title: Distributed Quantum Learning over Near-term Devices: Convergence Analysis and Security Design
comment: This paper is to be published in the IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications
summary: Distributed quantum learning (DQL) has emerged as a promising paradigm to scale quantum-enhanced machine learning by interconnecting multiple quantum devices. However, for efficient real-world deployment, it is essential to characterize how DQL converges under practical scenarios while simultaneously safeguarding multi-device quantum infrastructures from evolving security threats. Addressing these aspects in an integrated manner is key to ensuring both performance and resilience in large-scale DQL systems. Therefore, this paper presents a new DQL study where our innovation lies in: (i) conducting a holistic convergence analysis for DQL under practical settings, i.e., partial device participation, non-convex loss functions, and heterogeneous data distributions, (ii) developing a novel multi-layered post-quantum cryptographic architecture with a quantum neural network-powered adaptive mechanism that monitors conditions, evaluates threats, and adjusts parameters across three National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)-compliant levels. Our theoretical framework and empirical validation reveal two key insights: (i) the derived convergence bound uncovers a fundamental trade-off between convergence rate, measurement shots, and the size of the participating device subset; and (ii) findings from our evaluations on a physical testbed modeling quantum control architectures expose the performance limitations of static post-quantum security, while confirming that our adaptive framework effectively mitigates these overheads to preserve overall system efficiency. Specifically, the hardware experiments demonstrate that our dynamic security mechanism reduces total security execution time by approximately 49% relative to static high-security baselines, while maintaining a threat detection accuracy of over 91%. Furthermore, extensive simulations validate our theoretical analysis.....

AI.tldr: This paper presents a holistic analysis of distributed quantum learning (DQL) covering both convergence under practical conditions (partial device participation, non-convex losses, heterogeneous data) and a multi-layered adaptive post-quantum cryptographic framework. Theoretical bounds reveal trade-offs between convergence rate, measurement shots, and device subset size. Hardware experiments show a 49% reduction in security execution time with >91% threat detection accuracy.
AI.motivation: To enable efficient real-world deployment of distributed quantum learning, it is essential to simultaneously characterize convergence behavior under practical conditions and safeguard multi-device quantum infrastructures from evolving security threats in an integrated manner.
AI.method: (i) Holistic convergence analysis for DQL under partial device participation, non-convex loss functions, and heterogeneous data distributions; (ii) Development of a multi-layered post-quantum cryptographic architecture with a quantum neural network-powered adaptive mechanism that monitors conditions, evaluates threats, and adjusts parameters across three NIST-compliant security levels.
AI.result: The convergence bound reveals a fundamental trade-off between convergence rate, measurement shots, and participating device subset size. Hardware experiments demonstrate that the adaptive security framework reduces total security execution time by ~49% relative to static high-security baselines while maintaining >91% threat detection accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive framework effectively mitigates performance overheads of static post-quantum security to preserve overall system efficiency in DQL, validated by both physical testbed experiments and extensive simulations.

title: Efficient and SPAM-Robust Ansatz-Free Lindbladian Learning
comment: Senior Thesis for the Degree of Bachelor of Science, Computer Science and Physics. Defended May 29, 2026, California Institute of Technology. Supervised by Prof. Yu Tong and Prof. John Preskill. 81 pages, 5 figures
summary: Describing the dynamics of open systems is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation. Under Markovian assumptions, we can characterize dissipative dynamics via the Lindbladian. Using Bell sampling, we provide an efficient, ansatz-free Lindbladian learning algorithm with polynomial-time classical postprocessing. Motivated by the prevalence of state preparation and measurement (SPAM) noise on near-term devices, we also introduce the first efficient SPAM-robust protocol capable of learning the gauge-independent components of sparse Lindbladians to arbitrary precision in the presence of constant-order SPAM error. In doing so, we provide the first rigorous characterization of the gauge degrees of freedom in noisy Lindbladian learning, precisely identifying which components remain learnable under SPAM noise.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces efficient algorithms for learning Lindbladians (quantum dissipative dynamics) using Bell sampling, including the first SPAM-robust protocol that can learn sparse Lindbladians to arbitrary precision despite state preparation and measurement noise, along with a rigorous characterization of gauge degrees of freedom in noisy Lindbladian learning.
AI.motivation: Describing open system dynamics is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computation, and existing Lindbladian learning methods lack either efficiency, ansatz-free guarantees, or robustness to state preparation and measurement (SPAM) noise that is prevalent on near-term devices.
AI.method: The authors use Bell sampling to design an efficient, ansatz-free Lindbladian learning algorithm with polynomial-time classical postprocessing. They extend this to a SPAM-robust protocol that learns gauge-independent components of sparse Lindbladians to arbitrary precision under constant-order SPAM error, supported by a rigorous characterization of gauge degrees of freedom.
AI.result: A polynomial-time Lindbladian learning algorithm via Bell sampling, and the first efficient SPAM-robust protocol for learning sparse Lindbladians. The work also provides the first rigorous characterization of which Lindbladian components remain learnable under SPAM noise (gauge-invariant quantities).
AI.conclusion: The proposed methods enable efficient learning of open quantum system dynamics with provable guarantees, even in the presence of realistic SPAM errors, advancing fault-tolerant quantum computation capabilities.

title: Distribution Complexity of Electronic Structure Simulations on Quantum Supercomputers
summary: Efficient simulation of strongly-interacting fermionic systems on quantum processing units (QPUs) is a challenging task due to nonlocal mode entanglement generation. However, it is not yet well understood how the structure of entanglement governs the hardness of large-scale quantum chemistry simulations or the scaling of distributing such workloads. Here, we introduce an algorithm for estimating the distribution complexity of hybrid quantum-classical simulation for electronic structure Hamiltonians over heterogeneous high-performance architectures. Our algorithm relies on efficient analytical evaluation of the low entanglement boundaries for the orbital rotations and dephasing-induced localization within tensor fragments, in a double-factorized representation. Our entanglement estimation scales as $O(N^3)$ for each fragment, where $N$ is the number of orbitals. When QPUs are communicating via a quantum network, the cost of distribution per fragment is reduced quadratically from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N)$. Similarly, for hybrid quantum-classical approaches, with access to only conventional HPC interconnects, the worst-case cost is reduced from $O(\exp(N^2))$ to $O(\exp(N))$. We show that emergent entanglement patterns are induced by the interplay between coherent Gaussian orbital rotations and disordered Coulomb interactions. We discuss the underlying physical mechanisms that govern distribution complexity and introduce model systems that are tunable based on the localizability of fragments and the overlap of interfragment rotations. We characterize three different regimes of hardness for distribution complexity and classical simulability. The framework introduced here enables novel and more efficient quantum-classical application workflows towards utility-scale quantum computing.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an algorithm to estimate the distribution complexity of hybrid quantum-classical simulations for electronic structure Hamiltonians, showing that entanglement estimation scales as O(N³) per fragment and reduces distribution costs quadratically for QPU networks and exponentially for HPC interconnects.
AI.motivation: Efficient simulation of strongly-interacting fermionic systems on QPUs is challenging due to nonlocal mode entanglement, and the structure of entanglement's impact on large-scale quantum chemistry simulations and workload distribution scaling is not well understood.
AI.method: The algorithm relies on efficient analytical evaluation of low entanglement boundaries for orbital rotations and dephasing-induced localization within tensor fragments using a double-factorized representation, with O(N³) scaling per fragment.
AI.result: Distribution cost per fragment is reduced from O(N²) to O(N) for QPU networks and from O(exp(N²)) to O(exp(N)) for hybrid classical-HPC approaches. Three regimes of hardness for distribution complexity and classical simulability are characterized.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables novel and more efficient quantum-classical application workflows towards utility-scale quantum computing by characterizing emergent entanglement patterns from the interplay between coherent Gaussian orbital rotations and disordered Coulomb interactions.

title: Non-ergodicity effects in 1D localization
summary: It is well-known that the dimensionless Landauer resistance ρof an 1D disordered system obeys the log-normal distribution. The average value <ρ> for such distribution is not representative, since it strongly differs from the typical value ρ_{typ} in a specific sample. In fact, this conclusion should be revised due to effects of non-ergodicity. If L is the system size, and $K$ is the number of realizations of a random potential, then a situation for L\to\infty, K\to \infty depends on the order of limiting transitions. If the limit K\to \infty is taken firstly, then the log-normal distribution is valid for all L, if the condition ρ>>1 is fulfilled. If the number of realizations K is restricted, then a situation for L\to \infty is effectively described by the delta-function distribution, and <ρ>\approxρ_{typ}$. Transformation of the log-normal distribution can be observed with the use of experimental technique developed in the context of the universal conductance fluctuations. Non-ergodicity effects are essential for understanding of the difference between the theoretical predictions for the parameters of the log-normal distribution and the results of numerical and physical experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper revises the behavior of the Landauer resistance distribution in 1D disordered systems, showing that non-ergodicity effects cause the log-normal distribution to depend on the order of limits (system size L and number of realizations K), with implications for interpreting experimental and numerical results.
AI.motivation: To revise the conventional understanding that the log-normal distribution of the dimensionless Landauer resistance in 1D disordered systems is universally valid, by considering non-ergodicity effects arising from the order of limits between system size L and number of realizations K.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of the log-normal distribution of Landauer resistance under different limiting procedures: (i) K→∞ first yields log-normal distribution for all L when ρ>>1; (ii) restricted K yields delta-function distribution as L→∞, making <ρ>≈ρ_{typ}. Analysis connects to universal conductance fluctuations experimental techniques.
AI.result: The distribution of Landauer resistance depends critically on the order of limiting transitions L→∞ vs. K→∞. Non-ergodicity transforms the distribution from log-normal to delta-function under finite K, reconciling discrepancies between theoretical predictions and numerical/physical experiments.
AI.conclusion: Non-ergodicity effects are essential for understanding differences between theoretical log-normal distribution predictions and results from numerical and physical experiments; the conventional log-normal distribution is not universally applicable.

title: Parametric correlations in non-Hermitian quantum chaos: random matrix approach
summary: Motivated by the surge of interest in statistics of non-Hermitian random matrices as a framework for description of universal characteristics of dissipative chaotic quantum many-body systems, we address the problem of characterizing the parametric correlations of spectral densities. Considering parameter-dependent ensemble of complex Ginibre matrices we derive an explicit, closed-form expression for the parametric number covariance in the systems of symmetry class $\mathbf{A}$ for eigenvalues in a circular domain containing on average a finite number of eigenvalues in the spectral bulk. This behavior is expected to be universal, as further supported by numerical evidence for the real Ginibre ensemble, non-Hermitian Bernoulli Wigner matrices and bi-unitarily invariant ensembles. We also discuss a relation between parametric correlations of spectral densities and the distribution of the so-called eigenvector non-orthogonality factor, which attracted considerable interest in recent years.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an explicit closed-form expression for parametric number covariance in non-Hermitian random matrices (complex Ginibre ensemble), demonstrating universal behavior across different ensembles and relating it to eigenvector non-orthogonality.
AI.motivation: There is growing interest in non-Hermitian random matrices for describing universal characteristics of dissipative chaotic quantum many-body systems, and understanding parametric correlations of spectral densities is essential for characterizing these systems.
AI.method: The authors consider a parameter-dependent complex Ginibre matrix ensemble, derive an analytical closed-form expression for the parametric number covariance in circular domains within the spectral bulk, and validate universality via numerical simulations of real Ginibre, non-Hermitian Bernoulli Wigner, and bi-unitarily invariant ensembles.
AI.result: An explicit closed-form expression for the parametric number covariance is obtained for symmetry class A, and the result is shown to be universal across multiple non-Hermitian ensembles (complex Ginibre, real Ginibre, Bernoulli Wigner, bi-unitarily invariant).
AI.conclusion: Universal parametric correlations of spectral densities in non-Hermitian random matrices are established, with a connection to eigenvector non-orthogonality factors, relevant for understanding dissipative quantum chaos.

title: Communication Heterogeneity and Collective Consensus in Neural Cellular Automata
summary: Reaching global agreement from purely local interactions is a defining problem of collective intelligence, and most models of it assume that all agents share a single communication protocol. We ask what happens when they do not. Using a Neural Cellular Automaton in which a population of cells must solve the density classification task, agreeing on a global majority that no individual can observe, we introduce ``languages'' as sub-populations that read one another's messages through a translation with a tunable ``linguistic distance''. We find that linguistic distance slows consensus, that it produces mild divergence between groups rather than full fragmentation, and that a collective whose shared rule was trained under diverse protocols is robust to mismatch; a homogeneously trained one is not. The findings hold on both a ring and a two-dimensional grid, and admit a natural reading as Ising relaxation, in which a foreign-language region acts as a boundary defect that leaves the system in a higher-energy, partially ordered state. These patterns are qualitatively consistent with effects reported in human group studies, suggesting that distance between communication protocols is a minimal mechanism sufficient to produce them, without anything language-specific.

AI.tldr: This paper studies consensus formation in multi-agent systems where agents use different communication protocols (languages). Using Neural Cellular Automata on a density classification task, the authors show that linguistic distance slows consensus, causes mild divergence between groups but not full fragmentation, and that systems trained with diverse protocols are robust to mismatch while homogeneously trained ones are not. These findings, observed on both ring and 2D grid topologies, are interpretable as Ising relaxation dynamics and qualitatively match human group behavior patterns.
AI.motivation: To understand how collective agreement emerges when agents do not share a common communication protocol, moving beyond the standard assumption in collective intelligence models that all agents use the same language.
AI.method: Using a Neural Cellular Automaton (NCA) where a population of cells solves the density classification task. The authors introduce "languages" as sub-populations that communicate through translation with a tunable "linguistic distance" parameter, and compare training under homogeneous vs. diverse protocol conditions.
AI.result: Linguistic distance slows consensus; it produces mild divergence between groups rather than full fragmentation; collectively trained systems (diverse protocols) are robust to mismatch while homogeneously trained systems are not; these findings hold on both ring and 2D grid topologies.
AI.conclusion: The observed patterns are qualitatively consistent with human group studies and can be interpreted as Ising relaxation where foreign-language regions act as boundary defects leaving the system in a higher-energy, partially ordered state. Linguistic distance between communication protocols is a minimal, sufficient mechanism for producing these effects without requiring language-specific features.

title: Enhancing quantum processor capabilities during idle times
summary: We advocate an alternative paradigm to operate quantum computers that utilizes multipartite entanglement generated in dedicated auxiliary systems during idle times. This stored entanglement enhances the future capabilities of the quantum processor, as it can be flexibly used to assist and speed-up computations when needed. We identify classes of multipartite entangled resource states whose computational power are related to their entanglement features, and in turn to the complexity to generate them. During idle times, one can thus continuously work towards generating more and more powerful auxiliary multipartite entangled states. Idle times include both times prior to the start of a computation, but also any step during the execution of an algorithm where parts of the processor are not actively involved. To illustrate our approach, we consider architectures with limited connectivity, e.g. corresponding to a 1D geometry. We show that $d$-dimensional cluster states allow one to flexibly perform multiple long-distance two-qubit gates in parallel, where both the complexity to generate them, as well as the number of achievable gates increases with $d$.

AI.tldr: Proposes using idle times in quantum computers to generate multipartite entangled resource states (like cluster states) that can later speed up computations, particularly useful in limited-connectivity architectures.
AI.motivation: To utilize idle periods in quantum processors—both before computation and during algorithm execution—to generate entangled resource states that enhance computational capabilities, rather than letting those times go to waste.
AI.method: Proposes generating multipartite entangled states (e.g., d-dimensional cluster states) in auxiliary systems during idle times. The stored entanglement is then flexibly deployed to assist and accelerate computations, such as performing multiple long-distance two-qubit gates in parallel.
AI.result: In 1D-limited connectivity architectures, d-dimensional cluster states enable flexible parallel execution of multiple long-distance two-qubit gates. The complexity of generating these states and the number of achievable gates both scale with dimension d.
AI.conclusion: Idle-time entanglement generation offers a viable paradigm for enhancing quantum processors, where more complex entangled states (higher d) yield greater computational power, linking entanglement features to computational utility.

title: Multifractality at the Integer Quantum Hall Transition: Acquittal of the Parabolic Law
summary: Stationary wave functions at the integer quantum Hall transition are known to be multifractal, but the exact form of the multifractality spectrum has remained a subject of debate. While conformal field theory arguments predict a parabolic law, numerical simulations show deviations from parabolicity. We resolve this discrepancy by pointing out that powers of the local wave intensity fail to obey the Gaussian Free Field and Abelian Fusion Hypothesis assumed in earlier analysis. Rather, due to the non-Abelian nature of the underlying effective field theory, wave intensity correlators are dressed by insertions of background charge distributed uniformly in space. An exact expression for the $q$-moments of point-contact generated eigenstates is presented. Numerical tests are performed for the critical Chalker-Coddington network model on a rectangular torus. Our results are in precise agreement with the predictions of conformal symmetry realized as a level-4 current algebra.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves the long-standing discrepancy between theoretical predictions (parabolic multifractality) and numerical simulations at the integer quantum Hall transition by showing that non-Abelian effective field theory introduces background charge insertions that modify the multifractality spectrum, with exact results for q-moments confirmed by Chalker-Coddington network simulations.
AI.motivation: There was a discrepancy between conformal field theory predictions (parabolic multifractality spectrum) and numerical simulations showing deviations from parabolicity at the integer quantum Hall transition.
AI.method: The authors show that powers of local wave intensity do not obey Gaussian Free Field or Abelian Fusion Hypothesis due to the non-Abelian nature of the underlying effective field theory. Instead, wave intensity correlators are dressed by insertions of background charge uniformly distributed in space. They derive an exact expression for q-moments of point-contact generated eigenstates and test numerically using the critical Chalker-Coddington network model on a rectangular torus.
AI.result: Numerical tests on the Chalker-Coddington network model show precise agreement with predictions of conformal symmetry realized as a level-4 current algebra, resolving the discrepancy between theory and simulation.
AI.conclusion: The multifractality spectrum at the integer quantum Hall transition is governed by non-Abelian conformal field theory (level-4 current algebra) rather than a simple parabolic law, with background charge insertions dressing the wave intensity correlators.

title: Hierarchical separation of relaxation timescales from spectral localization bounds
summary: We investigate the dissipative dynamics of multilevel quantum systems strongly coupled either to a lossy cavity mode or directly to a bosonic environment. By deriving spectral localization bounds, we establish conditions under which strong system-bath coupling gives rise to a hierarchy of population relaxation timescales. Our approach builds on the reaction-coordinate polaron-transform framework. By mapping the original strong-coupling problem onto an effective weakly dissipative model, we analyze the spectrum of the resulting Liouvillian superoperator through localization bounds. For the generalized V model, we find that strong system-bath coupling gives rise to a bright-dark structure in the effective system-bath coupling operator: a single collective mode remains strongly coupled to the environment, while the remaining modes become progressively dark. Consequently, the dynamics separate into fast and slow sectors and, at finite coupling strengths, develop a hierarchy of population relaxation timescales. Numerical simulations based on both secular and non-secular quantum master equations corroborate the emergence of timescale separation and the pronounced slowing down of dissipative dynamics at strong coupling. Our results reveal a general mechanism underlying anomalously slow relaxation in strongly coupled open quantum systems and provide a route for engineering long-lived states through system-environment interactions.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates strongly coupled multilevel quantum systems and shows that strong system-bath coupling leads to a bright-dark mode structure, causing a hierarchy of relaxation timescales and anomalously slow relaxation. This is established via spectral localization bounds within a reaction-coordinate polaron-transform framework and validated by numerical simulations.
AI.motivation: To understand the general mechanism underlying anomalously slow relaxation in strongly coupled open quantum systems and to establish conditions under which strong coupling gives rise to a hierarchy of population relaxation timescales.
AI.method: The approach uses the reaction-coordinate polaron-transform framework to map the strong-coupling problem onto an effective weakly dissipative model. The spectrum of the resulting Liouvillian superoperator is analyzed through spectral localization bounds. Numerical simulations with both secular and non-secular quantum master equations are performed.
AI.result: For the generalized V model, strong system-bath coupling produces a bright-dark structure in the effective coupling operator: one collective mode remains strongly coupled (bright), while the others become dark. This yields fast and slow dynamical sectors and a hierarchy of population relaxation timescales at finite coupling strengths.
AI.conclusion: The results reveal a general mechanism for anomalously slow relaxation in strongly coupled open quantum systems and offer a route for engineering long-lived states through tailored system-environment interactions.

title: Exact Accumulated-Field Determined Steady States with Boundary-Controlled Relaxation in Dissipative Quantum Link Chains
summary: In open quantum lattice systems, changing the boundary condition would appear to alter both the steady state and the nonzero Liouvillian spectrum. Here we show that these two boundary-induced changes do not necessarily occur together in a globally reciprocal dissipative quantum link chain. The steady state is determined by an accumulated field defined by link-resolved dissipative asymmetries, and a gauge-generated transformation built from this field gives exact symmetry-resolved steady states with nonuniform, accumulated-field-dependent reduced matter occupations. We then construct a reciprocal cyclic boundary condition that preserves these matter occupations while changing the nonzero Liouvillian spectrum. Consequently, open and cyclic chains relax to the same reduced matter steady-occupation profile with different Liouvillian gaps, with the cyclic closure accelerating relaxation. In the strong-dissipation limit, this relaxation difference can be reduced to a spectral comparison of effective exclusion processes with open and cyclic boundaries.

AI.tldr: In globally reciprocal dissipative quantum link chains, the steady state depends only on link-resolved dissipative asymmetries (via an accumulated field), not on boundary conditions. Changing from open to cyclic boundaries preserves the steady-state matter occupations but modifies the nonzero Liouvillian spectrum, potentially accelerating relaxation. In the strong-dissipation limit, this reduces to comparing effective exclusion processes with open vs. cyclic boundaries.
AI.motivation: To understand whether boundary conditions affect steady states and relaxation dynamics independently in open quantum lattice systems, specifically challenging the assumption that changing boundaries always alters both.
AI.method: Analytical analysis of a globally reciprocal dissipative quantum link chain using a gauge-generated transformation built from an accumulated field defined by link-resolved dissipative asymmetries, enabling exact symmetry-resolved steady states.
AI.result: The steady state is boundary-independent (determined solely by link-resolved asymmetries), while cyclic boundaries change the nonzero Liouvillian spectrum and accelerate relaxation; in the strong-dissipation limit this maps to exclusion processes with different boundary conditions.
AI.conclusion: Boundary-induced changes to steady state and Liouvillian spectrum are decoupled in reciprocal dissipative quantum link chains, allowing engineering of relaxation rates without disturbing the steady-state matter occupation profile.

title: Unobservables and Decoherence from Complexity
summary: The interface between the quantum and the classical is an intriguing and, at times, hotly contested subject of ongoing research. The quantum regime is characterized by interference, made possible by the superposition principle, while such phenomena are absent in macroscopic, everyday experience. Here, we investigate the link of this absence (or, as we will argue, unobservability) to computational complexity. We show how the assumption that quantum systems cannot solve NP-complete problems efficiently implies that certain formally valid quantum measurements on finite-dimensional systems are unperformable. We study several consequences of this restriction. First, Pauli matrices in an inconveniently transformed basis are a simple example of unobservables. Furthermore, some quantum states are not connected by any physically realizable time evolution. Finally there are quantum states whose coherence cannot be observed, i.e. superpositions of pure quantum states which are indistinguishable from mixtures. We discuss the connection of this phenomenon to the presence of superselection sectors. Our results suggest that the apparent classicality of macroscopic systems may be partly due to limitations on measurements and time evolutions imposed by computational complexity.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that assuming quantum computers cannot efficiently solve NP-complete problems implies certain quantum measurements are unperformable, leading to unobservable Pauli operators, disconnected state spaces, and indistinguishable superpositions from mixtures—suggesting that macroscopic classicality may stem from computational complexity constraints.
AI.motivation: To bridge the quantum-classical divide by linking the absence of macroscopic quantum interference to computational complexity, proposing that the unobservability of certain quantum phenomena arises not from fundamental physical laws but from computational intractability.
AI.method: The authors assume that quantum systems cannot efficiently solve NP-complete problems (i.e., NP ⊈ BQP) and derive restrictions on quantum measurements and time evolutions. They analyze consequences including unobservable Pauli matrices, disconnected quantum state spaces under physically realizable dynamics, and indistinguishable coherent superpositions from mixed states, relating these to superselection sectors.
AI.result: The assumption that quantum computers cannot solve NP-complete problems efficiently leads to: (1) certain formally valid measurements (e.g., Pauli matrices in transformed bases) being unperformable; (2) some quantum states not being connectable by any physically realizable time evolution; (3) existence of quantum states whose coherence is unobservable (superpositions indistinguishable from mixtures), connected to superselection sectors.
AI.conclusion: The apparent classicality of macroscopic systems may be partially explained by computational complexity constraints on measurements and time evolutions, rather than purely by decoherence or fundamental superselection rules.

title: Percolation of Zero-Weight Paths and the Shape of the Phase Boundary in the Two-Dimensional Random-Bond Ising Model
summary: We explore the connection between the low-temperature boundary of the ferromagnetic phase in the two-dimensional $\pm J$ random-bond Ising model, where antiferromagnetic bonds occur with probability $p$ and a geometric transition dubbed ``zero-weight percolation''. We argue that the onset of this percolation characterized by the emergence of a percolating path containing an equal number of $+J$ and $-J$ bonds is incompatible with ferromagnetic ordering. Due to its purely geometrical nature, this percolation criterion is a property of a disorder realization and is independent of the temperature, which in turn suggests that the ferromagnetic phase boundary is vertical below the Nishimori point in the $(p,T)$ plane. Using a dynamic-programming algorithm combined with finite-size scaling, we identify the critical disorder at which zero-weight paths first percolate as $p_c = 0.1000(2)$, and we extract the associated critical exponents $ν= 1.26(1)$, $β/ν= 0.85(1)$, $γ/ν= 0.264(5)$, and fractal dimension $d_f \approx 1.11$. The value of $p_c$ is below the previously reported values of the critical disorder strength corresponding to the loss of the ferromagnetic order, both at zero temperature and the Nishimori point. Nevertheless, we argue that the percolation transition studied in this paper is behind the loss of ferromagnetism and thus provides a new, purely geometrical perspective on the stability of ferromagnetic order in disordered spin systems.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a "zero-weight percolation" transition in the 2D ±J random-bond Ising model, where percolating paths with equal numbers of +J and -J bonds emerge. Using dynamic programming and finite-size scaling, the critical disorder is found at p_c = 0.1000(2) with associated exponents. This percolation is argued to be the geometric mechanism behind the loss of ferromagnetic order, implying a vertical phase boundary below the Nishimori point.
AI.motivation: To understand the geometric origin of the ferromagnetic phase boundary in disordered spin systems, specifically exploring whether a purely structural percolation criterion based on bond-weight balance can explain the loss of ferromagnetic order independent of temperature.
AI.method: A dynamic-programming algorithm combined with finite-size scaling to identify the critical disorder at which zero-weight paths (containing equal numbers of +J and -J bonds) first percolate; extraction of critical exponents ν, β/ν, γ/ν, and fractal dimension d_f.
AI.result: Critical disorder p_c = 0.1000(2); critical exponents ν = 1.26(1), β/ν = 0.85(1), γ/ν = 0.264(5), fractal dimension d_f ≈ 1.11. The percolation threshold is below previously reported values for loss of ferromagnetic order at zero temperature and the Nishimori point.
AI.conclusion: The zero-weight percolation transition provides a new purely geometrical perspective on the stability of ferromagnetic order, suggesting the ferromagnetic phase boundary is vertical below the Nishimori point in the (p,T) plane.

title: Profiling the Effective Limits of Error Mitigation via Circuit Replication
summary:
Current era quantum computers continue to grow in both capability and capacity. Despite these advancements, errors induced by environmental noise severely limit practical applicability. Current research into error mitigation and correction to bridge the gap between current-era quantum computers and the execution of noise-sensitive workloads. These methods have significant performance and resource overheads, thereby greatly limiting the real-world benefits of their use. Circuit replication, as a naive form of error mitigation, is not new and has largely been ignored given the resource constraints of current quantum hardware. However, its simplicity is attractive as a means to supplement modern methods, reducing the overall performance overhead while still preserving error-mitigation capabilities. In this paper, we profile the effects of simple circuit replication under real-world noise profiles to better establish replication's limits as a supplemental mitigation strategy.
  Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for the Maxcut problem is explored for the analysis. For small graphs, we found that the average inference strength decreases by approximately 21.8% while the average standard deviation decreases by 108.8% compared to 6 replicates. For larger graphs, inference strength decreases by 35.4% while the average standard deviation decreased only 20.5%. Fewer replications did not affect smaller graphs, but degraded inference strength, with comparable benefits to standard deviation in larger graphs. These results show that replication has potential uses as a supplemental mitigation strategy for large-depth, highly variable workloads.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates simple circuit replication as a low-overhead supplemental error mitigation strategy for quantum computers, testing it on QAOA for Maxcut. Results show replication reduces inference strength (21.8% for small graphs, 35.4% for large) and standard deviation (108.8% for small, 20.5% for large), with potential for large-depth, high-variability workloads.
AI.motivation: Current error mitigation and correction methods impose significant performance and resource overheads, limiting practical quantum computing. Simple circuit replication has been overlooked due to hardware constraints, but its low overhead makes it attractive as a supplemental strategy.
AI.method: Profiling simple circuit replication under real-world noise profiles using QAOA for the Maxcut problem, comparing results across small and large graphs with varying numbers of replications.
AI.result: For small graphs: inference strength decreases ~21.8%, standard deviation decreases ~108.8% (vs 6 replicates). For large graphs: inference strength decreases ~35.4%, standard deviation decreases ~20.5%. Fewer replications had minimal impact on small graphs but degraded inference strength for large graphs.
AI.conclusion: Circuit replication shows potential as a supplemental error mitigation strategy, particularly for large-depth, highly variable workloads, though its effectiveness depends on graph size and replication count.

title: Scalable Physics-Inspired Transformers for Spin Glasses
summary: Efficient sampling of the Boltzmann distribution in frustrated spin glasses is central to statistical mechanics and combinatorial optimization. Despite advances in machine-learning-based approaches, two issues persist: limited understanding of why variational models fail to benefit from increased scale, unlike the monotonic scaling law of large language models; and high computational cost on large systems that negates advantages over classical sampling methods. Here, we develop a physics-inspired transformer with interpretable sparse attention and spin-tailored positional embeddings to address these challenges. By further leveraging FlashAttention for parallel ancestral sampling, it achieves up to two orders of magnitude speedup over vanilla variational autoregressive networks, enabling neural-network simulations of spin-glass systems to unprecedented sizes on a single GPU. It can resolve full probability distributions, free energies, and overlap statistics across temperatures, for Sherrington-Kirkpatrick and 2D or 3D Edwards-Anderson models, where existing machine-learning methods encounter limitations at certain temperatures. This framework thus establishes a scalable paradigm for frustrated spin-glass systems.

AI.tldr: A physics-inspired transformer with sparse attention and spin-tailored embeddings is developed for efficient sampling of Boltzmann distributions in frustrated spin glasses, achieving up to 100x speedup over vanilla variational autoregressive networks and enabling neural-network simulations at unprecedented system sizes on a single GPU.
AI.motivation: Existing machine-learning approaches to sampling Boltzmann distributions in spin glasses suffer from two key issues: (1) unclear understanding of why variational models fail to benefit from increased scale (unlike the monotonic scaling laws of LLMs), and (2) high computational costs on large systems that negate advantages over classical sampling methods.
AI.method: A physics-inspired transformer is developed featuring interpretable sparse attention and spin-tailored positional embeddings. It leverages FlashAttention to enable parallel ancestral sampling, achieving significant computational acceleration.
AI.result: The method achieves up to two orders of magnitude speedup over vanilla variational autoregressive networks, enabling neural-network simulations of spin-glass systems at unprecedented sizes on a single GPU. It resolves full probability distributions, free energies, and overlap statistics across temperatures for Sherrington-Kirkpatrick, 2D, and 3D Edwards-Anderson models, where existing ML methods fail at certain temperatures.
AI.conclusion: This framework establishes a scalable paradigm for frustrated spin-glass systems, overcoming both the scaling failure and computational cost issues that previously limited ML-based approaches.

title: Finite-Time Electrometry with a Quantum-Regime Single-Ion Phonon Laser
summary: The phonon laser realized in a trapped ion, i.e., a self-sustained mechanical oscillator, has demonstrated the unique characteristics in practically detecting externally applied electric signals without the prerequisite of sideband cooling. Entering the quantum regime via sideband cooling is expected to further improve its sensing performance. Here we report the first experimental realization of a quantum-regime single-ion phonon laser ($\bar{n}<10$) using a trapped $^{40}\mathrm{Ca}^+$ ion and demonstrate electrometry based on its phase-space symmetry-breaking response to weak resonant electric fields. By tuning the phonon-laser parameters, we reveal that the sensing performance is fundamentally governed by the finite-time relaxation dynamics of the underlying open quantum system. We find that a slow Liouvillian relaxation, correlated with the finite experimental interaction window, effectively enhances the dynamic susceptibility while maintaining the structural robustness of the limit cycle. This regime, when applied to the detection of electric fields, produces a shot-noise-limited peak sensitivity of $14.15 \pm 0.77~μ\mathrm{V/m}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ and a minimum detectable field variation of $δE_{\mathrm{min}} \approx 1.83~μ\mathrm{V/m}$. Our results establish quantum phonon lasers as a practical platform for advanced sensing and highlight the central role of Liouvillian dynamics in non-equilibrium electrometry.

AI.tldr: First experimental realization of a quantum-regime single-ion phonon laser (mean phonon number < 10) using a trapped ⁴⁰Ca⁺ ion, demonstrating ultra-sensitive electrometry via phase-space symmetry-breaking response to weak electric fields, achieving 14.15 μV/m/√Hz shot-noise-limited sensitivity and 1.83 μV/m minimum detectable field variation, governed by finite-time Liouvillian relaxation dynamics.
AI.motivation: To realize a quantum-regime phonon laser and demonstrate its practical application for sensitive electrometry, leveraging quantum mechanical properties to surpass classical sensing limits without requiring sideband cooling.
AI.method: Trapped ⁴⁰Ca⁺ ion phonon laser operated in the quantum regime (mean phonon number < 10); phase-space symmetry-breaking response to weak resonant electric fields is used as the sensing mechanism; analysis of finite-time Liouvillian relaxation dynamics governing sensing performance.
AI.result: Shot-noise-limited peak sensitivity of 14.15 ± 0.77 μV/m/√Hz and minimum detectable field variation δE_min ≈ 1.83 μV/m; discovery that slow Liouvillian relaxation within finite experimental windows enhances dynamic susceptibility while preserving limit-cycle structural robustness.
AI.conclusion: Quantum phonon lasers are established as a practical platform for advanced sensing; Liouvillian dynamics plays a central role in governing non-equilibrium electrometry performance.

title: Approximating velocity fields with planted attractors via Neural-ODEs for classification purposes
summary: In this work, Neural ODEs equipped with a curated collection of equilibrium points have been successfully employed for classification tasks.The planted attractors serve as indicators for the target classes, while the velocity field leveraging the universal approximation capabilities of the architecture shapes the dynamical landscape.This process defines the basins of attraction of the trained model, effectively directing each input provided as an initial condition toward its corresponding destination target.

AI.tldr: Neural ODEs with planted equilibrium points are used for classification, where attractors represent target classes and the velocity field shapes basins of attraction to direct inputs toward correct targets.
AI.motivation: To leverage Neural ODEs for classification by designing a dynamical system with planted equilibrium points that serve as attractors for target classes.
AI.method: Equipping Neural ODEs with a curated collection of equilibrium points (planted attractors) as indicators for target classes, and using the velocity field (with universal approximation capabilities) to shape the dynamical landscape of basins of attraction.
AI.result: The trained model successfully directs each input (provided as an initial condition) toward its corresponding destination target through the defined basins of attraction.
AI.conclusion: Neural ODEs with planted attractors can effectively perform classification tasks by shaping the dynamical landscape into basins of attraction that guide inputs to target classes.

title: Schur--Horn bound on field-free molecular orientation at finite temperature
summary: The maximum field-free orientation attainable from a \emph{thermal} molecular ensemble within a finite rotational subspace has not been characterised analytically. Here we derive a Schur--Horn-type upper bound on the field-free orientation $\avg{\cosθ}$ achievable by \emph{any} $M$-conserving unitary control acting on a Boltzmann ensemble truncated to rotational levels $J\le\Jmax$. The bound is the sum, over magnetic-quantum-number sectors, of the sorted Boltzmann weights paired with the sorted spectrum of $\cosθ$; it is purely kinematic, set by temperature, the rotational constant, and $\Jmax$ alone, and interpolates exactly between the zero-temperature subspace eigenvalue and a finite-temperature ceiling fixed by the rotational partition function. Benchmarked on LiH against the analytical $N$-subpulse resonant protocol of Hong \textit{et al.} [Phys.\ Rev.\ Research \textbf{7}, L012049 (2025)], it reveals three regimes: the protocol saturates the bound to within about $1.6\%$ for $T\le\SI{5}{\kelvin}$, loses roughly $10\%$ of its zero-temperature orientation at $T=B/\kB\approx\SI{10.8}{\kelvin}$, and leaves a $10$--$40\%$ gap above $\SI{10}{\kelvin}$. Optimising the subpulse areas and carrier phases within the fixed layout closes only $\approx7\%$ of that gap, the optimal phase offsets vanishing, which localises the dominant loss in the rigidity of the analytic layout rather than in the choice of areas or phases. The bound is a control-independent target for coherent-control design, applies unchanged to any linear polar molecule in a $^1Σ^+$ state, and is mapped across the $(\Jmax,T)$ plane.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a Schur–Horn-type upper bound on the maximum field-free orientation (⟨cosθ⟩) achievable by any M-conserving unitary control on a thermal molecular ensemble truncated to J≤Jmax. The bound is purely kinematic, depends only on temperature, rotational constant, and Jmax, and exactly interpolates between zero-temperature and finite-temperature limits. Benchmarking against a resonant protocol on LiH reveals three thermal regimes and shows that the dominant loss at high temperature stems from the rigidity of the analytic pulse layout, not parameter tuning.
AI.motivation: No analytical characterization existed for the maximum field-free orientation attainable from a thermal molecular ensemble within a finite rotational subspace under coherent control.
AI.method: Derives a Schur–Horn-type bound by pairing sorted Boltzmann weights with the sorted spectrum of cosθ across magnetic-quantum-number sectors. Benchmarked against the analytical N-subpulse resonant protocol of Hong et al. on LiH.
AI.result: The bound is saturated to ~1.6% for T≤5 K; at T≈10.8 K (B/kB), orientation drops ~10% relative to zero-temperature; above 10 K, a 10–40% gap remains. Optimizing subpulse areas and phases recovers only ~7% of this gap; optimal phase offsets vanish, indicating the analytic layout rigidity is the dominant loss source.
AI.conclusion: The bound is a control-independent, purely kinematic target for coherent-control design, applicable to any linear polar molecule in a ¹Σ⁺ state, and mapped across the (Jmax, T) plane.

title: Fundamental Limits of Stability Inference in High-Dimensional Complex Systems
summary:
Many complex systems, including ecosystems, neural circuits, and financial markets, are inferred to operate close to a threshold of instability, at which a small perturbation can propagate across the entire system. This proximity is often interpreted as functionally advantageous, yet it poses a question common to all these fields: from a finite, noisy recording, how precisely can the distance of a system from that threshold be estimated? Using the multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process as the canonical linear model of relaxation near a stable fixed point, we show that the attainable precision is governed by three factors: an effective measurement budget, set by the number of samples relative to the system dimension and the sampling interval; the signal-to-noise ratio, given by the magnitude of deterministic interactions relative to stochastic forcing; and the distance to criticality, which simultaneously sets the system's correlation times and degrades both of the preceding factors. As the slowest dynamical mode softens near the threshold, the curvature of the log-likelihood flattens along the direction that determines stability, so that the relative uncertainty on the estimated distance diverges as that distance vanishes. Critically, temporal correlations near instability reduce the effective number of independent observations far below the nominal sample count, and inference breaks down when this effective count falls below the system dimension, even when the raw data volume appears sufficient.
  A direct consequence is the existence of an optimal sampling interval that diverges as the system approaches criticality, with practical implications for experimental design.

AI.tldr: The precision of estimating a system's distance from instability is fundamentally limited by three factors: effective measurement budget (samples vs. dimension vs. sampling interval), signal-to-noise ratio, and distance to criticality—where correlation times degrade the other two factors, causing uncertainty to diverge and creating an optimal sampling interval that grows near criticality.
AI.motivation: Despite the widespread observation that complex systems (ecosystems, neural circuits, financial markets) operate near instability—often considered functionally advantageous—there is a fundamental open question: from finite, noisy recordings, how precisely can we estimate that system's distance from the instability threshold?
AI.method: The authors use the multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process as the canonical linear model of relaxation near a stable fixed point, then analyze the Fisher information (log-likelihood curvature) to derive how estimation precision depends on measurement budget, signal-to-noise ratio, and distance to criticality.
AI.result: Relative uncertainty on the estimated distance diverges as distance to criticality vanishes, because the log-likelihood curvature flattens along the stability-determining direction. Temporal correlations reduce the effective number of independent observations; inference breaks down when this effective count falls below the system dimension. An optimal sampling interval exists and diverges near criticality.
AI.conclusion: Fundamental limits exist on how precisely we can infer proximity to instability, with practical implications for experimental design: the optimal sampling strategy changes drastically as a system approaches criticality.

title: Bounded-depth spacetime lattice surgery for resource-efficient fault-tolerant quantum computation
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing based on lattice surgery requires place-and-route compilation with low spacetime overhead. Routing, in particular, faces a basic tension between suppressing path conflicts through greater spatial allocation and exploiting the time direction to realize ancilla-efficient spacetime routing. Existing approaches do not fully resolve this trade-off while retaining compatibility with inner factory layouts and termination guarantees. Here we introduce double-slice routing, a constant-depth spacetime-routing method that uses two consecutive time slices with a guarantee that its kink-parity correction terminates under both planar and stacked architectures. We numerically benchmark the resulting compiler on Hamiltonian-simulation workloads to show that double-slice routing reduces compilation cost by up to a factor of 2.4 over a single-slice baseline. Compared to projective routing, an existing method that allows an unbounded number of time slices per path, double-slice routing achieves smaller circuit volume with only a marginal execution-time penalty. Combined with a cultivation-compatible mapping optimization, the overall improvement reaches up to 7.5-fold over a naive single-slice compilation baseline. These results identify double-slice routing as a practically useful operating point in lattice-surgery compilation and show the substantial benefit in joint optimization of mapping and routing.

AI.tldr: Double-slice routing is a constant-depth spacetime-routing method for lattice-surgery-based fault-tolerant quantum computing that uses two consecutive time slices, guarantees kink-parity correction termination, and reduces compilation cost by up to 2.4× over single-slice baselines and up to 7.5× when combined with cultivation-compatible mapping optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing lattice-surgery routing methods fail to resolve the trade-off between suppressing path conflicts via spatial allocation and exploiting time direction for ancilla-efficient spacetime routing, while retaining compatibility with inner factory layouts and termination guarantees.
AI.method: The paper introduces double-slice routing, a constant-depth method using two consecutive time slices with guaranteed kink-parity correction termination under both planar and stacked architectures. It is combined with a cultivation-compatible mapping optimization and benchmarked on Hamiltonian-simulation workloads.
AI.result: Double-slice routing reduces compilation cost by up to 2.4× over a single-slice baseline, achieves smaller circuit volume than projective routing with marginal execution-time penalty, and combined with mapping optimization yields up to 7.5-fold improvement over naive single-slice compilation.
AI.conclusion: Double-slice routing is a practically useful operating point in lattice-surgery compilation, demonstrating substantial benefit from joint optimization of mapping and routing.

title: Synchronization in the quantum regime
summary: Can synchronization -- the widespread spontaneous emergence of coordinated dynamics in classical nonlinear systems -- also occur in the quantum regime? This question has recently sparked intense research into collective behavior and temporal self-organization in quantum systems. Typical quantum features such as the linearity of time evolution and the presence of quantum noise seem to hinder the appearance of synchrony at the microscopic level. At the same time, quantum coherence and quantum correlations may provide novel mechanisms for enhancing synchronization beyond its classical counterpart. We here survey recent theoretical and experimental advances in quantum synchronization, ranging from the characterization of synchronous oscillations and genuinely nonclassical forms of synchrony to many-body synchronization on quantum networks.

AI.tldr: This survey explores whether synchronization—a classic nonlinear phenomenon—can occur in quantum systems, reviewing recent theoretical and experimental advances on quantum synchronization, including nonclassical synchrony and many-body synchronization in quantum networks.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether spontaneous coordinated dynamics (synchronization) can emerge in the quantum regime despite features like linear time evolution and quantum noise that seem to hinder it, and to explore if quantum coherence and correlations can enhance synchronization beyond classical limits.
AI.method: A comprehensive survey of recent theoretical and experimental research on quantum synchronization, covering characterization of synchronous oscillations, genuinely nonclassical synchrony forms, and many-body synchronization on quantum networks.
AI.result: Quantum synchronization is possible and exhibits novel features beyond classical synchronization, with quantum coherence and correlations potentially enhancing synchronization, though quantum noise and linear dynamics pose challenges.
AI.conclusion: Synchronization can occur in the quantum regime, with unique quantum-enhanced mechanisms, opening new directions for collective behavior and temporal self-organization in quantum systems.

title: Machine Learning Optimal Quantum Error Correction Thresholds
summary: As quantum computers remain susceptible to noise, QEC is essential for preserving logical information during computations. However, the performance of QEC codes breaks down beyond certain noise thresholds, revealing fundamental limits on their ability to protect quantum information. These limits can be characterized using information-theoretic measures such as the coherent information, which quantifies the maximum rate at which logical information can be reliably transmitted through a noisy quantum channel. In this work, we establish a direct connection between the CI and the binary cross-entropy loss used when training neural network decoders. Specifically, we show that the CI constitutes a sharp lower bound on the achievable loss for decoders that track logical operators across noisy channels. To this end, we develop a transformer-based neural network model based on maximum likelihood decoding. We train this network to estimate the CI and evaluate its performance on the surface code under three noise models: code capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise. Our results demonstrate that the network accurately predicts CI and yields threshold estimates that closely match known theoretical limits. When used as a decoder, the network significantly outperforms the minimum weight perfect matching decoder in terms of logical error rate. We also introduce a novel soft post-selection scheme that independently treats uncertainty in both logical operators and relies on confidence-based filtering of the network's output. We prove that such post-selection strategies, based on the MLD cosets, are optimal, and demonstrate their scalability in terms of both logical error rate and abort probability. These findings establish transformer-based architectures as powerful tools for QEC and provide the first numerical evidence supporting the optimality and scalability of MLD-based post-selection.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a direct connection between coherent information (CI) and binary cross-entropy loss for training neural network decoders in quantum error correction (QEC). Using a transformer-based architecture for maximum likelihood decoding, they accurately predict CI and threshold estimates for the surface code under various noise models, outperforming MWPM decoders. They also introduce an optimal, scalable soft post-selection scheme based on MLD cosets.
AI.motivation: Quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but QEC codes break down beyond certain noise thresholds. Characterizing these fundamental limits—via information-theoretic measures like coherent information—is crucial, yet a direct connection between coherent information and practical neural network decoder loss functions was missing.
AI.method: A transformer-based neural network model is developed for maximum likelihood decoding. The network is trained to estimate coherent information, establishing a lower bound relationship between CI and binary cross-entropy loss. Performance is evaluated on the surface code under code capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise models. A soft post-selection scheme based on confidence-based filtering of MLD cosets is introduced.
AI.result: The network accurately predicts coherent information and yields threshold estimates matching known theoretical limits. As a decoder, it significantly outperforms minimum weight perfect matching (MWPM) in logical error rate. The post-selection scheme is proven optimal and demonstrates scalability in logical error rate and abort probability.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based architectures are powerful tools for QEC, and the results provide the first numerical evidence supporting the optimality and scalability of maximum likelihood decoding-based post-selection.

title: Assessing Cost Hamiltonian Reliability in Quantum Protein Structure Prediction
summary: In variational quantum algorithms, QAOA, and quantum annealing, the cost Hamiltonian defines the optimization landscape explored by the quantum hardware; however, in many application-driven formulations, this Hamiltonian is a simplified proxy for the true task-level objective. Using lattice-based quantum protein structure prediction as a case study, we investigate whether the contact-energy cost Hamiltonian commonly used in this setting is sufficiently aligned with structural accuracy, as measured by RMSD against experimentally determined structures. Through this specific problem, we show the importance of studying the reliability of the cost Hamiltonian independently from the quantum approach used. This work shows that, for small peptides and on average, the energy landscape of the considered cost Hamiltonian is not correlated well enough to the actual error to provide meaningful predictions. Moreover, this correlation was estimated through Monte-Carlo sampling for larger instances. It shows an increase of said correlation for larger problem instances and when more interaction shells are considered. This investigation illustrates the meaningfulness of investigating cost Hamiltonian relevance independently from the quantum algorithm used.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether the contact-energy cost Hamiltonian used in quantum protein structure prediction is sufficiently aligned with structural accuracy (RMSD). Using lattice-based quantum protein structure prediction as a case study, they find that for small peptides the energy landscape is not well correlated with actual error, but correlation improves for larger instances and when more interaction shells are considered.
AI.motivation: In variational quantum algorithms, QAOA, and quantum annealing, the cost Hamiltonian is often a simplified proxy for the true task-level objective. The authors aim to investigate whether this simplification leads to misalignment between the cost Hamiltonian and actual structural accuracy in protein structure prediction.
AI.method: Using lattice-based quantum protein structure prediction as a case study, the authors evaluate the correlation between the contact-energy cost Hamiltonian and structural accuracy measured by RMSD against experimentally determined structures. They perform Monte-Carlo sampling for larger instances to estimate this correlation.
AI.result: For small peptides, the energy landscape of the cost Hamiltonian is not correlated well enough with actual error to provide meaningful predictions. However, correlation increases for larger problem instances and when more interaction shells are considered.
AI.conclusion: It is important to study the reliability of the cost Hamiltonian independently from the quantum approach used. The findings illustrate the meaningfulness of investigating cost Hamiltonian relevance separately from the quantum algorithm employed.

title: Entanglement-entropy analysis of critical and topological quantum phases in a frustrated spin-1/2 Heisenberg ladder
summary: We investigate the ground-state phase diagram of a frustrated spin-1/2 Heisenberg ladder in the transverse magnetic field with an anisotropic inter-rung exchange coupling $α$. This bond-anisotropic parameter continuously interpolates among the Ising-like limit $α=0$, the isotropic point $α=1$, and the XY-dominated regime $α\gg 1$. Using density-matrix renormalization group calculations within a matrix-product-state framework, we analyze bipartite entanglement, magnetization, and spin correlations to characterize the emergent quantum phases. We identify six distinct ground-state phases, including rung-singlet, Haldane-like, Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid, canted Ising-ordered, XY-polarized, and ordered ferromagnetic states. While magnetization and local correlations provide a first insight into phase classifications, the finite-size scaling of the entanglement measures offers a more sensitive and unified diagnostics of both gapped and gapless regimes. In the gapless regime, we extract the central charge $c \simeq 1$, confirming Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid behavior, while at the transition between the canted Ising and ferromagnetic phases, we observe $c \simeq 1/2$, consistent with the Ising universality. Finally, we find that both the Haldane-like behavior and the extended critical Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid regime are strongly confined to the vicinity of the isotropic point $α= 1$.

AI.tldr: Using DMRG calculations, this study maps the ground-state phase diagram of a frustrated spin-1/2 Heisenberg ladder with anisotropic inter-rung coupling under a transverse magnetic field, identifying six distinct phases and characterizing their entanglement and critical properties.
AI.motivation: To understand how bond anisotropy (interpolating between Ising-like and XY-dominated limits) and a transverse magnetic field jointly shape the quantum phase diagram of a frustrated spin-1/2 Heisenberg ladder.
AI.method: Density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations within a matrix-product-state (MPS) framework, analyzing bipartite entanglement, magnetization, spin correlations, and finite-size scaling of entanglement measures.
AI.result: Six ground-state phases identified: rung-singlet, Haldane-like, Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid, canted Ising-ordered, XY-polarized, and ordered ferromagnetic. Central charge c≈1 in gapless regime (TLL) and c≈1/2 at the canted Ising–ferromagnetic transition (Ising universality). Haldane-like and TLL regimes are confined near α=1.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement measures provide more sensitive and unified diagnostics than magnetization/correlations alone for classifying gapped and gapless phases; the Haldane and TLL phases are strongly tied to the isotropic point.

title: Reducing measurement error with adaptivity
summary: We show that adaptivity, also called feed-forward, is a powerful resource in reducing the error of measurement circuits that combine multiple uses of a noisy measuring device. In previous work, it has been shown that error in measurements can be mitigated by using the measuring device multiple times. So far, the most effective protocols have been parallel measurement schemes, where all measurements are simultaneous. We extend this idea to adaptive measurement schemes, where the results of previous measurements can influence our choice of processing further down the circuit. We show that adaptive measurement circuits can in general reduce overall measurement errors further than any non-adaptive measurement circuit could with the same number of measurements. In particular, we show that for a large class of noisy two-outcome qubit measurements, such an adaptive advantage can exist when as few as three measurements are used. We also show that the adaptive advantage is unbounded across the class of noisy two-outcome qubit measurements, as the number of uses of the device increases. As part of this work, we devise and use methods for finding optimal measurement circuits in both the non-adaptive and adaptive cases. In addition, we prove general results about the limits of such circuits, both in measuring a qubit, and more generally, a qudit.

AI.tldr: Adaptive (feed-forward) measurement circuits can reduce measurement errors more effectively than non-adaptive parallel schemes for noisy qubit measurements, with advantages appearing with as few as three measurements and growing unboundedly with more uses.
AI.motivation: Previous work showed that using a noisy measuring device multiple times can mitigate measurement errors, but the most effective protocols were parallel (non-adaptive) schemes. The authors wanted to explore whether adaptivity (using previous measurement results to influence later processing) could provide additional error reduction beyond what non-adaptive circuits can achieve.
AI.method: The authors extended parallel measurement schemes to adaptive measurement circuits, where prior measurement outcomes influence subsequent choices. They developed methods for finding optimal measurement circuits for both non-adaptive and adaptive cases, and analyzed a large class of noisy two-outcome qubit measurements.
AI.result: Adaptive measurement circuits can generally reduce overall measurement errors further than any non-adaptive circuit using the same number of measurements. Adaptive advantage exists for a large class of noisy two-outcome qubit measurements with as few as three measurements, and this advantage is unbounded as the number of device uses increases.
AI.conclusion: Adaptivity (feed-forward) is a powerful resource for reducing measurement errors in noisy quantum devices, offering provable advantages over parallel schemes. General limits for such circuits were established for both qubit and qudit measurements.

title: Time-Bin BB84 QKD System Using Indium Phosphide and Silicon Nitride Photonic Integrated Circuits
comment: Accepted for presentation at European Conference on Optical Communications (ECOC) 2026
summary: We demonstrate a dual-chip InP-SiN photonic QKD system with on-chip pulse generation and reconfigurable decoding, implementing time-bin BB84 with finite-key security against coherent attacks. The system sustains a QBER below 4% and delivers secret keys at kbps rates over 150-250 km of fiber.

AI.tldr: A dual-chip InP-SiN photonic QKD system implementing time-bin BB84 with on-chip pulse generation and reconfigurable decoding achieves kbps secret key rates over 150-250 km fiber with QBER below 4% and finite-key security against coherent attacks.
AI.motivation: To realize a compact, integrated photonic QKD system that combines InP (gain/active components) and SiN (low-loss passive components) on dual chips, enabling on-chip pulse generation and reconfigurable decoding for practical long-distance quantum key distribution.
AI.method: Dual-chip InP-SiN photonic integration; on-chip pulse generation; reconfigurable decoding; time-bin BB84 protocol; finite-key security analysis against coherent attacks.
AI.result: QBER below 4%; secret key rates at kbps level over 150-250 km fiber.
AI.conclusion: The demonstrated dual-chip InP-SiN platform is viable for integrated QKD systems, offering stable performance (low QBER) and practical secret key rates over long-haul fiber distances with proven security.

title: Temporal processing of quantum states with hybrid quantum-classical reservoirs
comment: 17 pages (10 main article + 7 bibliography and appendix), 12 figures (8 main article + 4 appendix)
summary: A distinctive feature of Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) is the ability to directly embed quantum input states into the reservoir dynamics. However, the resulting output is fundamentally linear for a single input state, preventing QRC from naturally computing nonlinear functionals such as purity or entropy. We overcome this limitation with a quantum-classical hybrid architecture combining a qubit quantum reservoir with a classical echo state network (ESN), allowing both nonlinear functional approximation and effective temporal processing. We systematically study performance under two information regimes: full-tomography and partial information (single-axis measurements), with the latter demonstrating that the hybrid system outperforms its standalone components in both linear and nonlinear tasks due to the enhanced information retrieval provided by the quantum reservoir. Building on these results, we apply an online monitoring protocol that explicitly accounts for measurement back-action and finite measurement ensembles, enabling a realistic assessment of performance under experimental conditions. These results establish hybrid quantum-classical reservoir computing (HRC) architectures as a practical and scalable route for enhanced quantum machine learning on near-term qubit hardware.

AI.tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical reservoir computing architecture is proposed that combines a qubit quantum reservoir with a classical echo state network to overcome the linearity limitation of QRC, enabling nonlinear functional approximation and effective temporal processing, with superior performance demonstrated under partial information regimes and realistic experimental conditions.
AI.motivation: Quantum Reservoir Computing suffers from fundamental linearity in its output for single input states, preventing it from naturally computing nonlinear functionals like purity or entropy. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by introducing a hybrid architecture.
AI.method: A quantum-classical hybrid architecture is developed, combining a qubit quantum reservoir with a classical echo state network (ESN). Performance is systematically studied under full-tomography and partial information (single-axis measurements) regimes, and an online monitoring protocol accounting for measurement back-action and finite measurement ensembles is applied.
AI.result: The hybrid system outperforms its standalone components (pure QRC and pure ESN) in both linear and nonlinear tasks under the partial information regime, due to enhanced information retrieval provided by the quantum reservoir. Realistic experimental assessment is demonstrated via the online monitoring protocol.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid quantum-classical reservoir computing architectures are established as a practical and scalable route for enhanced quantum machine learning on near-term qubit hardware.

title: Efficient Verification of Entangled Measurements with Local States
summary: We develop a framework for quantum measurement verification (QMV) using only local state preparations. For locally transitive and irreducible projective measurements, we prove that symmetry reduces locality constrained QMV to quantum state verification of a single basis state, thereby reducing protocol design to the optimization of homogeneous verification operators. We apply the framework to generalized Bell measurements, single-parameter measurements on two qubits, elegant joint measurements, and stabilizer state induced measurements, and derive explicit local protocols together with closed form verification operators, success probabilities, and sample complexities. We further show that homogeneous QMV protocols can estimate measurement fidelity directly from observed passing frequencies.

AI.tldr: A framework for quantum measurement verification (QMV) using only local state preparations is developed, proving that for locally transitive and irreducible projective measurements, symmetry reduces QMV to quantum state verification of a single basis state. Explicit local protocols and closed-form expressions are derived for several measurement types.
AI.motivation: To develop a systematic framework for verifying quantum measurements using only local state preparations, which is more experimentally feasible than global operations.
AI.method: The authors leverage symmetry properties (local transitivity and irreducibility) to reduce measurement verification to state verification of a single basis state, then optimize homogeneous verification operators. They apply this to generalized Bell measurements, two-qubit single-parameter measurements, elegant joint measurements, and stabilizer-induced measurements.
AI.result: Explicit local protocols with closed-form verification operators, success probabilities, and sample complexities are derived. Homogeneous QMV protocols can estimate measurement fidelity directly from observed passing frequencies.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a practical, symmetry-based approach to quantum measurement verification using only local resources, with analytical results for important measurement classes.

title: Quantum Beam-Splitter Cooling and Thermometry in Large Trapped-Ion Crystals
summary: We propose and characterize a protocol for rapid near-ground state cooling of the center-of-mass (c.m.) mode of a large trapped ion crystal. When the initial mean thermal occupation of the mode $\bar{n}_i$ is small compared to the number of ions $N$, a red sideband drive implements a beam-splitter type SWAP operation between the mode and the collective spin of the $N$ ions, with the latter effectively serving as a quantum harmonic oscillator. Subsequently, a reset of the spins removes the entropy, leading to near-ground state cooling of the c.m. mode. We term this protocol as quantum beam-splitter cooling (QBSC). We analyze the impact of several practical imperfections on the final temperature achievable under QBSC, including finite ion number, off-resonant carrier and blue-sideband contributions, and the impact of the sideband drives arising from spectator modes. In addition, we outline practical strategies to eliminate the carrier drive. Furthermore, we show that measuring the population statistics of the ions at the end of the SWAP operation can enable near-optimal quantum beam-splitter thermometry (QBST), with the classical Fisher information approaching the quantum Fisher information of a thermal state. We discuss the connection of QBSC with continuous sideband cooling and compare QBST with a recently proposed rapid adiabatic passage-based thermometry scheme. Our work constitutes an example of harnessing many-body effects to open new routes to laser cooling and thermometry in large trapped ion crystals.
