AI.tldr: The paper proposes quantum beam-splitter cooling (QBSC), a protocol for rapidly cooling the center-of-mass mode of large trapped ion crystals by swapping excitations between the mode and a collective spin (acting as a quantum harmonic oscillator) via red sideband drive, then resetting the spins. It also introduces quantum beam-splitter thermometry (QBST) for near-optimal temperature measurement.
AI.motivation: To achieve rapid near-ground state cooling of the center-of-mass mode in large trapped ion crystals, overcoming limitations of conventional cooling methods by harnessing many-body collective effects.
AI.method: The protocol uses a red sideband drive to implement a beam-splitter type SWAP operation between the c.m. mode and the collective spin of N ions (treated as a quantum harmonic oscillator), followed by spin reset to remove entropy. The analysis includes imperfections such as finite ion number, off-resonant carrier and blue-sideband contributions, and spectator mode effects. For thermometry, population statistics measurement after SWAP yields classical Fisher information approaching the quantum Fisher information.
AI.result: QBSC enables near-ground state cooling when initial mean thermal occupation is small compared to N. Practical imperfections are characterized, and strategies to eliminate the carrier drive are outlined. QBST achieves near-optimal thermometry with classical Fisher information approaching the quantum Fisher information bound.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates harnessing many-body effects to create new laser cooling and thermometry routes for large trapped ion crystals, connecting QBSC with continuous sideband cooling and comparing QBST with adiabatic passage-based thermometry.

title: Bell inequalities tailored to optimal global randomness certification
comment: See also the related works by R. D'Avino et al and M. Farkas et al. today on arXiv.org
summary: We present two novel families of bipartite Bell inequalities designed to achieve optimal global randomness certification for an arbitrary number of outputs $d$. We first use symmetry arguments to argue that their maximal quantum violations certify $2\log d$ random bits. For the first family, we construct a quantum realization using $d\times d$ maximally entangled states which provides a quantum violation that we conjecture to be optimal for any $d$. It is then numerically shown that the obtained quantum violation certifies optimal global randomness, up to numerical precision, for $d=3,4$. For the second family, we provide the optimal quantum violation and its quantum realization for any $d$, again using $d\times d$ maximally entangled states and projective measurements over at least two unbiased bases on one of the parties. We self-test this realization for $d=3$, which implies the optimal certification of two fully random trits.

AI.tldr: Two families of bipartite Bell inequalities are presented that certify 2 log d random bits using d×d maximally entangled states, with optimal quantum violations proven for the second family and numerically verified for the first family up to d=4, including self-testing for d=3 yielding two fully random trits.
AI.motivation: To achieve optimal global randomness certification for an arbitrary number of outputs d using Bell inequalities, addressing the need for efficient and provably secure random number generation in quantum information processing.
AI.method: Two families of bipartite Bell inequalities are introduced using symmetry arguments. The first family conjectures optimal quantum violation via d×d maximally entangled states with numerical verification for d=3,4. The second family provides provably optimal quantum violation using maximally entangled states and projective measurements over at least two unbiased bases on one party. Self-testing is performed for d=3.
AI.result: Maximal quantum violations certify 2 log d random bits. For the first family, optimal quantum violation is conjectured and numerically confirmed for d=3,4. For the second family, optimal quantum violation is proven for any d. Self-testing for d=3 certifies two fully random trits.
AI.conclusion: The two families of Bell inequalities achieve optimal global randomness certification for arbitrary d, with the second family fully analytically solved and the first family numerically supported up to d=4. The self-testing result for d=3 establishes a rigorous certification of two random trits.

title: Maximal global device-independent randomness from projective measurements in every dimension
comment: Comments welcome! See also the related work by I. Perito et al. today on arXiv.org
summary: Device-independent random number generation (DIQRNG) is the most secure form of generating private randomness using quantum physical processes. Its strength lies in producing numbers that are impossible to predict by any eavesdropper restricted by the laws of quantum theory. Moreover, security is proven solely from observed measurement statistics, without the need to characterise or trust the devices used in random number generation. Implementing DIQRNG is, however, costly, as it requires high-quality entangled systems. It is therefore important to make the best use of available resources. In this work, we show that using projective measurements -- which are most readily implementable experimentally -- one can certify $2\log(d)$ bits of device-independent randomness from a bipartite system of local dimension $d$ for every $d \ge 2$, thus reaching the theoretically maximum possible rate of DIQRNG. We provide explicit protocols reaching $2\log(d)$ bits based on mutually unbiased bases. Furthermore, we compute numerical bounds on the rate for the case of imperfect implementations, showing that our protocols are robust to experimental noise.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that using projective measurements on bipartite quantum systems of local dimension d, one can certify 2log(d) bits of device-independent randomness per system, achieving the theoretical maximum rate for DIQRNG. The protocols use mutually unbiased bases and are robust to experimental noise.
AI.motivation: Device-independent random number generation (DIQRNG) is the most secure form of private randomness but is costly due to requiring high-quality entangled systems. The authors aim to maximize the randomness rate from available resources, specifically to reach the theoretical maximum of 2log(d) bits per bipartite system of local dimension d.
AI.method: The authors propose explicit protocols based on mutually unbiased bases using projective measurements (most readily implementable experimentally). They provide analytical proofs for achieving 2log(d) bits of device-independent randomness and compute numerical bounds for imperfect implementations to assess robustness to experimental noise.
AI.result: The protocols achieve 2log(d) bits of device-independent randomness from a bipartite system of local dimension d for every d ≥ 2, reaching the theoretically maximum possible rate of DIQRNG. Numerical bounds show the protocols are robust to experimental noise in imperfect implementations.
AI.conclusion: Using projective measurements with mutually unbiased bases, one can achieve the optimal DIQRNG rate of 2log(d) bits per bipartite system, and the protocols remain effective under realistic noisy conditions.

title: Noise robustness of three outcome Bell certified quantum randomness
comment: See also the related work by I. Perito et al. today on ArXiv.org
summary: We investigate device-independent certification of global randomness based on Bell inequality violations in bipartite scenarios with three outcomes per party. Our goal is to determine whether multi-outcome measurements allow one to surpass the amount of randomness achievable with binary outputs in realistic scenarios. We begin by analyzing several known Bell expressions and evaluating their robustness against noise for randomness certification. We then introduce a systematic method for generating new Bell expressions within structured families and perform a large-scale numerical study. We find that a substantial number of inequalities certify significant amounts of min-entropy. In particular, we identify simple inequalities that achieve near-maximal global randomness while involving a reduced number of measurement settings, thus improving the balance between certified randomness and number of inputs. Moreover, the vast majority of nontrivial certificates exhibit robustness against realistic noise, maintaining positive certified randomness away from the ideal regime. These results demonstrate that strong device-independent randomness expansion in multi-outcome scenarios is not restricted to carefully engineered inequalities, but arises generically within suitably constructed families of Bell expressions.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates device-independent randomness certification using multi-outcome (three-outcome) Bell inequality violations, finding that many simple inequalities can certify near-maximal global randomness with good noise robustness, and that such randomness is generic rather than requiring specially engineered inequalities.
AI.motivation: To determine whether multi-outcome measurements allow surpassing the amount of randomness achievable with binary outputs in realistic device-independent scenarios, and to explore the generic behavior of randomness certification beyond carefully engineered inequalities.
AI.method: Analyzed known Bell expressions for noise robustness, introduced a systematic method for generating new Bell expressions within structured families, and performed large-scale numerical study of min-entropy certification.
AI.result: Identified simple inequalities achieving near-maximal global randomness with reduced measurement settings; vast majority of nontrivial certificates maintain positive certified randomness away from the ideal regime.
AI.conclusion: Strong device-independent randomness expansion in multi-outcome scenarios arises generically within suitably constructed families of Bell expressions, not limited to specially engineered inequalities.

title: Collective enhancement in sideband cooling of ion crystals
summary: Low-entropy motional states of ion Coulomb crystals are an essential prerequisite for a plethora of applications and are typically prepared by laser cooling. As larger crystals are operated in the quantum regime, it remains unclear, and has recently become debated, whether increasing the ion number can be beneficial for cooling. Here, we investigate theoretically and experimentally many-ion sideband cooling and the role of collective effects in different spin-motion coupling regimes. For weak coupling, the many-body effects are insignificant. In the strong-coupling regime, however, the spin and motional subsystems undergo a coherent state swap, enabling cooling by a suitably timed laser pulse. Using planar Coulomb crystals with up to 91 ions, we demonstrate that the residual mean phonon occupation after one such pulse scales as $1/N^2$ with the number of ions. By iterating the pulses, we measure mean phonon occupations $<2\cdot10^{-4}$. For large crystals in the coherent regime, we further show that the spin-motion dynamics becomes largely independent of the initial phonon statistics. Through spin measurements, the state-swap mechanism can be utilized to probe the phonon distribution in the mode.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates many-ion sideband cooling and collective effects in spin-motion coupling, demonstrating that residual phonon occupation scales as 1/N² with ion number, achieving mean phonon occupations <2×10⁻⁴ in planar Coulomb crystals with up to 91 ions.
AI.motivation: Low-entropy motional states of ion Coulomb crystals are essential for quantum applications, but it remains debated whether increasing ion number benefits cooling. The authors aim to resolve this question by investigating many-ion sideband cooling and collective effects across different coupling regimes.
AI.method: The study combines theoretical analysis and experimental demonstration of many-ion sideband cooling using planar Coulomb crystals (up to 91 ions). They examine weak and strong spin-motion coupling regimes, utilizing coherent state-swap dynamics and iterative laser pulses.
AI.result: In the strong-coupling regime, residual mean phonon occupation after one pulse scales as 1/N². Iterating pulses yields mean phonon occupations <2×10⁻⁴. Spin-motion dynamics becomes largely independent of initial phonon statistics for large crystals in the coherent regime.
AI.conclusion: Collective effects in the strong-coupling regime enable enhanced cooling with increasing ion number, contrary to concerns that larger crystals hinder cooling. The state-swap mechanism can also be used to probe phonon distribution via spin measurements.

title: Entanglement engineering in magnomechanical system via cross-Kerr interaction and mechanical parametric amplification
summary: Quantum entanglement in cavity magnomechanical system has a wide range of applications in modern quantum technologies. In this work, we propose a theoretical scheme to generate and enhance quantum entanglement through cross-Kerr nonlinearity and mechanical parametric amplification (MPA) in a magnomechanical system. Our system is made of a magnonic mode that is simultaneously driving the acoustic phononic and the center-of-mass motion (CMM) phonon in a yttrium iron garnet sphere. The acoustic mode and the center-of-mass mechanical (CMM) mode are weakly coupled via the phonon hopping rate $J_m$. Moreover, the magnonic and phononic modes interact through cross-Kerr interaction, while the phononic mode is additionally driven via a Mechanical Parametric Amplification (MPA). Without the mechanical coupling ($J_m = 0$) and the MPA, the generation of entanglement among the subsystems requires a relatively strong effective cross-Kerr coupling. However, when phonon hopping and MPA are accounted, quantum entanglement can be generated even for weak values of the cross-Kerr coupling strength, revealing the key role of these interactions in the engineering of quantum correlations in our proposal. Furthermore, the related purity of the generated entangled states remains high for the same parameter's regime, revealing that the generated quantum entanglement is established without significantly increasing the mixing of the involved states in the system. Our work suggests how robust and stable quantum correlations can be engineered in magnomechanical structures based on nonlinear interactions. These results are useful for modern quantum applications including quantum information processing, quantum communication, and quantum computational tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a theoretical scheme to generate and enhance quantum entanglement in a cavity magnomechanical system using cross-Kerr nonlinearity and mechanical parametric amplification (MPA), showing that phonon hopping and MPA enable entanglement even at weak cross-Kerr coupling while maintaining high state purity.
AI.motivation: To generate and enhance robust quantum entanglement in magnomechanical systems for applications in quantum technologies, particularly overcoming the need for strong nonlinear couplings.
AI.method: A theoretical scheme employing cross-Kerr nonlinearity between magnonic and phononic modes, mechanical parametric amplification (MPA) on the phononic mode, and phonon hopping (J_m) between acoustic and center-of-mass mechanical modes in a yttrium iron garnet (YIG) sphere.
AI.result: Phonon hopping and MPA enable quantum entanglement even for weak cross-Kerr coupling strength, whereas without them strong nonlinear coupling is required. The generated entangled states maintain high purity in the same parameter regime.
AI.conclusion: Robust and stable quantum correlations can be engineered in magnomechanical structures via nonlinear interactions, useful for quantum information processing, communication, and computation.

title: Quantum work statistics and coherence effects in quenched bosonic Josephson junctions
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures. Comments and feedback are welcome
summary: We investigate the non-equilibrium work statistics originating from a sudden quench in a bosonic Josephson junction. In particular, by employing the Holstein-Primakoff approximation, the work statistics are analytically characterized in the weak-interaction regime, where the dynamics map onto a time-dependent quantum harmonic oscillator. For a junction initialized in the ground state of the pre-quench Hamiltonian, we demonstrate that the work statistics are governed by a negative binomial distribution, as occurs in fully-connected models driven across a critical point. Furthermore, we also consider initial superposition states containing quantum coherences in the energy basis. To characterize the corresponding work distributions, we employ Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobabilities (KDQ). Even in the simplest case, when the junction is initialized in a superposition of the ground and second excited states, the KDQ distribution of work exhibits negative or complex values, reflecting non-classical features. Moreover, the coherence content of the initial state can be optimized to enhance the extractable work extracted from the quench, beyond classical bounds. Finally, we propose an experimental interferometric protocol to directly measure the characteristic function of the work distribution in experimentally accessible settings.

AI.tldr: This paper analytically characterizes non-equilibrium work statistics in a bosonic Josephson junction after a sudden quench, showing a negative binomial distribution for ground-state initializations and using Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobabilities to reveal negative/complex values for coherent superposition states, with implications for enhancing extractable work.
AI.motivation: To understand non-equilibrium work statistics in a bosonic Josephson junction, particularly how quantum coherences in initial superposition states affect work distributions and extractable work beyond classical limits.
AI.method: Holstein-Primakoff approximation to map dynamics onto a time-dependent quantum harmonic oscillator in the weak-interaction regime; analytical characterization of work statistics using negative binomial distribution for ground-state initializations and Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobabilities (KDQ) for initial superposition states.
AI.result: Work statistics follow a negative binomial distribution for ground-state-initialized junctions; KDQ distributions exhibit negative or complex values for superpositions; coherence can be optimized to enhance extractable work beyond classical bounds; an interferometric protocol is proposed to measure the characteristic function.
AI.conclusion: Quantum coherences in initial states can be leveraged to enhance work extraction in bosonic Josephson junctions, with KDQ providing a framework to characterize non-classical features, and the proposed interferometric protocol offers experimental accessibility.

title: Optimal GHZ-State Distribution in LOSR Quantum Networks via Local Decoding from Information Sets
summary: Distributing multipartite entanglement is a prerequisite for scalable quantum networks. Networks restricted to local operations and shared randomness (LOSR) avoid the quantum-memory and latency costs associated with the real-time classical communication required by LOCC-based networks. However, when only bipartite sources are available, LOSR networks cannot prepare useful GHZ states. In earlier work, we conjectured that multipartite sources overcome this limitation and supported this claim with a single numerical example. In this work, we prove the conjecture for regular and uniform networks of arbitrary size. By identifying the hyperedges of the network with the coordinates of a linear code, we show that whenever the edges incident to each node form an information set, a fixed collection of local unitaries, namely the local decoders of the code, transforms the source state into an (N)-party GHZ state with fidelity (d^{m-M}), without requiring any classical communication. Here, (m) denotes the number of edges incident to each node and (M) the total number of edges in the network. For the complete ((N-1))-uniform hypergraph (K_N^{(N-1)}), this fidelity reduces to (1/d). We further prove that this value is optimal among all local-unitary strategies and exceeds the best fidelity achievable using only bipartite sources. For example, in the four-node case, the optimal fidelity is (1/2), compared with the bipartite bound of (1/8). These results demonstrate that multipartite sources, together with shared randomness, can replace real-time classical communication for entanglement distribution.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that multipartite entanglement sources, combined with local operations and shared randomness (LOSR), can prepare high-fidelity GHZ states in regular uniform networks of any size, overcoming limitations of bipartite-only sources. Using a linear code framework, they achieve fidelity \(d^{m-M}\) and show this is optimal for local-unitary strategies, exceeding bipartite bounds (e.g., 1/2 vs 1/8 for four nodes). This eliminates the need for real-time classical communication in entanglement distribution.
AI.motivation: Scalable quantum networks require distributing multipartite entanglement. LOSR networks avoid costly real-time classical communication needed by LOCC networks, but bipartite-only LOSR networks cannot produce useful GHZ states. The authors aim to prove that multipartite sources overcome this limitation.
AI.method: The authors identify hyperedges of a regular uniform network with coordinates of a linear code. They show that when edges incident to each node form an information set, local decoders of the code transform the source state into an N-party GHZ state with fidelity \(d^{m-M}\) using only local unitaries and no classical communication.
AI.result: For the complete \((N-1)\)-uniform hypergraph \(K_N^{(N-1)}\), the fidelity reduces to \(1/d\). This value is optimal among all local-unitary strategies and exceeds the best fidelity achievable with bipartite sources (e.g., 1/2 vs 1/8 for four nodes).
AI.conclusion: Multipartite sources with shared randomness can replace real-time classical communication for entanglement distribution in regular uniform networks, enabling scalable quantum network architectures without the overhead of LOCC-based schemes.

title: A Correlation Aware Quantum Feature Map for Variational Quantum Classification
summary:
Quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising research area for learning complex data patterns. However, most existing quantum feature maps employ fixed encoding strategies that do not explicitly consider the relationships among features within a dataset. In this study, we propose a Correlation Aware Quantum Feature Map (CAQFM) which integrates feature dependencies into the quantum encoding process. The proposed approach utilizes Pearson, Spearman, Kendall Tau, Mutual Information, and Distance Correlation measures to identify relationships among features. Dependencies exceeding a predefined threshold are incorporated into the quantum circuit through controlled quantum gates, enabling the construction of richer quantum representations that better reflect the underlying structure of the data.
  The proposed method is evaluated using a Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) on three benchmark datasets, namely breast cancer diagnosis, credit default prediction, and student placement classification. Simulation results demonstrate that correlation based quantum encoding can improve classification performance compared to conventional encoding strategies. In particular, the Spearman and Kendall Tau based CAQFM variants achieved the highest predictive performance and consistently outperformed standard quantum feature maps. The findings indicate that incorporating dependency information from classical data into quantum feature maps facilitates the generation of more discriminative quantum representations and enhances the effectiveness of variational quantum classifiers.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CAQFM, a correlation-aware quantum feature map that integrates feature dependencies (using Pearson, Spearman, Kendall Tau, Mutual Information, Distance Correlation) into quantum encoding via controlled gates, and shows improved classification performance on VQC across three benchmark datasets, with Spearman and Kendall Tau variants performing best.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum feature maps use fixed encoding strategies that ignore relationships among features within a dataset, limiting the expressiveness of quantum representations.
AI.method: CAQFM computes multiple correlation measures (Pearson, Spearman, Kendall Tau, Mutual Information, Distance Correlation) between features; dependencies exceeding a threshold are encoded via controlled quantum gates into a variational quantum classifier (VQC).
AI.result: On breast cancer diagnosis, credit default prediction, and student placement datasets, correlation-based encoding outperforms conventional strategies, with Spearman and Kendall Tau CAQFM variants achieving the highest predictive performance consistently.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating classical feature dependency information into quantum feature maps produces more discriminative quantum representations and enhances the effectiveness of variational quantum classifiers.

title: Systematic derivation of Tsirelson bounds in arbitrary dimensions
summary: The study of Bell nonlocality and the bounds of quantum correlations, the so-called Tsirelson bounds, is fundamental to quantum information science and the exploration of the limits of quantum theory. While quantum bounds for qubit systems have been extensively characterized, determining tight quantum bounds for correlations attainable with high-dimensional quantum states and measurements remains a significant challenge. In this work, we propose a systematic derivation of bipartite Tsirelson and local bounds written in terms of sum-of-squares decompositions. Using this method, we discover novel bounds and recover established results for maximally entangled states of qubits and qu$d$its.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a systematic method to derive bipartite Tsirelson and local bounds using sum-of-squares decompositions, discovering new quantum correlation bounds and recovering known results for maximally entangled states.
AI.motivation: Determining tight quantum bounds (Tsirelson bounds) for correlations achievable with high-dimensional quantum states and measurements remains a significant challenge, motivating the need for a systematic derivation method.
AI.method: The authors propose a systematic approach to derive bipartite Tsirelson and local bounds based on sum-of-squares decompositions.
AI.result: The method discovers novel bounds and recovers established results for maximally entangled states of qubits and qudits.
AI.conclusion: The sum-of-squares decomposition approach provides a systematic framework for deriving tight quantum correlation bounds in high-dimensional quantum systems.

title: No-signaling values of quantum games--an operator algebra perspective
summary: The aim of this work is to study two-prover quantum games (i.e., games with quantum inputs and outputs) from an operator-algebraic and operator-space point of view. We characterize several notions of the value of such games by formulating them in terms of tensor norms in the category of operator spaces. The main results of the paper concern the description of the so-called no-signalling value of these games, for which we not only provide a precise operator-space formulation, but also establish close connections between this study and some problems in operator algebras. In particular, we show how the recent counterexample to Grothendieck's theorem for operator spaces given in \cite{Ara} can be understood as a direct consequence of results in quantum information theory. We also obtain new upper bounds on the gap between the no-signalling value and the quantum value of two-prover quantum games, improving the best previously known estimates.

AI.tldr: This paper studies two-prover quantum games using operator-algebraic and operator-space approaches, characterizes game values via tensor norms, provides an operator-space formulation of the no-signalling value, connects to operator algebra problems, and improves upper bounds on the gap between no-signalling and quantum values.
AI.motivation: To study two-prover quantum games from an operator-algebraic and operator-space perspective, establishing connections between quantum information theory and operator algebras.
AI.method: Characterizing notions of game value via tensor norms in the category of operator spaces; formulating the no-signalling value using operator-space theory.
AI.result: (1) A precise operator-space formulation of the no-signalling value of two-prover quantum games. (2) Showing that a recent counterexample to Grothendieck's theorem for operator spaces follows directly from results in quantum information theory. (3) New upper bounds on the gap between no-signalling and quantum values, improving prior estimates.
AI.conclusion: The operator-space approach provides a unifying framework for analyzing two-prover quantum games, reveals deep connections between quantum information theory and operator algebras, and yields improved quantitative results on the no-signalling vs. quantum value gap.

title: Instabilities of the continuous superradiant laser
summary: We investigate the intensity stability of the superradiant laser. Our study focuses on the architecture where a continuous beam of atoms in an electronically excited state crosses the mode of a high-finesse Fabry-Perot cavity, which has been proposed as a new architecture of an active optical clock. We show that such superradiant laser can become unstable and develop chaotic behavior. We derive an analytical criterion for this instability and find that it may only occur when the lifetime of photons in the cavity is significantly shorter than the lifetime of atoms. This criterion allows for refining the necessary parameters to run a superradiant laser as a frequency reference in the optical domain. In particular, we point-out the consequences of the instability on intensity fluctuations and laser linewidth. On the other hand, we also point out that the superradiant laser, when in the unstable regime, can become an interesting playground for studying chaos. At the mean-field level, there is a direct mapping to the Bénard instability associated with fluid turbulence; however quantum fluctuations associated with photon out-coupling and atom re-filling substantially modify the expected behaviors. Finally, we point-out the existence of a regular self-pulsing regime at large atom numbers.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the intensity stability of superradiant lasers using a continuous beam of excited atoms crossing a high-finesse cavity. It shows that such lasers can develop chaotic instability when cavity photon lifetimes are much shorter than atomic lifetimes, derives an analytical instability criterion, and identifies a regular self-pulsing regime at large atom numbers. The instability has implications for frequency reference applications and provides a playground for studying chaos with quantum effects modifying classical Bénard instability analogies.
AI.motivation: To understand the intensity stability of superradiant lasers proposed as active optical clocks, specifically to identify and characterize instability regimes that could affect their performance as frequency references.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of an instability criterion for superradiant lasers with a continuous beam of excited atoms crossing a high-finesse Fabry-Perot cavity, combined with mean-field analysis and consideration of quantum fluctuations from photon out-coupling and atom re-filling.
AI.result: Superradiant lasers can become unstable and develop chaotic behavior when the cavity photon lifetime is significantly shorter than the atomic lifetime. An analytical criterion for this instability is derived. At large atom numbers, a regular self-pulsing regime exists. Quantum fluctuations substantially modify the expected behaviors compared to the classical Bénard instability analogy.
AI.conclusion: The instability criterion provides refined parameters for operating superradiant lasers as stable frequency references, with consequences for intensity fluctuations and laser linewidth. In the unstable regime, the system serves as a quantum-modified playground for studying chaos.

title: Exceptional Points revealed by the integrated imaginary scattering eigenphase
summary: We propose and analytically demonstrate that the eigenphases of the scattering matrix provide direct, phase-sensitive signatures of exceptional points in open PT-symmetric systems. Using a one-dimensional PT-symmetric quantum dimer with balanced gain and loss, coupled to continuum leads, we track the evolution of the scattering eigenphases across the PT-exact to PT-broken transition. The imaginary parts of the eigenphases develop localized structures of opposite sign as the exceptional point is approached, reflecting the emergence of gain/loss asymmetry in the scattering eigenmodes. We introduce the integrated imaginary scattering eigenphase G(gamma), which condenses this information into a single experimentally accessible scalar. G(gamma) is negligibly small in the PT-exact phase and undergoes a sharp transition -- a pronounced inflection followed by saturation into a plateau -- near the exceptional point. The inflection point of G(gamma) precedes gamma_{EP} and coincides with the maximum amplitude of the transmission resonances, revealing that peak gain/loss asymmetry and eigenstate coalescence are governed by independent conditions in open systems -- a direct fingerprint of their finite coupling to the continuum. Because the analysis is formulated entirely at the level of the S-matrix -- without reference to any specific physical realization -- the results are universally applicable across wave systems, including photonic, acoustic, and microwave platforms where phase-resolved measurements are available.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that eigenphases of the scattering matrix directly signal exceptional points in open PT-symmetric systems. An integrated scalar G(γ) is introduced that transitions sharply near the exceptional point, revealing that gain/loss asymmetry and eigenstate coalescence are governed by independent conditions due to finite coupling to the continuum. The S-matrix-based formulation is universally applicable across wave systems.
AI.motivation: To identify phase-sensitive, experimentally accessible signatures of exceptional points in open PT-symmetric systems, overcoming limitations of intensity-only measurements by leveraging scattering eigenphase information.
AI.method: Analytical demonstration using a one-dimensional PT-symmetric quantum dimer with balanced gain and loss, coupled to continuum leads. Tracking scattering eigenphases across PT-exact to PT-broken transition; introducing integrated imaginary scattering eigenphase G(γ) as a scalar diagnostic.
AI.result: Imaginary eigenphases develop localized opposite-sign structures near the exceptional point. G(γ) is negligible in PT-exact phase and undergoes a sharp inflection-to-plateau transition near the EP. The inflection point precedes γ_EP and coincides with peak transmission resonance amplitude.
AI.conclusion: Gain/loss asymmetry and eigenstate coalescence are independent in open systems due to finite continuum coupling. The S-matrix approach is universally applicable across photonic, acoustic, and microwave platforms.

title: Finite-shot operating windows for probabilistic error cancellation and Clifford data regression
summary: Quantum error mitigation on noisy devices is limited not only by residual bias but also by the shot noise and calibration errors introduced by the mitigation procedure itself. We derive finite-shot mean-square-error boundaries for probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), Clifford data regression (CDR), and no mitigation for noisy Pauli-observable estimates. Exact PEC removes the target bias under an exact noise inverse at the price of a quasi-probability variance overhead, whereas population linear CDR can have smaller target-shot variance but retains a calibration floor when the training and target noise responses do not match. This competition yields a finite CDR-dominant operating window whose upper endpoint scales as $B_{\mathrm{PEC}=\mathrm{CDR}}(p)\propto 1/(δ_1^2p)$, where $δ_1$ is the first-order CDR calibration mismatch. We further prove a target-response projection theorem showing that response-blind affine CDR removes the first-order bias only when the target noise response is affine in the ideal target value; otherwise a nonzero projection error gives an irreducible local calibration floor. The same mean-square-error formulation extends to second-order calibration, commuting Pauli Hamiltonians, finite CDR training shots, and residual PEC model bias. A closed-form two-qubit calculation and QAOA simulations support the predicted no-mitigation, CDR-dominant, and PEC-dominant regimes.

AI.tldr: This paper derives finite-shot mean-square-error boundaries for quantum error mitigation techniques (PEC, CDR, and no mitigation), revealing a CDR-dominant operating window and proving a target-response projection theorem that limits affine CDR when noise responses are non-affine.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental limits of quantum error mitigation when accounting for shot noise and calibration errors, beyond just residual bias, and to compare the finite-sample performance of PEC versus CDR.
AI.method: Derivation of finite-shot mean-square-error boundaries for PEC, CDR, and no mitigation; proof of a target-response projection theorem; closed-form two-qubit calculations and QAOA simulations.
AI.result: Exact PEC removes bias but incurs quasi-probability variance overhead; CDR reduces variance but retains a calibration floor when training and target noise responses mismatch. A CDR-dominant window exists with upper endpoint scaling as B ∝ 1/(δ₁²p). Affine CDR only removes first-order bias when the target noise response is affine; otherwise an irreducible local calibration floor persists.
AI.conclusion: The MSE formulation generalizes to second-order calibration, commuting Pauli Hamiltonians, finite CDR training shots, and residual PEC model bias; simulations confirm three regimes: no-mitigation, CDR-dominant, and PEC-dominant.

title: Continuous-variable model for arbitrary image propagation via Dirac-comb expansion in Four-Wave Mixing
summary: We develop a macroscopic continuous-variable model of stimulated four-wave mixing (4WM) yielding closed-form expressions for the mean intensity, variance, and covariance of bright probe and conjugate beams, valid for arbitrary transverse profiles of the pump and seed to all orders in the nonlinear interaction strength. The model uses a Dirac-comb expansion of the pump field, making the photon statistics computable pixel-by-pixel from one set of expressions. In the plane-wave limit, we recover the phase-insensitive amplifier results. Beyond this limit, the formalism explicitly demonstrates the spatial routing of information observed in earlier experiments: the seed angular spectrum is transferred to the twin-beam intensities, whereas the angular spectrum of the squared pump field is transferred to the spatial cross-correlation between the probe and conjugate. We characterize the parameter window of high-fidelity image transfer in the covariance, which is controlled by the seed-to-pump waist ratio and the interaction strength. Our model provides, in one analytical framework, a theoretical account of experiments encoding information in the bright intensities or non-locally in the spatial cross-correlations.

AI.tldr: A macroscopic continuous-variable model of stimulated four-wave mixing is developed, yielding closed-form expressions for mean intensity, variance, and covariance of probe and conjugate beams. Using a Dirac-comb expansion, it computes photon statistics pixel-by-pixel, recovers plane-wave amplifier results, demonstrates spatial routing of information, and characterizes the parameter window for high-fidelity image transfer in the covariance.
AI.motivation: To provide a unified analytical framework that explains experiments encoding information either in bright intensities or non-locally in spatial cross-correlations, going beyond the plane-wave limit to capture spatial routing phenomena observed in earlier experiments.
AI.method: A macroscopic continuous-variable model of stimulated four-wave mixing using a Dirac-comb expansion of the pump field, enabling pixel-by-pixel computation of photon statistics (mean intensity, variance, covariance) for arbitrary transverse pump/seed profiles to all orders in nonlinear interaction strength.
AI.result: Closed-form expressions valid for arbitrary transverse profiles; recovery of phase-insensitive amplifier results in the plane-wave limit; demonstration that the seed angular spectrum transfers to twin-beam intensities while the squared pump angular spectrum transfers to spatial cross-correlation; characterization of the parameter window (seed-to-pump waist ratio and interaction strength) for high-fidelity image transfer in covariance.
AI.conclusion: The model provides a comprehensive analytical framework that unifies theoretical understanding of both local (bright intensity) and non-local (spatial cross-correlation) information encoding in four-wave mixing experiments.

title: Evaluation of Variational Quantum Classifiers (VQC) for Cyberattack Detection in the NISQ Era
summary: This paper investigates the effectiveness and structural limits of Variational Quantum Classifiers (VQC) for detecting network anomalies in the era of Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) systems. Using the official 20\% research subset of the NSL-KDD dataset, a 4-qubit classifier featuring a 24-parameter trainable ansatz was developed, utilizing amplitude encoding to embed 16 principal components. On a held-out partition of this subset, the model achieved a consistent binary-classification accuracy of 88\%. A comparative evaluation with two fundamentally different optimizers, COBYLA and SPSA, found that the observed performance plateau is not attributable to convergence to local minima, a result we interpret as consistent with an encoding-related expressibility limit rather than an optimization artifact. An architectural parity comparison with a classical neural network (a Tiny MLP with four nodes, achieving 97\% accuracy) highlighted the expressiveness gap associated with data overcompression into restricted quantum states. The model was trained on a class-balanced set spanning the 22 raw NSL-KDD attack categories and evaluated in-sample as a probe of representational capacity: under this configuration the VQC reached only 9\% accuracy and exhibited a degenerate mode collapse onto a small subset of classes. We interpret this behavior as consistent with the loss of linear separability induced by excessive compression in the quantum probability space, while explicitly noting that our experiments do not isolate the encoding from the ansatz depth, optimizer budget, and measurement-decoding scheme (see Limitations). Motivated by these observations and by Cover's theorem, we outline an alternative paradigm: a 16-qubit VQC with angle encoding that expands the Hilbert-space representation rather than relying on aggressive classical dimensionality reduction.

AI.tldr: A 4-qubit VQC with amplitude encoding achieves 88% binary accuracy on NSL-KDD but only 9% on 22-class classification due to expressibility limits from data overcompression, motivating a 16-qubit angle-encoding approach.
AI.motivation: To investigate the effectiveness and structural limits of Variational Quantum Classifiers (VQC) for network anomaly detection in NISQ-era systems, specifically examining whether performance plateaus stem from optimization issues or fundamental encoding/expressibility constraints.
AI.method: Developed a 4-qubit VQC with 24-parameter trainable ansatz using amplitude encoding on 16 principal components from NSL-KDD dataset; compared COBYLA and SPSA optimizers; contrasted with a 4-node Tiny MLP; tested on binary (88% accuracy) and 22-class (9% accuracy, mode collapse) settings.
AI.result: Binary classification achieved 88% accuracy (plateau not from local minima); Tiny MLP reached 97%; 22-class VQC collapsed to 9% with degenerate output distribution; performance gap attributed to encoding-related expressibility limits and loss of linear separability from overcompression.
AI.conclusion: Current amplitude-encoding VQC suffers from expressibility limits due to aggressive dimensionality reduction; proposes a 16-qubit angle-encoding VQC to expand Hilbert-space representation, motivated by Cover's theorem.

title: On a Central Limit Theorem and Sanov's principle for quantum neural networks
summary: In this work, we study the fluctuations of a Mixture of Experts (MoE) generated by a quantum neural network trained via gradient flow on supervised learning problems. Our main results establish the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), and Sanov's principle for an MoE as the number of experts diverges. We demonstrate that the fluctuations of the empirical measure of its parameters close to its corresponding limit probability measure solve a linear transport equation. As a byproduct, we show that the MoE converges to a limit function which solves an evolution equation governed by the neural tangent kernel associated with the quantum neural network.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the fluctuations of a Mixture of Experts (MoE) model generated by a quantum neural network trained via gradient flow, establishing a Central Limit Theorem and Sanov's principle as the number of experts diverges, and showing that fluctuations solve a linear transport equation while the MoE converges to a limit function governed by the neural tangent kernel.
AI.motivation: To understand the statistical behavior and fluctuations of Mixture of Experts models when generated by quantum neural networks, particularly in the limit of many experts.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis using gradient flow training of a quantum neural network-based MoE, deriving Central Limit Theorem and Sanov's principle for the empirical measure of parameters as the number of experts tends to infinity.
AI.result: Established CLT and Sanov's principle for MoE with diverging expert count; fluctuations of the empirical measure solve a linear transport equation; MoE converges to a limit function governed by the neural tangent kernel associated with the quantum neural network.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical framework for understanding the limiting behavior and fluctuations of quantum neural network-based MoE models, connecting them to transport equations and neural tangent kernel theory.

title: Feedback-Controlled Magnon-Atom Entanglement and Photon Statistics
summary: Quantum systems face inherent challenges in achieving precise control, and solving the Schrödinger equation is often intractable for complex hybrid platforms. Here, for the first time, we introduce a magnon into a feedback-controlled quantum system. To solve the dynamics numerically and efficiently, we employ a Long Short-Term Memory network, a machine learning approach, to propagate the probability amplitudes to the steady state. By applying coherent feedback, we effectively stabilize the intracavity state. Our results reveal that the photon-photon correlation function and the concurrence, a measure of magnon-atom entanglement, exhibit periodic oscillations with the cavity-mirror distance, and that feedback significantly enhances both antibunching and bunching when the detuning is varied. These findings not only demonstrate the power of artificial intelligence in quantum dynamics simulation, but also open a promising route for on-demand quantum state engineering in hybrid magnonic systems, with potential applications in quantum networks and quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a magnon into a feedback-controlled quantum system for the first time, using a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to efficiently simulate quantum dynamics. Coherent feedback stabilizes the intracavity state, and results show periodic oscillations in photon-photon correlation and concurrence with cavity-mirror distance, with feedback enhancing antibunching/bunching under detuning variation.
AI.motivation: Quantum systems face inherent challenges in achieving precise control, and solving the Schrödinger equation is often intractable for complex hybrid platforms. The authors aim to address this by introducing a magnon into a feedback-controlled quantum system and employing machine learning for efficient simulation.
AI.method: The authors employ a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, a machine learning approach, to propagate probability amplitudes to the steady state. Coherent feedback is applied to stabilize the intracavity state.
AI.result: The photon-photon correlation function and concurrence (magnon-atom entanglement measure) exhibit periodic oscillations with cavity-mirror distance. Feedback significantly enhances both antibunching and bunching when detuning is varied.
AI.conclusion: The findings demonstrate the power of artificial intelligence in quantum dynamics simulation and open a promising route for on-demand quantum state engineering in hybrid magnonic systems, with potential applications in quantum networks and quantum information processing.

title: Dynamical Decoupling using Universal Optimal Tracking
comment: 10 pages plus appendix and bibliography; 10 figures
summary: Dynamical decoupling (DD) is a widely used and resource-efficient technique for error suppression, but conventional DD relies on periodically repeating a short pulse block to refocus the qubit state during idle periods. Imperfections in this block cause residual errors to accumulate, ultimately degrading state recovery over long idle times. Here, we introduce a universal optimal tracking approach that extends the original tracking concept to a fully state-independent setting for designing DD sequences. By monitoring the qubit's evolution at predefined waypoints during optimization, the method dynamically compensates residual errors while preserving regular refocusing. Experimental demonstrations on a superconducting-qubit platform confirm the suppression of error accumulation under static control imperfections, in agreement with numerical predictions. Complementary simulations further show that optimal-tracking-based sequences maintain strong performance under time-dependent noise. These results establish optimal tracking as a practical and hardware-agnostic approach to designing short, robust DD sequences suitable for noisy quantum devices.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an optimal tracking approach for dynamical decoupling that dynamically compensates residual errors from imperfect pulses, demonstrated on superconducting qubits and validated via simulations under time-dependent noise.
AI.motivation: Conventional dynamical decoupling relies on periodic pulse blocks whose imperfections cause residual error accumulation over long idle times, degrading qubit state recovery.
AI.method: A universal optimal tracking approach is introduced that monitors qubit evolution at predefined waypoints during optimization, dynamically compensating residual errors while maintaining regular refocusing, in a fully state-independent setting.
AI.result: Experimental demonstrations on a superconducting-qubit platform confirm suppression of error accumulation under static control imperfections; simulations further show strong performance under time-dependent noise.
AI.conclusion: Optimal tracking is established as a practical, hardware-agnostic approach for designing short, robust DD sequences suitable for noisy quantum devices.

title: Common causes for quantum identical particles
summary: Violations of Bell's inequalities imply that joint probabilities generated by non-commutative measurements on two (non-identical) quantum particles do not have a single common cause. But joint probabilities generated for such non-identical particles via commutative measurements do have non-trivial common cause variables. We focus on commutative measurements and consider two identical quantum particles, whose density matrices and observables (hermitian operators) are necessarily permutation-symmetric. It is natural to demand that the common cause describing joint probabilities is also permutation symmetric, i.e., it acts symmetrically on both particles. Looking at various ways of defining joint probabilities from the same measurement data, we conclude that either symmetric common causes need not exist (i.e., that the particles can be hiddenly distinguishable), or that symmetric screening variables exist, but they are trivial, i.e., no single common cause can explain all single-measurement correlations.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether permutation-symmetric common causes exist for joint probabilities of identical quantum particles under commutative measurements. It finds that such symmetric common causes either do not exist (implying hidden distinguishability) or are trivial (failing to explain all single-measurement correlations).
AI.motivation: To extend the common cause principle (motivated by Bell's inequalities) from non-identical to identical quantum particles, specifically examining whether permutation symmetry of particles imposes constraints on the existence of symmetric common causes for joint probabilities from commutative measurements.
AI.method: The paper considers commutative measurements on two identical quantum particles, where density matrices and observables are permutation-symmetric. It examines various definitions of joint probabilities from the same measurement data and analyzes the existence and non-triviality of symmetric common cause variables.
AI.result: Either symmetric common causes do not exist (suggesting particles can be hiddenly distinguishable), or symmetric screening variables exist but are trivial — no single common cause can explain all single-measurement correlations.
AI.conclusion: For identical particles under commutative measurements, permutation symmetry of the common cause is either impossible or insufficient to account for observed correlations, challenging the common cause principle in the quantum domain.

title: First-Quantized Relativistic Quantum Simulation with Periodic and Dirichlet Boundary Conditions
comment: This manuscript is a significantly revised and extended version of preprint arXiv:2509.22579, with an updated author list
summary: In this work, we present a methodology for first-quantized relativistic quantum simulation on one-dimensional finite domains under the two boundary conditions most commonly used in lattice models: periodic boundary conditions (PBC) and Dirichlet boundary conditions (DBC). Starting from the positive-energy relativistic kinetic operator, we construct weakly relativistic lattice Hamiltonians whose leading correction requires the boundary-consistent discretized momentum moments $\langle \hat{P}^{2}\rangle$ and $\langle \hat{P}^{4}\rangle$. These moments are reconstructed in the PBC Hamiltonian from moments of a unitary cyclic translation while the DBC Hamiltonian uses the open-chain finite-difference. In a qubit-register implementation, it can be evaluated as the corresponding cyclic translation estimator plus boundary-local terms that remove the unphysical wrap-around link. The resulting energy-estimation workflow uses translation measurements for the kinetic terms, a small number of endpoints and near-endpoints overlap probabilities for DBC, and position-basis sampling for diagonal potentials. We valdate the framework of the relativistic quantum simulation in various benchmark potentials such as no potential and a cosine potential for PBC as well as an infinite square well and a harmonic potential for DBC, with finite-shot sampling tests. These benchmarks show good agreement between the estimator reconstruction and direct matrix evaluation while separating the finite-grid discretization, weak-relativistic truncation, and measurement errors.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a methodology for first-quantized relativistic quantum simulation on 1D finite domains under periodic (PBC) and Dirichlet (DBC) boundary conditions, constructing weakly relativistic lattice Hamiltonians from the positive-energy kinetic operator. It uses boundary-consistent discretized momentum moments reconstructed via cyclic translation (PBC) or open-chain finite-difference (DBC), with energy estimation via translation measurements, endpoint probabilities, and position-basis sampling. Benchmarks validate the framework against no potential, cosine, infinite square well, and harmonic potentials.
AI.motivation: To enable first-quantized relativistic quantum simulation on finite lattices with correct boundary conditions, addressing the challenge of constructing boundary-consistent discretized momentum moments for the weakly relativistic kinetic operator.
AI.method: Construct weakly relativistic lattice Hamiltonians using the positive-energy relativistic kinetic operator with leading corrections from ⟨P̂²⟩ and ⟨P̂⁴⟩. For PBC, reconstruct moments via unitary cyclic translation; for DBC, use open-chain finite-difference with boundary-local terms to remove unphysical wrap-around links. Energy estimation uses translation measurements for kinetic terms, endpoint overlap probabilities for DBC, and position-basis sampling for potentials.
AI.result: Benchmarks on no potential, cosine potential (PBC), infinite square well, and harmonic potential (DBC) show good agreement between estimator reconstruction and direct matrix evaluation, with separation of finite-grid discretization, weak-relativistic truncation, and measurement errors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed methodology successfully enables relativistic quantum simulation on finite 1D lattices under both PBC and DBC, with validated accuracy across benchmark potentials.

title: Prethermal cooling with many-body quantum quenches
summary: Many-body quantum quenches are typically associated with heating. In this work, we show that quantum quenches that perform positive work on the system can still lead to effective cooling of low-energy degrees of freedom if the quench energy is deposited in long-lived high-energy excitations. We discuss this explicitly for a quench of the hopping term t in the strong-coupling (U >> t) fermionic Hubbard model at half filling, where the quench induces a very long-lived non-equilibrium doublon density. The associated prethermal state persists for a time exponentially large in (U/t)^2. During this time window, we find an effective prethermal temperature that is reduced by the square of the ratio of final to initial hopping amplitude with respect to the initial temperature. This manifests as an effective fluctuation-dissipation relation that holds for doublon-number conserving operators. In a practical implementation the Hubbard system acts as a refrigerant to cool a target system provided the coupling conserves doublon number. Our protocol can be thought of as a quantum quench many-body generalization of adiabatic demagnetization.

AI.tldr: Quantum quenches in the fermionic Hubbard model can cool low-energy degrees of freedom by depositing work energy into long-lived doublon excitations, creating a prethermal state with an effective temperature lower than the initial temperature, analogous to adiabatic demagnetization.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that quantum quenches, typically associated with heating, can instead cool low-energy degrees of freedom when quench energy is stored in long-lived high-energy excitations (doublons) in the strongly interacting Hubbard model.
AI.method: Analysis of a quantum quench of the hopping term t in the strong-coupling (U >> t) fermionic Hubbard model at half filling, deriving an effective prethermal temperature reduced by the square of the ratio of final to initial hopping amplitude, and establishing a fluctuation-dissipation relation for doublon-number conserving operators.
AI.result: The quench creates a long-lived non-equilibrium doublon density; the prethermal state persists for a time exponentially large in (U/t)^2; the effective prethermal temperature scales as (t_final/t_initial)^2 times the initial temperature, which is a reduction when t_final < t_initial.
AI.conclusion: The Hubbard system can act as a refrigerant to cool a target system if the coupling conserves doublon number; the protocol is a many-body generalization of adiabatic demagnetization.

title: Dynamical Tipping in a Quantum Limit Cycle
summary: Nonequilibrium systems maintain spatiotemporal order through energy dissipation and entropy production. Here, we demonstrate this principle by engineering a quantum limit cycle that emerges from the interplay between a first-order absorbing-state phase transition and feedback mechanism coupling order and control parameters. The quantum limit cycle manifests dynamical correlations driven by multiplicative quantum noise and periodic traverses through tipping points, which act as a robust early-warning signal for state transitions. This periodic crossing results in the enhanced dynamical susceptibility and transient rise of long-range correlations near each tipping event and their subsequent disappearance away from it. These critical transitions are accompanied by a sharp increase in the energy dissipation rate, leading to a stepwise accumulation of dynamical entropy production over time. Our results provide a way for realizing dynamical fluctuations and long-range correlations in strongly interacting driven-dissipative open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: A quantum limit cycle emerges from an absorbing-state phase transition coupled with feedback, exhibiting periodic tipping points, enhanced susceptibility, transient long-range correlations, and stepwise entropy production—offering a route to dynamical order in open quantum systems.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate how nonequilibrium systems maintain spatiotemporal order through energy dissipation and entropy production, specifically by engineering a quantum limit cycle in an open quantum system.
AI.method: Engineering a quantum limit cycle via the interplay of a first-order absorbing-state phase transition and a feedback mechanism that couples order and control parameters, driven by multiplicative quantum noise.
AI.result: The quantum limit cycle shows periodic traverses through tipping points, enhanced dynamical susceptibility, transient long-range correlations near tipping events, sharp increases in energy dissipation rate, and stepwise accumulation of dynamical entropy production.
AI.conclusion: These periodic critical transitions serve as robust early-warning signals and provide a mechanism for realizing dynamical fluctuations and long-range correlations in strongly interacting driven-dissipative open quantum systems.

title: Demonstration of a Monolithic and Fully Telecom-Fiber-Compatible Tunable Source of Polarization Entangled Photon Pairs Based on a van der Waals Material
summary: We present a tunable, single-mode-optical-fiber-based source of polarization entangled photon pairs for the near-infrared telecommunication band that is deployable in standard infrastructure. The photon pairs are generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) in a submicron-scale thin film of the inversion-broken rhombohedral polytype of the transition metal dichalcogenide molybdenum disulfide (3R-MoS$_2$), located between two fiber connectors. By exploiting the intrinsic symmetries of the second-order nonlinear susceptibility tensor of 3R-MoS$_2$, this hybrid approach offers control over the generated two-photon polarization state through the incident pump polarization. Most notably, two of the four maximally entangled Bell states, as well as fully co-polarized pairs can be produced. This represents a substantial improvement in terms of tunability and simplicity over established fiber-integrated sources, which require additional optical elements, precise alignment, or careful engineering of design parameters. Additionally, a nonlinear drop in the background photoluminescence signal of 3R-MoS$_2$ is observed at low pump powers, allowing us to reach a coincidences-to-accidentals ratio (CAR) of $(8.3\pm1.8)\times10^{3}$, the highest value recorded for SPDC in van der Waals materials to date.

AI.tldr: A fiber-integrated source of polarization-entangled photon pairs using 3R-MoS₂ for SPDC, enabling tunable generation of Bell states and co-polarized pairs with record-high CAR.
AI.motivation: To develop a deployable, tunable, and simple fiber-integrated source of polarization-entangled photon pairs in the telecom band without requiring additional optical elements or precise alignment.
AI.method: SPDC in a submicron 3R-MoS₂ thin film placed between two fiber connectors; polarization state control via incident pump polarization exploiting the second-order nonlinear susceptibility tensor symmetries.
AI.result: Generation of two maximally entangled Bell states and co-polarized pairs; record CAR of (8.3±1.8)×10³ for SPDC in van der Waals materials; nonlinear photoluminescence drop at low pump powers.
AI.conclusion: The 3R-MoS₂-based fiber source offers superior tunability and simplicity over existing fiber-integrated entangled photon sources, with record performance metrics.

title: Shuttling in Bidimensional Segmented Ion-Trap Quantum Processors with T-Junctions
summary: Shuttle-based trapped ion quantum processors typically employ a one-dimensional (1D) linear architecture to transport ion-qubits between one ore more laser interaction zones where the quantum gates are implemented, along with several qubit register storage segments. The two-dimensional (2D) quantum CCD architecture employs also T- or X-junctions for an improved scaling and efficiency. Here, we explore the shuttling layer in the compilation of quantum algorithm typical building blocks in such architecture. To weight the effort of linear shuttle and junction shuttle, we introduce individual cost functions for each operation. This allows comparing the total cost for quantum circuit building blocks such as the QFT, Carry, Adder, Shift, and Comparator circuits. We study their scaling properties with increased qubit numbers. At equivalent transport cost for junction and linear shuttling, we show that 2D architectures outperform the 1D linear trap with the ratio improving as the number of ions increases. Finally, we discuss the use of cells, such that the entire processor is constructed from a 2D array of such interconnected cells. The work aims to optimize quantum processor architectures, implementing a co-design that fits to the specific task and scaling up in a shuttle-efficient way.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes shuttling costs in 1D vs 2D trapped ion quantum processors, showing that 2D architectures outperform 1D linear traps when junction and linear shuttling costs are equivalent, with the performance gap widening as qubit numbers increase, and discusses modular cell-based processor designs.
AI.motivation: To systematically compare the shuttling overhead of 1D linear vs 2D quantum CCD architectures in trapped ion quantum processors, and to develop cost functions that enable architecture-aware compilation of quantum algorithms.
AI.method: Introduces individual cost functions for linear shuttle and junction shuttle operations; applies these cost models to analyze the total cost of building-block quantum circuits (QFT, Carry, Adder, Shift, Comparator); studies scaling properties with increasing qubit numbers.
AI.result: At equivalent transport costs for junction and linear shuttling, 2D architectures outperform 1D linear traps, with the performance ratio improving as the number of ions increases.
AI.conclusion: The work aims to optimize quantum processor architectures through co-design approaches that match the architecture to specific tasks and scale efficiently in terms of shuttling operations, potentially using a 2D cell-based array.

title: Quantifying and Probing Multipartite Entanglement via Minimum Entanglement Drop
comment: 13 pages,4 figure.Accepted by Physical Review A
summary: Quantifying genuine multipartite entanglement remains a significant challenge. We propose a multipartite entanglement monotone defined by the minimum entanglement drop -- the reduction in global one-to-group entanglement upon tracing out a single particle. We formulate a computationally efficient variant using tangle and negativity to ensure non-vanishing values for W-class states, and rigorously prove it is a valid monotone under local operations and classical communication. In the tripartite regime, the minimum tangle drop is physically equivalent to the minimum pairwise concurrence. We establish an operational framework where the entanglement drop acts as a structural probe: by assessing sensitivity to qubit loss, it identifies inseparable clusters, extracting connectivity fingerprints that uniquely differentiate graph topologies within the same local Clifford equivalence class. Integrating this mapping with classical shadows enables efficient experimental estimation and dynamic tracking of entanglement network evolution. We derive exact analytical solutions for n-qubit W states under environmental noise, revealing robust scaling behaviors. Finally, we acknowledge limitations, noting that diagnostic sensitivity strictly vanishes for highly robust states such as the 5-qubit error-correcting code.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multipartite entanglement monotone based on minimum entanglement drop (reduction in global one-to-group entanglement when tracing out a single particle), formulates computationally efficient variants using tangle and negativity, proves its monotonicity under LOCC, establishes an operational framework for using entanglement drop as a structural probe to identify inseparable clusters and differentiate graph topologies, derives analytical solutions for n-qubit W states under noise, and acknowledges limitations for highly robust states like the 5-qubit error-correcting code.
AI.motivation: Quantifying genuine multipartite entanglement remains a significant challenge, motivating the need for new monotones that are both theoretically valid and computationally practical.
AI.method: The method defines a multipartite entanglement monotone via minimum entanglement drop, introduces computationally efficient variants using tangle and negativity, provides rigorous proof of monotonicity under LOCC, establishes operational framework linking entanglement drop to graph topology via connectivity fingerprints, and combines with classical shadows for experimental estimation.
AI.result: The minimum tangle drop in the tripartite regime is physically equivalent to minimum pairwise concurrence; exact analytical solutions for n-qubit W states under noise reveal robust scaling behaviors; the method uniquely differentiates graph topologies within the same local Clifford equivalence class; diagnostic sensitivity strictly vanishes for highly robust states such as the 5-qubit error-correcting code.
AI.conclusion: The entanglement drop framework provides a valid, computationally efficient monotone for multipartite entanglement, enables structural probing of entanglement networks, and is experimentally feasible via classical shadows, though limited for certain error-correcting code states.

title: Acceleration of Free Electrons by Photonic Time-Crystals
summary: We study the quantum interaction between free electrons and photons in a time-varying media, and find that periodic modulation exponentially amplifies electron-photon coupling within momentum gaps, enabling arbitrarily large momentum transfer. By preparing the light in a two-mode squeezed vacuum state, the electron momentum grows faster than its spectral spreading, establishing time-modulated photonic media as a platform for accelerating free-electrons and shaping their quantum state.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how time-varying photonic media with periodic modulation exponentially amplify electron-photon coupling, enabling large momentum transfer, and demonstrates that using two-mode squeezed vacuum light allows electron momentum to grow faster than spectral spreading, offering a platform for accelerating free electrons and shaping their quantum states.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to explore quantum interactions between free electrons and photons in time-varying media, specifically to understand how periodic modulation can enhance electron-photon coupling and enable significant momentum transfer, potentially leading to new methods for electron acceleration and quantum state control.
AI.method: The method involves theoretically studying the quantum interaction of free electrons and photons in time-varying media with periodic modulation. The analysis focuses on momentum gaps where coupling is amplified exponentially. The light field is prepared in a two-mode squeezed vacuum state to examine electron momentum growth relative to spectral spreading.
AI.result: The key result is that periodic modulation exponentially amplifies electron-photon coupling within momentum gaps, enabling arbitrarily large momentum transfer. Additionally, using two-mode squeezed vacuum light, the electron momentum grows faster than its spectral spreading.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that time-modulated photonic media serve as a promising platform for accelerating free electrons and shaping their quantum state.

title: Quantum Error Suppression via Symmetry-Averaged Virtual Distillation
summary: Reliable quantum simulation is limited by both algorithmic approximations and hardware noise, which usually coexist in the output of near-term and early fault-tolerant quantum devices. Existing error-suppression strategies often target these error sources separately. Here, we introduce symmetry-averaged virtual distillation (SAVD), an error-suppression protocol that applies symmetry averaging before virtual distillation and treats both imperfections at the density-matrix level. The protocol constructs a symmetry-averaged output ensemble from symmetry-labeled implementations, leaving the symmetry-invariant target contribution unchanged while averaging residual components over symmetry-related branches. Virtual distillation (VD) is then applied to this averaged ensemble, rather than to the raw output state, to amplify its dominant eigencomponent. We analyze the resulting spectral suppression mechanism and identify the role of symmetry averaging as a state-preconditioning layer for VD. Numerical demonstrations on an isotropic Heisenberg chain show improved accuracy in the presence of both coherent algorithmic errors and hardware noise. Our results provide a general symmetry-based architecture for enhancing quantum simulations.

AI.tldr: SAVD combines symmetry averaging and virtual distillation to suppress both algorithmic and hardware errors in quantum simulations, demonstrating improved accuracy on an isotropic Heisenberg chain.
AI.motivation: Existing error-suppression strategies typically target algorithmic approximations and hardware noise separately, but both coexist in near-term and early fault-tolerant quantum devices. A unified approach is needed.
AI.method: SAVD first constructs a symmetry-averaged output ensemble from symmetry-labeled implementations, leaving the symmetry-invariant target unchanged while averaging residual components. Virtual distillation is then applied to this averaged ensemble to amplify its dominant eigencomponent.
AI.result: Numerical demonstrations on an isotropic Heisenberg chain show improved accuracy in the presence of both coherent algorithmic errors and hardware noise.
AI.conclusion: SAVD provides a general symmetry-based architecture for enhancing quantum simulations by jointly suppressing both imperfection sources at the density-matrix level.

title: Fine-Tuning Large Language Models for Quantum Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit abilities beyond natural language modelling and text generation. Recent advances in their reasoning capabilities have spurred interest in applying LLMs to complex scientific tasks requiring deep domain expertise and sophisticated reasoning. Quantum computing, as a highly specialised field with significant knowledge barriers and hardware constraints, could greatly benefit from such advancements. However, a key open question that first must be answered is: How can we develop fine-tuning pipelines that instil genuine quantum reasoning in LLMs, rather than task-specific pattern matching? We study this question through quantum circuit simulation as a training objective, where the model must predict the measurement probability distribution resulting from a sequence of quantum gate operations. We propose and compare two fine-tuning pipelines: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on explicit gate-by-gate state-vector simulation traces, and (2) a two-stage SFT+Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) approach that sequentially applies SFT followed by GRPO with verifiable rewards. Our findings show that SFT achieves near-perfect in-distribution and gate-count extrapolation accuracy, significantly outperforming both the base model and the GPT-OSS-120B baseline. SFT+GRPO trades some in-distribution precision for better generalisation to larger qubit systems that SFT alone cannot handle. Both pipelines significantly outperform the baselines, demonstrating that targeted fine-tuning on explicit reasoning traces is an effective strategy for advancing quantum reasoning in LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how to instill genuine quantum reasoning in LLMs through fine-tuning pipelines using quantum circuit simulation as a training objective. Two approaches are compared: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on explicit gate-by-gate state-vector traces, and a two-stage SFT+Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) method. SFT achieves near-perfect in-distribution and extrapolation accuracy, while SFT+GRPO trades some precision for better generalization to larger qubit systems.
AI.motivation: To determine how to develop fine-tuning pipelines that instill genuine quantum reasoning in LLMs (rather than task-specific pattern matching), motivated by the potential of LLMs to assist in the specialized field of quantum computing which has significant knowledge barriers and hardware constraints.
AI.method: Two fine-tuning pipelines are proposed and compared: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on explicit gate-by-gate state-vector simulation traces, and (2) a two-stage SFT+Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) approach that sequentially applies SFT followed by GRPO with verifiable rewards. Quantum circuit simulation is used as the training objective where the model predicts measurement probability distributions from sequences of quantum gate operations.
AI.result: SFT achieves near-perfect in-distribution and gate-count extrapolation accuracy, significantly outperforming both the base model and GPT-OSS-120B baseline.
