SFT+GRPO trades some in-distribution precision for better generalization to larger qubit systems that SFT alone cannot handle. Both pipelines significantly outperform the baselines.
AI.conclusion: Targeted fine-tuning on explicit reasoning traces is an effective strategy for advancing quantum reasoning in LLMs, with SFT+GRPO offering a trade-off that enables better generalization to larger systems at the cost of some precision.

title: Detector-Grade Germanium as a Low-Disorder Host for Indium-Acceptor Spin Qubits: A Five-Qubit Materials-to-Architecture Design Study
summary: Acceptor-bound hole spins in germanium (Ge) offer a promising but underexplored route to semiconductor quantum information processing. We present a theory-guided design study of a detector-grade Ge acceptor-spin platform based on intentionally incorporated indium (In) acceptors in ultra-high-purity Ge. The proposed materials strategy combines a residual impurity background near $10^{10} \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ with a target In density of approximately $2\times10^{14} \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, corresponding to an acceptor spacing of about 170 nanometer. A 1 $μ$m-long active channel with a suitable transverse mode volume can contain about five acceptors on average, enabling a statistically selected post-fabrication register rather than a deterministically placed chain. We analyze the physical basis, device architecture, strain and disorder limits, coupling hierarchy, modeling workflow, fabrication pathway, and scaling prospects. Our results indicate that detector-grade Ge can suppress uncontrolled bulk electrostatic and strain disorder to levels compatible with acceptor-hole qubits, while the spin--orbit-active valence-band manifold supports all-electrical control and dipolar or phonon-mediated coupling. Direct exchange is treated as a close-pair or gate-enhanced interaction rather than the generic mean-spacing coupling. Phononic crystal engineering is identified as a second-stage enhancement for suppressing unwanted acoustic modes and enabling selected cavity-mediated interactions after baseline control, readout, and nearest-neighbor coupling are validated. Remaining challenges include statistical acceptor placement, interface disorder, charge noise, readout integration, and experimental validation. This work identifies detector-grade Ge In-acceptor qubits as a credible intermediate architecture between donor-based impurity qubits and fully gate-defined Ge hole-spin hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a theory-guided design study of a detector-grade germanium (Ge) acceptor-spin quantum information platform using intentionally incorporated indium acceptors. With ultra-high-purity Ge (~10¹⁰ cm⁻³ residual impurities) and a target In density of ~2×10¹⁴ cm⁻³ (170 nm spacing), a 1 μm active channel contains ~5 acceptors on average. The work analyzes the physical basis, device architecture, strain/disorder limits, coupling hierarchy, modeling, fabrication, and scaling, concluding that detector-grade Ge can suppress disorder to levels compatible with acceptor-hole qubits, supporting all-electrical control and dipolar/phonon-mediated coupling.
AI.motivation: Acceptor-bound hole spins in germanium are a promising but underexplored route to semiconductor quantum information processing. The authors aim to bridge the gap between donor-based impurity qubits and fully gate-defined Ge hole-spin qubits by proposing a detector-grade Ge platform with intentional indium acceptors.
AI.method: The study employs a theory-guided design approach, analyzing the detector-grade Ge materials platform (ultra-high purity, controlled In doping), device architecture (1 μm active channel), strain and disorder limits, coupling hierarchy (exchange, dipolar, phonon-mediated), and a modeling workflow. The platform relies on statistical rather than deterministic acceptor placement.
AI.result: Detector-grade Ge can suppress uncontrolled bulk electrostatic and strain disorder to levels compatible with acceptor-hole qubits. The spin-orbit-active valence-band manifold enables all-electrical control and dipolar/phonon-mediated coupling, while direct exchange is treated as a close-pair or gate-enhanced interaction. Phononic crystal engineering is identified as a second-stage enhancement.
AI.conclusion: Detector-grade Ge In-acceptor qubits represent a credible intermediate architecture between donor-based impurity qubits and fully gate-defined Ge hole-spin hardware. Remaining challenges include statistical acceptor placement, interface disorder, charge noise, readout integration, and experimental validation.

title: Iterative quantum phase estimation with cQED encoding
summary: Quantum phase estimation is a cornerstone algorithm for determining eigenvalues of unitary operators or Hamiltonians with Heisenberg-limited precision. Conventional implementations rely on deep controlled-unitary operations together with an inverse quantum Fourier transform, resulting in substantial circuit depth and hardware overhead. Here, we propose a conceptually simple and experimentally feasible alternative that exploits the toolbox of circuit quantum electrodynamics. The protocol extracts the phase through a sequence of binary threshold tests, eliminating the need for an inverse quantum Fourier transform. A bosonic mode serves as an efficient quantum memory in which the binary digits of the phase are encoded into the direction of phase-space rotations. These digits are then read out sequentially via high-fidelity homodyne measurements. We show that the protocol achieves Heisenberg scaling in estimation precision while simultaneously providing exponentially suppressed failure probability. By replacing the ancillary circuit with a bosonic degree of freedom, the scheme significantly reduces hardware complexity and offers a practical route toward implementing high-precision quantum phase estimation on circuit quantum electrodynamics platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new quantum phase estimation protocol using circuit quantum electrodynamics that avoids deep controlled-unitary circuits and inverse quantum Fourier transform by encoding phase digits into bosonic mode rotations and reading them via homodyne measurements, achieving Heisenberg scaling with exponentially suppressed failure probability and reduced hardware complexity.
AI.motivation: Conventional quantum phase estimation requires deep controlled-unitary operations and an inverse quantum Fourier transform, leading to substantial circuit depth and hardware overhead that hinder practical implementation.
AI.method: The protocol replaces ancillary qubit circuits with a bosonic mode as quantum memory, extracts phase through binary threshold tests (eliminating inverse QFT), encodes binary digits of the phase into the direction of phase-space rotations of the bosonic mode, and reads them out sequentially via high-fidelity homodyne measurements.
AI.result: The protocol achieves Heisenberg-limited scaling in estimation precision while simultaneously providing exponentially suppressed failure probability, with significantly reduced hardware complexity compared to conventional approaches.
AI.conclusion: The scheme offers a practical, experimentally feasible route toward implementing high-precision quantum phase estimation on circuit quantum electrodynamics platforms by trading deep ancillary circuits for a bosonic degree of freedom.

title: Optimizing Pump Conditions of Parametric Amplifiers for Fast Multiplexed Readout of Superconducting Qubits
summary: Low-noise parametric amplifiers are widely used as the first-stage amplifier in qubit readout chains. The performance of parametric amplifiers depends sensitively on the choice of the pump condition. We propose a strategy for determining the pump condition that is tailored for fast multiplexed readout. Choosing the amplifier pump to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvement at the readout frequency of the limiting qubit--the qubit that requires the longest readout time to reach a target SNR--minimizes the total multiplexed readout time. We demonstrate our pump calibration strategy experimentally on a five-qubit multiplexed readout chain with a traveling-wave parametric amplifier. Using our strategy, we reduce the multiplexed readout time by 320 ns compared to optimizing the average SNR improvement on all qubits, without degrading the target SNR for any qubit.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a pump calibration strategy for parametric amplifiers that maximizes SNR improvement at the readout frequency of the limiting qubit (the one needing the longest readout time), thereby minimizing total multiplexed readout time. Experimental demonstration on a five-qubit system shows a 320 ns time reduction without degrading SNR.
AI.motivation: Parametric amplifiers are critical for qubit readout, but their performance depends sensitively on pump conditions. Existing pump optimization strategies (e.g., maximizing average SNR) are not tailored for fast multiplexed readout, where the slowest qubit determines total time.
AI.method: The strategy optimizes the amplifier pump to maximize SNR improvement specifically at the readout frequency of the limiting qubit—the qubit that requires the longest readout time to reach a target SNR. This is experimentally validated on a five-qubit multiplexed readout chain using a traveling-wave parametric amplifier.
AI.result: Using the proposed strategy, multiplexed readout time was reduced by 320 ns compared to optimizing the average SNR improvement across all qubits, without degrading the target SNR for any qubit.
AI.conclusion: Tailoring the pump condition to the limiting qubit is an effective and practical strategy for minimizing multiplexed readout time in superconducting qubit systems.

title: Transient Information Partition in Coherent Exciton-Phonon-Photon Dynamics
summary: We study transient information partition in a coherent exciton-phonon-photon system using subsystem-resolved quantum mutual information (QMI). By employing a model with excitonic, phononic, and photonic degrees of freedom, we analyze the dynamics in the $J$-$ν$ plane, where $J$ characterizes excitonic delocalization and $ν$ denotes the exciton-phonon coupling strength. By comparing time-averaged QMI maps with the absorbed photon number, we show that optical activity alone does not determine the character of the light-induced transient state. The exciton-centered information partition identifies a broad crossover between polariton-like and polaron-like transient responses, depending on whether excitonic information is mainly shared with the photon or phonon subsystem. In contrast, the phonon-centered partition reveals a sharper boundary-adjacent redistribution ridge near the boundary between the zero- and one-exciton ground-state sectors. This ridge is absent from both the ground-state sector map and the photon-absorption map, indicating that it is neither a static sector boundary nor an enhancement of optical absorption. A variational strength-function analysis connects the ridge to a region-II-like finite-energy polaronic excitation whose dominant spectral weight lies near the one-phonon energy, and thus the ridge represents a hidden transient correlation structure in which a limited amount of phonon-related information is preferentially shared with the photon subsystem before being predominantly allocated to exciton-phonon dressing. These results show that QMI-based information partition provides a correlation-based framework for characterizing coherent light-induced transient states in which optical and material degrees of freedom jointly participate quantum mechanically.

AI.tldr: Using subsystem-resolved quantum mutual information (QMI), the study analyzes transient information partitioning in a coherent exciton-phonon-photon system, revealing hidden correlation structures beyond optical absorption alone.
AI.motivation: To understand how quantum information is partitioned among excitonic, phononic, and photonic subsystems in light-induced transient states, and to determine whether optical activity alone can characterize these states.
AI.method: Subsystem-resolved quantum mutual information (QMI) analysis in the J-ν plane (excitonic delocalization vs. exciton-phonon coupling), combined with time-averaged QMI maps, absorbed photon number analysis, and variational strength-function analysis.
AI.result: Optical activity alone does not determine transient state character; exciton-centered partition reveals a broad polariton-like to polaron-like crossover; phonon-centered partition shows a sharp boundary-adjacent redistribution ridge absent from ground-state and absorption maps, linked to a region-II-like finite-energy polaronic excitation near one-phonon energy.
AI.conclusion: QMI-based information partition provides a correlation-based framework for characterizing coherent light-induced transient states where optical and material degrees of freedom jointly participate quantum mechanically.

title: Spectral and thermodynamic properties of supersymmetric quantum systems with self-adjoint deformed momentum
summary: We establish a rigorous framework for quantum systems with geometric deformations by constructing a strictly self-adjoint deformed momentum operator through the generalized extended momentum operator (GEMO) formalism. Unlike previous approaches relying on boundary-condition hermiticity, our method ensures intrinsic self-adjointness for both linear ($μ(x)=αx$) and quadratic ($μ(x)=αx^{2}$) deformations within a unified non-Hermitian supersymmetric factorization scheme. This yields exact analytical spectra while revealing hidden $\mathfrak{su}(1,1)$ symmetry structures. Crucially, we provide the first complete thermodynamic characterization of such systems by analytically evaluating the partition function via the Euler--Maclaurin approximation. Geometric deformation fundamentally reshapes the density of states $ρ(E)$, producing distinct thermal signatures: a divergent heat capacity peak for linear deformation due to state accumulation near a maximal energy, and a saturation $C/k_{\mathrm{B}}\to 0.6$ (below the Dulong--Petit limit) for quadratic deformation. These results establish geometric deformation as a tunable parameter for engineering quantum thermodynamic responses in curved nanostructures.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a rigorous self-adjoint formulation for quantum systems with geometric deformations using the GEMO formalism, derives exact spectra revealing hidden $\mathfrak{su}(1,1)$ symmetry, and provides the first complete thermodynamic characterization where linear deformation yields a divergent heat capacity peak and quadratic deformation saturates $C/k_{\mathrm{B}}\to 0.6$, establishing geometric deformation as a tunable thermodynamic parameter.
AI.motivation: To establish a rigorous self-adjoint framework for quantum systems with geometric deformations, overcoming limitations of previous boundary-condition hermiticity approaches, and to provide the first complete thermodynamic characterization of such deformed systems.
AI.method: Construction of a strictly self-adjoint deformed momentum operator via the generalized extended momentum operator (GEMO) formalism, combined with non-Hermitian supersymmetric factorization for both linear ($\mu(x)=\alpha x$) and quadratic ($\mu(x)=\alpha x^2$) deformations. The partition function is analytically evaluated using the Euler–Maclaurin approximation.
AI.result: Exact analytical spectra with hidden $\mathfrak{su}(1,1)$ symmetry structures are obtained. For linear deformation: a divergent heat capacity peak from state accumulation near a maximal energy. For quadratic deformation: saturation of heat capacity at $C/k_{\mathrm{B}}\to 0.6$, below the Dulong–Petit limit.
AI.conclusion: Geometric deformation serves as a tunable parameter for engineering quantum thermodynamic responses in curved nanostructures, with distinct thermal signatures depending on the deformation type.

title: Emergence of Boolean Facts from Markovian Coarse-Graining in Relational Quantum Causal Processes
comment: Under review at Letters in Mathematical Physics
summary: We formulate an operator-algebraic mechanism by which exact Boolean records can arise from local completely positive quantum operations without being imposed as microscopic structure. The kinematic input is an algebraic process functional assigning probabilities to local normal completely positive operations in a finite operational context. From the predual response of a target algebra to source interventions, relative to a background strategy class, we define an influence algebra; exact events are then, by definition, the projections in its center. The dynamical question is whether nontrivial centers can be generated by coarse-graining rather than inserted through split-record laboratories. We address this question using state-preserving normal unital completely positive coarse-graining channels. If the Cesaro means of such a channel converge to a Choi-Effros infrared range and the range is asymptotically abelian in the GNS seminorm, then the represented infrared algebra is a commutative von Neumann algebra. Its projection lattice is therefore a complete Boolean algebra. We also give a finite-sector block-primitive criterion, motivated by locality and scrambling, which implies this asymptotic abelianness with exponential suppression of off-sector coherences and intra-sector fluctuations. The result is a conservative mathematical statement: classical facts are not identified with arbitrary projections of a Type-III local algebra, but with central projections selected by an asymptotically abelian completely positive infrared limit.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an operator-algebraic framework where exact Boolean (classical) records emerge from local quantum operations through coarse-graining, rather than being assumed as primitive structure. The authors show that under certain conditions (Cesàro convergence of coarse-graining channels to a Choi-Effros infrared range that is asymptotically abelian), the resulting infrared algebra is a commutative von Neumann algebra, whose projection lattice forms a complete Boolean algebra.
AI.motivation: To explain how classical Boolean records—typically assumed as microscopic structure or imposed via split-record laboratory setups—can emerge dynamically from purely local completely positive quantum operations, without ad hoc classical assumptions at the fundamental level.
AI.method: The paper (1) defines an algebraic process functional assigning probabilities to local normal CP operations; (2) constructs an influence algebra from the predual response of a target algebra to source interventions; (3) identifies exact events as central projections; (4) studies state-preserving normal unital CP coarse-graining channels; (5) analyzes Cesàro means converging to a Choi-Effros infrared range; (6) establishes asymptotic abelianness in the GNS seminorm; and (7) provides a finite-sector block-primitive criterion for locality and scrambling that ensures exponential suppression of off-sector coherences.
AI.result: When the Cesàro means of a coarse-graining channel converge to a Choi-Effros infrared range and this range is asymptotically abelian in the GNS seminorm, the represented infrared algebra is a commutative von Neumann algebra, whose projection lattice is a complete Boolean algebra. A finite-sector block-primitive criterion, motivated by locality and scrambling, yields asymptotic abelianness with exponential suppression of off-sector coherences and intra-sector fluctuations.
AI.conclusion: Classical facts are not arbitrary projections of a Type-III local algebra; instead, they are central projections selected by an asymptotically abelian completely positive infrared limit. This provides a conservative mathematical mechanism for the emergence of exact Boolean records from quantum operations.

title: StableShots: Online Shot Stopping for Quantum Circuit Execution
summary: Quantum circuit execution estimates output distributions by repeated measurements, yet developers commonly choose a fixed shot budget before execution. This static choice is brittle: low budgets can under-sample the distribution, while high budgets waste measurements. In this paper, we present StableShots, a black-box online stopping rule for static quantum circuits. The method executes a fixed circuit in small batches, monitors the total-variation distance between cumulative empirical distributions, and stops after repeated evidence of local stability. We evaluate StableShots on 180 QSimBench traces spanning six circuit families, six sizes from 4 to 14 qubits, and five noisy IBM simulated backends. With validation-only calibration and 100 repeated backend-holdout splits, the selected configuration reaches TVD <= 0.05 on all held-out test evaluations with median 7,650 shots, whereas fixed-shot baselines either fail more often or spend substantially more shots.

AI.tldr: StableShots is a black-box online stopping rule for quantum circuits that adaptively determines the number of measurement shots by monitoring empirical distribution stability in batches, achieving TVD ≤ 0.05 with median 7,650 shots across 180 circuit benchmarks, outperforming fixed-shot baselines in both accuracy and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Static shot budgets for quantum circuit execution are brittle: low budgets under-sample the distribution, while high budgets waste measurements. Developers need an adaptive method to determine when sufficient shots have been collected.
AI.method: StableShots executes a fixed circuit in small batches, monitors the total-variation distance (TVD) between cumulative empirical distributions across batches, and stops after repeated evidence of local stability. Calibration uses validation-only data with 100 repeated backend-holdout splits.
AI.result: Evaluated on 180 QSimBench traces (six circuit families, 4–14 qubits, five noisy IBM backends). The selected configuration reaches TVD ≤ 0.05 on all held-out test evaluations with median 7,650 shots, outperforming fixed-shot baselines that either fail more often or spend substantially more shots.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive shot allocation via online stability monitoring is both more reliable and more efficient than fixed-shot budgets for quantum circuit output distribution estimation.

title: Fundamental Irreversibility from Discrete Time
summary: In 1964, Yu. A. Gol'fand proposed an extension of quantum mechanics to discrete time, predicting intrinsic non-unitarity and entropy increase. While historically significant, this formalism predates the modern theory of open quantum systems. In this work, we rigorously recast Gol'fand's discrete evolution equation as a Completely Positive Trace-Preserving (CPTP) quantum channel and derive its continuous-time coarse-grained limit. We demonstrate that the dynamics converge to a specific Lindblad master equation characterized by a fundamental time scale $τ$, which induces decoherence in both the energy basis and a fundamental operator basis $W$. We analyze the thermodynamic implications using Spohn's entropy production formalism, proving that the discrete time step induces a strictly positive entropy production rate driven by the decay of quantum coherences, thereby providing a microscopic foundation for the arrow of time independent of environmental coupling. Furthermore, we quantify the loss of quantum coherence via fidelity decay and purity loss, establishing exact constraints for fault-tolerant quantum computing. We further investigate the impact of this intrinsic decoherence on Discrete Time Crystals (DTCs), showing that Gol'fand dynamics impose a fundamental lifetime limit on time-translation symmetry breaking phases. Finally, we utilize precision data from optical lattice clocks, matter-wave interferometry, and neutrino oscillations to place stringent upper bounds on $τ$. Our results constrain the fundamental time discretization to $τ\lesssim 10^{-26}$ s, significantly tightening previous limits and offering a testable framework for quantum gravity phenomenology.

AI.tldr: This paper recasts Gol'fand's discrete-time quantum mechanics as a CPTP channel, derives its Lindblad master equation limit, proves it yields positive entropy production (providing a microscopic arrow of time), analyzes implications for fault-tolerant quantum computing and discrete time crystals, and places an upper bound τ ≲ 10⁻²⁶ s using precision experiments.
AI.motivation: To rigorously reformulate Gol'fand's 1964 discrete-time quantum formalism within modern open quantum systems theory, and to explore its thermodynamic, computational, and phenomenological consequences.
AI.method: Recasting Gol'fand's discrete evolution as a CPTP quantum channel; deriving continuous-time coarse-grained limit to a Lindblad master equation; applying Spohn's entropy production formalism; analyzing fidelity decay, purity loss; using data from optical lattice clocks, matter-wave interferometry, and neutrino oscillations to bound τ.
AI.result: The discrete time step τ induces decoherence in the energy basis and a fundamental operator basis W; strictly positive entropy production rate emerges from coherence decay; fundamental lifetime limits for DTCs are established; τ ≲ 10⁻²⁶ s is obtained from experimental data.
AI.conclusion: Gol'fand dynamics provide a testable framework for quantum gravity phenomenology, with an intrinsic arrow of time independent of environment coupling, and impose constraints relevant for quantum computing and time crystal stability.

title: Probing the Weak-Driving Quantum Speed Limit via Drift-Aware Shooting Methods
summary: A central goal of quantum optimal control is to achieve high-fidelity and low-energy control pulses. When quantum optimal control methods optimize every point of a pulse discretized over small time steps independently this can yield high fidelity control but also results in broadband and energy-hungry waveforms. We extend MAGICARP -- a shooting method inspired by Pontryagin's maximum principle on energy that generates an entire pulse from a small set of parameters, making it smooth and energy-efficient by construction -- from driftless systems to closed systems with the constant drift Hamiltonian of two exchange-coupled spins in an external magnetic field. The optimization proceeds in stages: the dressed states of the drift Hamiltonian structure the target, an initial shooting optimization is performed in the rotating-wave frame, and an exact laboratory-frame refinement follows. Benchmarked against Krotov and GRAPE at matched gate infidelity, MAGICARP consistently achieves the lowest energy and a conserved pulse area, concentrates its spectral weight on the gate-relevant transitions, and is the most robust to fluctuations in the exchange coupling; GRAPE independently converges to essentially the same pulse, while Krotov's method pays an order-of-magnitude energy premium. Moreover, a large statistical survey of unselected optimization runs resolves a weak-driving quantum speed limit for two exchange-coupled electron spins: low-amplitude realizations of the two-qubit quantum Fourier transform cease to exist below a critical gate time $T^*$ set by the drift's interaction rate, and the minimum control energy diverges on approach to this limit. The divergence obeys a simple two-parameter area-pole law, $E_2^{\mathrm{law}}(T)=A/T+B/(T-T^*)$, whose first term is the time-optimal area cost and whose second term is a pole at the speed limit.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the MAGICARP method for quantum optimal control to exchange-coupled spins in a magnetic field, achieving smooth, energy-efficient pulses that are robust and approach a quantum speed limit where control energy diverges following a two-parameter area-pole law.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum optimal control methods optimize each time step independently, yielding high-fidelity but broadband, energy-hungry pulses. The goal is to generate smooth, energy-efficient pulses with minimal parameters while maintaining high fidelity.
AI.method: MAGICARP, a shooting method based on Pontryagin's maximum principle, is extended from driftless to closed systems with constant drift (exchange-coupled spins in external magnetic field). Optimization proceeds in stages: dressed states structure the target, initial shooting in rotating-wave frame, then exact laboratory-frame refinement. Benchmarked against Krotov and GRAPE.
AI.result: MAGICARP achieves lowest energy and conserved pulse area, concentrates spectral weight on gate-relevant transitions, and is most robust to exchange coupling fluctuations. GRAPE converges to essentially the same pulse; Krotov pays an order-of-magnitude energy premium. A weak-driving speed limit T* is discovered below which low-amplitude realizations of the two-qubit QFT cease to exist.
AI.conclusion: The minimum control energy diverges approaching T* following a two-parameter area-pole law E(T)=A/T+B/(T-T*), with the first term being time-optimal area cost and the second a pole at the speed limit.

title: Collective Mpemba-Type Relaxation in Degenerate Bosonic Modes Coupled to a Common Thermal Reservoir
summary: We investigate collective Mpemba-type relaxation in a degenerate family of bosonic modes coupled to a common thermal reservoir. Starting from a fully symmetric M-mode description and employing a representative mean-field reduction, we derive effective master equations for weak-coupling Markovian, strong-coupling Caldeira-Leggett, and weak-coupling non-Markovian regimes. In the weak-coupling Markovian limit, relaxation separates into an incoherent thermal channel decaying at rate gamma and a collective coherent channel decaying at rate M gamma, yielding an explicit Mpemba crossing time determined by the initial-state preparation. In the strong-coupling Caldeira-Leggett regime, transient quadrature dynamics enriches the relaxation pattern, delaying crossings in the overdamped sector and generating multiple crossings in the underdamped sector. In the non-Markovian regime, reservoir memory reshapes the same channel-competition mechanism through time-dependent decay rates and a Lamb shift, producing delayed and clustered crossing windows. Numerical results based on the energy and the Kullback-Leibler divergence reveal Mpemba and anti-Mpemba behavior, criterion dependence, and multiple transient reorderings induced by collective coherence, quadrature dynamics, and reservoir memory.

AI.tldr: The paper studies collective Mpemba-type relaxation in a family of bosonic modes coupled to a common thermal reservoir. Analyzing three regimes (weak-coupling Markovian, strong-coupling Caldeira-Leggett, and weak-coupling non-Markovian), it finds that relaxation dynamics involve competing decay channels, leading to Mpemba and anti-Mpemba effects, multiple crossings, and criterion-dependent transient reorderings.
AI.motivation: To understand how collective effects, coherence, quadrature dynamics, and reservoir memory influence Mpemba-type relaxation (where a hotter system cools faster than a colder one) in a bosonic multi-mode system.
AI.method: The authors start from a fully symmetric M-mode description, employ a mean-field reduction, and derive effective master equations for three regimes: weak-coupling Markovian, strong-coupling Caldeira-Leggett, and weak-coupling non-Markovian. They analyze relaxation via energy and Kullback-Leibler divergence.
AI.result: In the weak-coupling Markovian regime, relaxation separates into an incoherent thermal channel (decay rate γ) and a collective coherent channel (decay rate Mγ), yielding an explicit Mpemba crossing time dependent on initial state. In the strong-coupling Caldeira-Leggett regime, transient quadrature dynamics produce delayed crossings in the overdamped sector and multiple crossings in the underdamped sector. In the non-Markovian regime, time-dependent decay rates and a Lamb shift generate delayed and clustered crossing windows. Numerical results show Mpemba and anti-Mpemba behavior, criterion dependence, and multiple transient reorderings.
AI.conclusion: Collective coherence, quadrature dynamics, and reservoir memory significantly enrich Mpemba-type relaxation, leading to multiple crossings and criterion-dependent effects beyond simple single-mode scenarios.

title: Probing Single-Particle Spatial Extent With Helical Neutron Wavefronts
summary: Distinguishing transverse coherence length from single-particle wavepacket extent is fundamentally challenging, as both manifest through spatial broadening of observed intensity profiles in conventional experiments. Here we introduce a method based on helical neutron wavefronts that enables this separation. Helical neutron states produce annular intensity profiles whose peak radius depends on the transverse wavepacket extent, while coherence length only contributes to profile broadening. In our experimental geometry we measure a beam divergence of ~1.1 mrad, corresponding to a transverse coherence length of ~180 nm. In contrast, the same measurement places a lower bound of >= 2 um on the spatial extent of the individual neutron wavepackets, more than an order of magnitude larger than the coherence length. These results provide direct experimental evidence that transverse coherence length and single-particle wavepacket extent are distinct physical quantities, resolving a longstanding source of confusion in the neutron literature.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a method using helical neutron wavefronts to separately measure transverse coherence length and single-particle wavepacket extent. Results show the wavepacket extent (≥2 μm) is an order of magnitude larger than the coherence length (~180 nm), proving they are distinct physical quantities.
AI.motivation: Distinguishing transverse coherence length from single-particle wavepacket extent has been fundamentally challenging, as both manifest as spatial broadening in conventional experiments, causing longstanding confusion in the neutron literature.
AI.method: The method uses helical neutron wavefronts, where annular intensity profiles have a peak radius dependent on transverse wavepacket extent, while coherence length only contributes to profile broadening, enabling separation of the two quantities.
AI.result: Measured beam divergence of ~1.1 mrad (transverse coherence length ~180 nm) and a lower bound of ≥2 μm for single-particle wavepacket extent, showing the latter is more than an order of magnitude larger.
AI.conclusion: Transverse coherence length and single-particle wavepacket extent are distinct physical quantities, resolving a longstanding source of confusion in neutron literature.

title: The Physics Behind Symmetrization
comment: Forthcoming in a special issue of Entropy (Quantum Mereologies and Quantum Inspired Set Theories and Logics)
summary: It is often asserted that quantum states for same-type particles must be symmetrized due to ``label redundancy,'' i.e. the assumption that the permutations of labels in direct-product states do not reflect any real physical distinction and thus their permutations constitute an ``exchange degeneracy''. This assumption is directly challenged by the case of scattering of same-type particles such as electrons, which involves two physically distinct scattering channels effectively corresponding to permutation of the labels. I discuss this counterexample with critical attention to an extant portrayal in the literature that omits pertinent physical content. I further note ways in which the assumption that symmetrization must be universally imposed is not supported by actual calculations of particle interactions, nor by seemingly viable particle states based on preparations and outcomes.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the necessity of symmetrizing quantum states for identical particles, arguing that the assumption of "label redundancy" is contradicted by physically distinct scattering channels (e.g., electron-electron scattering) and is not supported by actual calculations of particle interactions or by states based on preparations and outcomes.
AI.motivation: To critically examine and challenge the long-held assumption that quantum states for identical particles must be symmetrized due to "label redundancy" or "exchange degeneracy."
AI.method: The author presents the counterexample of scattering of same-type particles (e.g., electrons), which involves two physically distinct scattering channels that effectively correspond to label permutation, and critically reviews how the literature has portrayed this issue while omitting pertinent physical content.
AI.result: The assumption of universal symmetrization is not supported by actual calculations of particle interactions, nor by seemingly viable particle states based on preparations and outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The necessity of universally imposing symmetrization on identical particle states is questionable, as it conflicts with physically meaningful distinctions in scattering processes and lacks support from practical calculations and state preparation considerations.

title: Making Quantum Networks Work: Routing, Calibration, and Programmable Quantum Repeaters
summary:
The quantum internet enables distribution of quantum states across distant nodes, supporting secure communication, distributed computing, and quantum sensing. Unlike classical networks, it is constrained by the no cloning theorem, probabilistic entanglement generation, decoherence, and hardware drift, making classical abstractions inadequate. Scalable quantum networking therefore requires new architectures, protocols, and optimisation methods that explicitly account for these limitations.
  This thesis studies the architecture, routing, and operation of quantum networks under realistic constraints, focusing on bipartite entanglement distribution over quantum repeater networks. Key metrics include end to end fidelity, throughput, scalability, and fairness. At the network layer, routing strategies are developed beyond assumptions of homogeneous nodes and full network knowledge. Routing under heterogeneous repeater efficiencies shows how partial knowledge of node quality improves fidelity and reduces path blocking. A grey box routing approach is then introduced, where path selection relies only on topology and end to end estimates, achieving robustness and fairness without detailed link information.
  At the link layer, calibration and hardware drift are addressed through a calibration aware model separating activation and calibration phases. For linear repeater chains, an optimal calibration schedule is derived to balance operation time and calibration overhead. This is extended to general topologies with shared links, where a greedy orchestration heuristic is proposed.
  Finally, the thesis connects network protocols with hardware via an instruction set architecture for programmable quantum repeater nodes based on NV centers, enabling coherent programmability and linking physical operations to higher layer protocols.

AI.tldr: This thesis develops architectures, routing protocols, and operational strategies for scalable quantum repeater networks under realistic constraints such as heterogeneity, decoherence, and hardware drift. It introduces grey-box routing, calibration-aware link-layer scheduling, and an instruction set architecture for programmable NV-center-based nodes.
AI.motivation: Classical networking abstractions fail under quantum constraints (no-cloning, probabilistic entanglement, decoherence, hardware drift). Scalable quantum networking requires new architectures and methods that explicitly address these limitations.
AI.method: (1) Network layer: routing strategies under heterogeneous repeater efficiencies and grey-box routing using topology and end-to-end estimates. (2) Link layer: calibration-aware model separating activation and calibration phases, with optimal scheduling for linear chains and greedy orchestration for general topologies. (3) Hardware-software interface: instruction set architecture for programmable NV-center-based repeater nodes.
AI.result: Partial knowledge of node quality improves fidelity and reduces path blocking. Grey-box routing achieves robustness and fairness without detailed link information. Optimal calibration schedules balance operation time and overhead. Greedy orchestration extends to general topologies with shared links.
AI.conclusion: Practical quantum networking requires cross-layer co-design spanning heterogeneous routing, calibration-aware link management, and programmable hardware abstractions to enable scalable bipartite entanglement distribution.

title: No Reference-Free Generalization in Quantum Machine Learning
summary: Quantum machine learning is often motivated by the exponentially large state space of quantum systems, but this promise leaves a basic generalization problem unresolved: how can a learner assign different meanings to unseen quantum directions when the training data provide no preferred basis, measurement frame, or other orienting structure? We address this identifiability problem by formulating supervised learning without an external quantum reference frame, so that predictions cannot depend on an arbitrary choice of Hilbert-space coordinates. This requirement forces the learned classifier to preserve every unitary symmetry left unbroken by the training data. We prove that whenever the training states fail to span the full Hilbert space, all pure states orthogonal to their span must receive the same prediction -- even when those states are mutually orthogonal and perfectly distinguishable once an appropriate measurement is supplied. The limitation is therefore not caused by state discrimination, optimization, or computational power, but by missing reference information. We further establish a robust version under weak symmetry breaking and show that learning generic unstructured concepts on multiqubit systems requires exponentially many independently oriented training directions. Numerical illustrations visualize the resulting prediction collapse and its controlled relaxation. Our results identify feature maps, measurement bases, Hamiltonians, locality, symmetry priors, architectures, and sufficiently diverse training states as operational resources for generalization. The central implication is that Hilbert-space dimension alone is not a learnable feature space: successful QML must specify the physical structure that gives unseen quantum directions semantic meaning.

AI.tldr: Without an external quantum reference frame, supervised learning in Hilbert space suffers an identifiability problem: any pure state orthogonal to the training data's span must receive the same prediction, even if those states are perfectly distinguishable. This implies that Hilbert-space dimension alone is not a sufficient feature space; QML requires explicit physical structure (e.g., preferred bases, symmetries, locality) to generalize.
AI.motivation: Quantum machine learning promises advantages from exponentially large Hilbert spaces, but lacks a basic principle: how can a learner assign different meanings to unseen quantum directions when training data provide no preferred basis, measurement frame, or orienting structure? This missing reference information causes a fundamental identifiability problem.
AI.method: The paper formulates supervised learning without an external quantum reference frame, enforcing that predictions cannot depend on arbitrary Hilbert-space coordinates. This symmetry requirement forces the learned classifier to preserve all unitary symmetries unbroken by the training data. The analysis includes proofs of prediction collapse, a robust version under weak symmetry breaking, and scaling arguments for multiqubit systems.
AI.result: All pure states orthogonal to the training span receive identical predictions regardless of distinguishability. Learning generic unstructured concepts on multiqubit systems requires exponentially many independently oriented training directions. Numerical experiments illustrate the prediction collapse and its controlled relaxation.
AI.conclusion: Hilbert-space dimension alone is not a learnable feature space. Successful QML must specify physical structure—feature maps, measurement bases, Hamiltonians, locality, symmetry priors, architectures, and sufficiently diverse training data—that gives unseen quantum directions semantic meaning.

title: Lattice-quantile estimation of π and convex-region integrals from coined two-dimensional quantum walks
summary: Monte Carlo integration is fundamentally limited by the M^(-1/2) rate that the Cramer-Rao bound imposes on any sample-mean estimator of an expectation value, regardless of how the samples are drawn. Coined discrete-time quantum walks (DTQWs) are known to spread ballistically - their position variance scales as T^2 against the diffusive T of classical random walks - yet this faster spreading has not been exploited for numerical integration. We show that coupling the ballistic scaling of a 2D DTQW to the Hardy-Huxley asymptotic for Gauss circle lattice counts produces estimators whose dominant error is a deterministic number-theoretic residual controlled by walk depth T, not a statistical fluctuation controlled by sample count M. The construction replaces the empirical mean of a sample-mean estimator with the ratio N(R-hat)/R-hat^2 of a lattice count to the square of a radial position quantile, a structural change that sidesteps the Cramer-Rao barrier. A single batch of measurements then propagates through classically precomputed multipliers to cover an entire family of integrals simultaneously. We develop the framework for convex smooth domains via Kraetzel's lattice asymptotic and for smooth integrals with convex or annular super-level sets via Cavalieri's principle, and provide a parameter-free identity for the bias floor (validated to within 1.5x across all tested depths). Every experiment is benchmarked against the classical random walk with the identical estimator to isolate the quantum contribution; the framework is oracle-free in the QAE sense (no controlled unitary encoding the integrand is required) and structurally distinct from quantum amplitude estimation and Szegedy-walk approaches. These ratios compare measurement counts at fixed precision and do not include quantum circuit execution cost.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a novel Monte Carlo integration method using 2D discrete-time quantum walks (DTQWs) that bypasses the classical M^(-1/2) statistical convergence barrier by replacing empirical sample means with deterministic lattice-count ratios, achieving error controlled by walk depth rather than sample count.
AI.motivation: Monte Carlo integration is limited by the Cramer-Rao bound's M^(-1/2) convergence rate for sample-mean estimators, regardless of sampling strategy. The ballistic spreading of DTQWs (variance ~ T^2) has not been exploited for numerical integration, presenting an opportunity to overcome this fundamental limitation.
AI.method: The method replaces the empirical mean of sample-mean estimators with N(R̂)/R̂² — the ratio of a lattice count to the square of a radial position quantile — coupling the ballistic scaling of 2D DTQWs to the Hardy-Huxley asymptotic for Gauss circle lattice counts. A single measurement batch propagates through classically precomputed multipliers to cover entire families of integrals. The framework handles convex smooth domains via Kraetzel's lattice asymptotic and smooth integrals via Cavalieri's principle, with a parameter-free identity for the bias floor.
AI.result: The dominant error becomes a deterministic number-theoretic residual controlled by walk depth T, not a statistical fluctuation controlled by sample count M, sidestepping the Cramer-Rao bound. The bias floor identity is validated to within 1.5× across all tested depths. Benchmarks against classical random walks with identical estimators isolate the quantum contribution, showing improved measurement count ratios at fixed precision.
AI.conclusion: This DTQW-based integration framework is structurally distinct from quantum amplitude estimation and Szegedy-walk approaches, is oracle-free (no controlled unitary encoding the integrand), and offers a fundamentally different scaling regime where deterministic errors dominate over statistical fluctuations, potentially enabling faster numerical integration.

title: Probabilistic Storage and Retrieval of Quantum Superchannels for "Retrospective'' Intervention
summary: Storing an unknown quantum computation in a quantum state and retrieving it at a desired later time is a challenging task, hindered by the no-programming theorem of quantum computations. In the previous studies on the task of probabilistic storage-and-retrieval (pSAR) of quantum channels, the maximum probability of exactly retrieving a single unknown unitary channel from a quantum state in which the unknown unitary has been encoded via multiple calls to the unknown unitary channel is derived. In this work, we consider a higher-order version of pSAR, the probabilistic storage-and-retrieval of definite-causal unitary superchannels, which are physically modeled by sequences of unitary channels with open slots where arbitrary channels can be inserted between the unitary channels for intervention. This task requires activating the ``retrospective'' intervention functionality on the superchannel, beyond its normal intervention functionality. We propose two protocols: partial teleportation, which is optimal for a small number of storage queries, and staircase backstitch, which achieves unit success probability asymptotically as the number of queries increases. We also derive a universal inversion protocol for unitary superchannels.

AI.tldr: This paper studies probabilistic storage-and-retrieval (pSAR) of definite-causal unitary superchannels, proposing two protocols—partial teleportation (optimal for few queries) and staircase backstitch (asymptotically perfect)—and deriving a universal inversion protocol for unitary superchannels.
AI.motivation: To extend the probabilistic storage-and-retrieval framework from unitary channels to higher-order operations (unitary superchannels), enabling retrospective intervention on sequences of unitary channels with open slots.
AI.method: Two protocols are proposed: (1) partial teleportation, optimal for small numbers of storage queries, and (2) staircase backstitch, which achieves unit success probability asymptotically. Additionally, a universal inversion protocol for unitary superchannels is derived.
AI.result: Partial teleportation achieves optimal success probability for few queries; staircase backstitch approaches unit success probability as the number of queries grows. A universal inversion protocol for unitary superchannels is also derived.
AI.conclusion: The work generalizes pSAR to higher-order quantum operations, providing protocols with provable performance and a universal inversion technique, advancing the understanding of quantum memory for unknown computations.

title: Vibe Calibration: Autonomous Bring-up of a 112-Qubit Superconducting Quantum Processor by a Skill-Orchestrating Language Agent
summary: Superconducting quantum computing is one of the most mature solid-state platforms for quantum computation, with processors exceeding one hundred qubits. Yet further scaling toward fault-tolerant quantum computing is increasingly constrained by calibration complexity. Conventional scripts are brittle to anomalous signals, and expert judgment is bounded by cognitive bandwidth and serial operation time, failing to keep pace with system scale. Here we report Vibe Calibration, an autonomous calibration system orchestrated by large language model agents, which distills expert tacit knowledge into reusable Skills. Each Skill is organized as a decision tree that packages parameterized measurement commands, quantitative acceptance criteria, and audit records, enabling autonomous execution and self-healing. We capture this knowledge through a three-phase human-in-the-loop distillation process and fine-tune a large language model on validated trajectories. On a 112-qubit processor with frequency-tunable transmons, the system autonomously completes calibration of 108 out of 112 qubits in 4.7 hours, achieving a 4--5$\times$ speedup over manual calibration of the full 112 qubits. A cross-validated comparison with expert manual calibration on a 16-qubit subset shows agreement on 14 out of 16 qubits. More importantly, the model demonstrates transferable calibration workflows across devices. While low-level control scripts require minor interface adaptation for different hardware platforms, the core decision logic and task orchestration generalize to new processors, demonstrating a reusable laboratory interface rather than a memorized script.This work demonstrates, for the first time, fully autonomous calibration of a hundred-qubit superconducting processor through reusable and auditable Skills, removing a critical barrier to scalable quantum hardware operation.

AI.tldr: Vibe Calibration is an autonomous calibration system for superconducting quantum processors, orchestrated by LLM agents, that distills expert tacit knowledge into reusable Skills. It achieves 4-5× speedup over manual calibration on a 112-qubit processor, completing 108/112 qubits in 4.7 hours, and demonstrates transferable workflows across devices.
AI.motivation: Conventional calibration scripts are brittle to anomalous signals, and expert judgment is bounded by cognitive bandwidth and serial operation time, failing to keep pace with the scaling of quantum processors beyond one hundred qubits. This creates a critical barrier to fault-tolerant quantum computing.
AI.method: The system distills expert tacit knowledge into reusable Skills via a three-phase human-in-the-loop distillation process. Each Skill is organized as a decision tree with parameterized measurement commands, quantitative acceptance criteria, and audit records. A fine-tuned LLM agent orchestrates autonomous execution and self-healing.
AI.result: On a 112-qubit processor with frequency-tunable transmons, the system autonomously calibrated 108/112 qubits in 4.7 hours (4-5× speedup). Cross-validation on a 16-qubit subset showed agreement with expert manual calibration on 14/16 qubits. The model demonstrated transferable calibration workflows across different hardware platforms.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates the first fully autonomous calibration of a hundred-qubit superconducting processor through reusable and auditable Skills, removing a critical barrier to scalable quantum hardware operation and showing that the core decision logic and task orchestration generalize to new processors.

title: Quantum Otto engine with decoupled idle levels in a non-Hermitian XY model
summary: We study a quantum Otto cycle in a two-qubit non-Hermitian XY model with a staggered imaginary magnetic field. The energy spectrum of this system naturally decouples into a pair of working levels that depend on the external field and a pair of idle levels that are completely independent of it, thereby providing the first concrete microscopic realization of the idle-level quantum heat engine architecture proposed by de~Oliveira and Jonathan [Phys. Rev. E 104, 044133 (2021)] in a physical spin model. Tuning the non-Hermitian parameter eta_0 drives a continuous transition from a dissipative regime with negative net work and net heat absorption from the hot reservoir into a genuine heat engine mode, while simultaneously enhancing both output work and efficiency. As eta_0 increases within the stable PT-unbroken phase, the engine efficiency rises significantly, reaching a substantial fraction of the Carnot limit. This effect originates from the compression of the idle-level gap, which redistributes the level occupation weights in the hot and cold equilibrium states and thereby modulates the absorbed heat. The numerator of the net work expression is independent of eta_0, but the denominator depends on eta_0 indirectly through hyperbolic cosine functions -- this is the mathematical root of the idle-level control mechanism. We provide a detailed analysis of the robustness of these findings against parameter variations, a critical comparison of the non-Hermitian control with the Hermitian limit, and a concrete experimental proposal for trapped-ion quantum simulators. Our results demonstrate that non-Hermiticity serves as an indispensable tool for steering both the operation mode and the performance of a quantum engine.

AI.tldr: This paper realizes the idle-level quantum heat engine architecture in a two-qubit non-Hermitian XY model with a staggered imaginary magnetic field. By tuning the non-Hermitian parameter, the system transitions from a dissipative regime to a genuine heat engine with enhanced efficiency approaching the Carnot limit, due to compression of the idle-level gap that redistributes occupation weights. The effect is demonstrated analytically and via a trapped-ion experimental proposal.
AI.motivation: To provide the first concrete microscopic realization of the idle-level quantum heat engine architecture (proposed by de Oliveira and Jonathan) in a physical spin model, and to explore whether non-Hermiticity can serve as a control tool for steering the operation mode and performance of quantum thermal machines.
AI.method: A quantum Otto cycle is analyzed in a two-qubit non-Hermitian XY model with a staggered imaginary magnetic field. The energy spectrum decouples into working levels (field-dependent) and idle levels (field-independent). The non-Hermitian parameter η₀ is tuned to control the idle-level gap, modulating level occupation weights and absorbed heat. Analytical expressions for work and efficiency are derived and compared with the Hermitian limit.
AI.result: Tuning η₀ drives a continuous transition from a dissipative regime (negative net work) to a genuine heat engine mode, simultaneously enhancing output work and efficiency. Efficiency rises significantly within the stable PT-unbroken phase, reaching a substantial fraction of the Carnot limit. The net work numerator is η₀-independent, but the denominator depends on η₀ via hyperbolic cosine functions, mathematically enabling idle-level control.
AI.conclusion: Non-Hermiticity is an indispensable tool for controlling both the operation mode and the performance of quantum heat engines. The findings are robust against parameter variations and are experimentally realizable in trapped-ion quantum simulators.

title: A Three-Layer Architecture for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
summary: Fault tolerance is an indispensable prerequisite for constructing large-scale universal quantum computers. Drawing philosophies from classical computer architecture, this paper presents a hardware-agnostic three-layer high-level architectural framework for generic fault-tolerant quantum computation. Guided by the real execution workflows of fault-tolerant quantum algorithms, the proposed model is decoupled from specific physical qubit hardware platforms and quantum error correction codes, serving as a universal abstract standard rather than a platform-specific implementation scheme. Special attention is devoted to the intermediate Fault-Tolerance Layer, which serves as the architectural bridge between application-level logical programs and hardware-level execution. We systematically characterize its five internal components, the interfaces and data exchanged among them, and the execution, correction, and adaptation paths that together enable logical synthesis, fault-tolerant resources management, decoding, and runtime fault-tolerant control. An end-to-end example is further provided to illustrate the full-stack operating pipeline of fault-tolerant quantum algorithms under this framework. Given the increasing emphasis on modular, heterogeneous, and cross-layer fault-tolerant quantum systems, our architecture provides a unified foundational model for organizing such designs.

AI.tldr: A hardware-agnostic three-layer architectural framework for generic fault-tolerant quantum computation is proposed, with a detailed focus on the intermediate Fault-Tolerance Layer that bridges logical programs and hardware execution, featuring five internal components for logical synthesis, resource management, decoding, and runtime control.
AI.motivation: Fault tolerance is essential for large-scale universal quantum computers, and a unified, hardware-agnostic architectural model is needed to organize increasingly modular, heterogeneous, and cross-layer fault-tolerant quantum systems.
AI.method: Drawing from classical computer architecture, the paper presents a three-layer high-level framework decoupled from specific physical qubit platforms and quantum error correction codes, systematically characterizing the intermediate Fault-Tolerance Layer with five internal components, interfaces, and execution/correction/adaptation paths.
AI.result: A universal abstract architectural standard for fault-tolerant quantum computation is established, with an end-to-end example illustrating the full-stack operating pipeline under this framework.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architecture provides a unified foundational model for organizing modular, heterogeneous, and cross-layer fault-tolerant quantum systems, serving as a universal abstract standard rather than a platform-specific implementation scheme.

title: Hierarchy of mixed symmetry protected topological states in extended cluster states under subsystem decoherence
summary: We study the effect of subsystem decoherence to an extended cluster state which is a symmetry protected topological (SPT) phase. The model includes many subsystem $Z_2$ symmetries. We report that subsystem decoherence induces local charge fluctuations, leading to a mixed SPT state in the unaffected subsystems. If we start from the extended cluster state, hierarchical mixed-state SPT phases emerge in response to step-by-step subsystem decoherences. These mixed-state SPT phases keep strong symmetries the symmetry of which is protecting symmetries for the initial cluster SPT. Moreover, these SPTs can be characterized by Rényi-2 string orders. Then, as the subsystems are progressively decohered, the hierarchy of mixed-state SPT phases terminates in a $Z_2$ strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SWSSB) state on the final remaining subsystem, where a long-range entangled state appears, namely a glassy Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state. Our work demonstrates that decoherence is not merely a destructive process, but can induce and organize series of nontrivial mixed-states. This reveals a systematic route from mixed-state SPT order to SWSSB with the glassy GHZ-type long-range entanglement.

AI.tldr: Subsystem decoherence in an extended cluster SPT state induces hierarchical mixed-state SPT phases characterized by Rényi-2 string orders, culminating in a Z2 strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SWSSB) state with glassy GHZ long-range entanglement.
AI.motivation: To understand how decoherence, rather than being purely destructive, can systematically induce and organize nontrivial mixed-state quantum phases, specifically exploring the transition from mixed-state SPT order to SWSSB.
AI.method: The authors study an extended cluster state with multiple subsystem Z2 symmetries under step-by-step subsystem decoherence, analyzing the resulting mixed states via strong symmetries, Rényi-2 string order parameters, and the emergence of SWSSB.
AI.result: Subsystem decoherence induces hierarchical mixed-state SPT phases preserving strong symmetries; these phases are characterized by Rényi-2 string orders. Progressive decoherence terminates in a Z2 SWSSB state, which is a glassy GHZ-type long-range entangled state.
AI.conclusion: Decoherence can systematically generate a hierarchy of mixed-state topological orders, bridging SPT phases and SWSSB with glassy long-range entanglement, revealing a structured route from mixed-state SPT to symmetry-broken entangled states.

title: Geometric Response in Open Quantum Systems: Coherence, Curvature, and Susceptibility
summary: We develop a response-geometric framework for open quantum systems by decomposing the stationary-state response tensor into symmetric and antisymmetric sectors. The symmetric sector defines a metric-like response tensor governing local susceptibility, while the antisymmetric sector defines a curvature two-form associated with nonreciprocal response and geometric work. We show that the work curvature is precisely the antisymmetric component of the response tensor, establishing a fluctuation--response relation that extends the geometric structure of equilibrium thermodynamics to nonequilibrium steady states, and reveals a response geometry with both metric and symplectic sectors. In equilibrium, the antisymmetric sector vanishes by reciprocity, recovering the familiar metric geometry of thermodynamic response. Open quantum systems admit a broader structure in which reciprocal and nonreciprocal responses coexist on the same control manifold. We illustrate this with a driven dissipative qubit under pure dephasing, where finite curvature emerges from the misalignment between the Hamiltonian eigenbasis and the pointer basis selected by the environment, without requiring strong driving or engineered reservoirs. Comparison with the Bures metric shows that response geometry and information geometry characterize distinct properties of the stationary-state manifold: the former governs susceptibility and geometric work, the latter quantifies state distinguishability. Geometric work thus emerges as a measurable signature of nonreciprocal response in open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a response-geometric framework for open quantum systems, decomposing the stationary-state response tensor into metric (symmetric, reciprocal) and symplectic (antisymmetric, nonreciprocal) sectors. It shows the antisymmetric sector defines work curvature, establishes a fluctuation-response relation for nonequilibrium steady states, and illustrates geometric work in a driven dissipative qubit under pure dephasing.
AI.motivation: To extend the geometric structure of equilibrium thermodynamics (where response is purely metric and reciprocal) to nonequilibrium steady states of open quantum systems, where nonreciprocal responses emerge and a broader geometric framework with both metric and symplectic sectors is needed.
AI.method: Decompose the stationary-state response tensor into symmetric (metric-like) and antisymmetric (curvature two-form) components. Establish a fluctuation-response relation linking the antisymmetric sector to geometric work. Compare with the Bures metric to distinguish response geometry from information geometry. Illustrate with a driven dissipative qubit under pure dephasing.
AI.result: The antisymmetric component of the response tensor defines work curvature, establishing a fluctuation-response relation for nonequilibrium steady states. In a driven dissipative qubit, finite curvature emerges from misalignment between Hamiltonian eigenbasis and the pointer basis selected by the environment, without requiring strong driving or engineered reservoirs. Response geometry and information geometry characterize distinct properties of the stationary-state manifold.
AI.conclusion: Geometric work emerges as a measurable signature of nonreciprocal response in open quantum systems. The framework reveals that open quantum systems admit a coexistence of reciprocal and nonreciprocal responses on the same control manifold, generalizing equilibrium thermodynamic geometry.

title: Liouvillian Geometry of Multidimensional Spectra: Pathway Transport and Observational Holonomy in Open Quantum Systems
summary: Liouville pathways provide the conceptual foundation for interpreting multidimensional spectroscopies, yet are typically treated as fixed objects that evolve independently between optical interactions. In open quantum systems, this picture is incomplete. Environmental interactions continuously redistribute amplitude among pathways during every free-evolution interval, generating transport that leaves measurable signatures in the nonlinear spectroscopic response. We develop a geometric framework in which pathway transport is governed by a Liouvillian connection, its associated curvature, and the resulting observational holonomy. The framework applies to open quantum systems in which the environment selects a pointer basis distinct from the observational basis used to construct the spectroscopic response. This basis incompatibility induces transport among Liouville pathways, generating characteristic spectral distortions and a nontrivial Liouvillian curvature. Using a Duhamel expansion of the Liouvillian propagator, we derive a reconstruction procedure that identifies the transport operators responsible for the observed redistribution of pathway weight, accurate throughout the full range of basis misalignment. This perspective reframes spectral features as determined not only by which pathways exist but by how amplitude is transported among them. Spectral distortions, peak shifts, and otherwise-forbidden pathway contributions become geometric signatures of a curved Liouville-space manifold rather than phenomenological broadening corrections, identifying pathway geometry as a complementary layer of organization in nonlinear spectroscopy.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a geometric framework for understanding how environmental interactions cause amplitude redistribution among Liouville pathways during multidimensional spectroscopy, introducing the concepts of Liouvillian connection, curvature, and observational holonomy to explain spectral distortions as geometric signatures rather than phenomenological corrections.
AI.motivation: The standard Liouville pathway framework treats pathways as fixed, independently evolving objects between optical interactions, which is incomplete for open quantum systems where environmental interactions continuously redistribute amplitude among pathways during free-evolution intervals.
AI.method: The authors develop a geometric framework where pathway transport is governed by a Liouvillian connection with associated curvature and observational holonomy. They employ a Duhamel expansion of the Liouvillian propagator to derive a reconstruction procedure that identifies transport operators responsible for observed pathway weight redistribution.
AI.result: Basis incompatibility between the environment's pointer basis and the observational basis induces transport among Liouville pathways, generating characteristic spectral distortions and nontrivial Liouvillian curvature. The reconstruction procedure accurately identifies transport operators across the full range of basis misalignment.
AI.conclusion: Spectral distortions, peak shifts, and otherwise-forbidden pathway contributions are reframed as geometric signatures of a curved Liouville-space manifold rather than phenomenological broadening corrections, identifying pathway geometry as a complementary organizational layer in nonlinear spectroscopy.

title: The Quantum Hamming Bound in Arbitrary Local Dimension
summary: The quantum Hamming bound is the finite-length sphere-packing count for exact quantum error correction: the code dimension times the number of correctable local error patterns must fit inside the ambient Hilbert space. For nondegenerate codes this follows from disjoint error spheres. Degeneracy is the only obstruction, because distinct physical errors can coincide on the code subspace and turn sphere packing into an overcount. The central finite-length question has been whether this overcount can ever invalidate the Hamming inequality. Earlier linear-programming, asymptotic, and structural results left a pointwise finite-length problem for arbitrary exact subspace codes. Writing $Q=q^2$ for the Hamming-scheme alphabet, the nonbinary range begins at $Q=9$; here we prove the bound for every $q\ge3$, while the binary endpoint is governed by a distinct $Q=4$ charging geometry. For every nontrivial exact subspace code in this range, any possible violation reduces to a two-center Hamming-ball intersection inequality normalized by the Lloyd response. For $q\ge4$, the Lloyd-square linear program has a uniform half-gap after reduction to alphabet $Q\ge16$ and critical length $n=4t+1$. Qutrits form the boundary: the half-gap disappears, but the bridge is handled by a quadratic-filtered Lloyd square, an exact coefficient-certificate reduction, and a Stein-tangent positivity argument. Thus degeneracy may merge error sectors, but not enough to beat the Hamming count. This proves the nonbinary part of the finite-length quantum Hamming bound; together with the independent binary endpoint theorem, it gives the result in arbitrary local dimension.

AI.tldr: This paper proves the finite-length quantum Hamming bound for all nonbinary quantum error-correcting codes (q≥3), showing that degeneracy cannot produce enough overcount to violate the sphere-packing bound, with qutrits (q=3) as the critical boundary case requiring specialized techniques.
AI.motivation: The central open question is whether degeneracy (where distinct physical errors coincide on the code subspace) can ever invalidate the Hamming inequality for exact subspace codes in the finite-length regime, since this effect turns sphere-packing into an overcount.
AI.method: The proof reduces any possible violation to a two-center Hamming-ball intersection inequality normalized by the Lloyd response. For q≥4, a uniform half-gap is obtained via the Lloyd-square linear program after reduction to alphabet Q≥16 and critical length n=4t+1. For q=3 (qutrits), the half-gap disappears and is handled by a quadratic-filtered Lloyd square, exact coefficient-certificate reduction, and Stein-tangent positivity argument.
AI.result: The nonbinary part of the finite-length quantum Hamming bound is proved for every q≥3. Together with the binary endpoint theorem, this gives the result for arbitrary local dimension.
AI.conclusion: Degeneracy may merge error sectors, but not enough to beat the Hamming count, thus the quantum Hamming bound holds for all exact subspace codes in arbitrary local dimension.

title: Hierarchical Logical Processor on the Rotated Surface Code with Shuttle Buses
summary: Quantum platforms with beyond-planar connectivity provide new opportunities for fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC). While quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes offer high encoding efficiency, their direct implementation requires non-local couplings in every round of syndrome extraction, incurring additional physical error and implementation complexity. To reduce the frequency of such couplings, we propose the Hierarchical Logical Processor (HLP), which concatenates a high-rate quantum CSS code with the rotated surface code (RSC). HLPs can achieve beyond-RSC encoding efficiency while requiring long-range connectivity only once every $Θ(d_0)$ rounds of level-0 error correction, where $d_0$ denotes the base-code distance, substantially reducing the frequency of non-local couplings relative to direct implementations of qLDPC codes. HLPs introduce elongated RSC patches called shuttle buses. Using transversal hybrid-unit CNOT gates, a single shuttle bus can simultaneously couple to multiple standard RSC patches. This capability enables efficient level-1 syndrome extraction with suppressed level-1 error correlations and supports highly parallel logical Pauli measurements. We perform circuit-level simulations of several concrete HLP constructions and benchmark both logical memory and logical Pauli measurement performance. At a physical error rate of $10^{-3}$, an HLP based on the [[256,194,4]] code achieves 3-4 times higher qubit efficiency than the standard RSC. Compared with the yoked surface code on the same level-1 code, this HLP reduces the space overhead per logical qubit by 100-200 physical qubits and shortens the logical error-correction cycle time by a factor of 20-30.

AI.tldr: Proposes the Hierarchical Logical Processor (HLP), which concatenates high-rate quantum CSS codes with the rotated surface code, achieving beyond-surface-code encoding efficiency while requiring long-range connectivity only once every Θ(d₀) rounds, with simulations demonstrating 3-4× higher qubit efficiency at 10⁻³ physical error rate and 20-30× faster logical error-correction cycles compared to yoked surface codes.
AI.motivation: Quantum platforms with beyond-planar connectivity offer new FTQC opportunities, but direct qLDPC code implementation requires non-local couplings in every syndrome extraction round, incurring additional physical error and complexity. The goal is to reduce the frequency of such non-local couplings while maintaining high encoding efficiency.
AI.method: Proposes HLP that concatenates a high-rate quantum CSS code (level-1) with the rotated surface code (level-0). Introduces elongated RSC patches called shuttle buses that use transversal hybrid-unit CNOT gates to simultaneously couple to multiple standard RSC patches, enabling efficient level-1 syndrome extraction with suppressed error correlations and highly parallel logical Pauli measurements.
AI.result: At 10⁻³ physical error rate, an HLP based on the [[256,194,4]] code achieves 3-4× higher qubit efficiency than standard RSC. Compared to yoked surface code on the same level-1 code, this HLP reduces space overhead per logical qubit by 100-200 physical qubits and shortens logical error-correction cycle time by factor of 20-30.
AI.conclusion: HLP substantially reduces the frequency of non-local couplings relative to direct qLDPC implementations (requiring long-range connectivity only once every Θ(d₀) rounds), while achieving beyond-RSC encoding efficiency, making it a promising architecture for fault-tolerant quantum computation on platforms with limited beyond-planar connectivity.

title: Generalization of catability for parity-less cat states
summary: We extend the nullifier-based certification framework of catability from parity-defined coherent cat states to parity-less Kerr cat states. Since Kerr cats cannot be distinguished by parity alone, we replace the parity component of the original nullifier with a displaced-parity operator that captures their characteristic interference structure. The resulting generalized catability remains directly observable and can be evaluated from a finite number of photon-number measurements without full state tomography. Numerical benchmarks show that the method faithfully certifies Kerr-cat features, produces accurate approximations of ideal Kerr cat states, and is more resilient to optical loss than fidelity-based certification. We also identify an exact anti-linear nullifier based on complex conjugation, providing an ideal algebraic description of Kerr cat states. Our results broaden the scope of catability and provide an experimentally practical approach to the characterization of Kerr cat states.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes the nullifier-based certification framework (catability) from parity-defined coherent cat states to parity-less Kerr cat states by replacing parity with a displaced-parity operator. The method is experimentally practical, loss-resilient, and can be evaluated from finite photon-number measurements without full tomography. An exact anti-linear nullifier based on complex conjugation is also identified.
AI.motivation: Existing certification methods (catability) apply only to parity-defined coherent cat states.
