AI.method: Density functional formalism with Kohn-Sham equation solved via generalized pseudospectral method; work function-based exchange potential; Wigner and LYP correlation functionals; analysis of Shannon entropy (position and momentum spaces), Fisher information, Fisher-Shannon plane, and Collin's conjecture.
AI.result: Energy increases with decreasing potential width; S_r exhibits minima while S_p and I_r show maxima; potential depth amplifies these effects. The Fisher-Shannon plane indicates progressive electronic density localization and compression, weakening relative electron correlation effects. A non-linear loop-like feature emerges in Collin's conjecture.
AI.conclusion: Gaussian confinement allows controlled manipulation of electronic energies and density distributions; the combined analysis of Shannon entropy, Fisher information, and correlation functionals provides a comprehensive picture of confinement-induced electronic structure changes; many results are presented for the first time.

title: Structure-Aware Variance Reduction for Unbiased Randomized Hamiltonian Simulation
summary: Randomized Hamiltonian simulation methods are often governed by a trade-off between systematic bias and sampling overhead. We study how classical variance-reduction techniques can be applied to such methods without changing their mean channel, and therefore without introducing additional bias. As a motivating unbiased estimator, we formulate continuous time-evolution probabilistic angle interpolation (continuous TE-PAI), a quasiprobabilistic random-circuit protocol whose remaining Monte Carlo error is purely statistical. Continuous TE-PAI removes Trotter discretization error with finite-depth random circuits, whereas deterministic Trotterization does so only in the infinite-depth limit. Further, in tensor-network simulations, we demonstrate that discretization error can cause an unphysical exponential growth in the bond dimension required for Trotterized simulations, whereas comparable-depth continuous TE-PAI circuits avoid this growth. We then show that the variance of randomized product-formula-based estimators admits a canonical decomposition into a classical counting component and a quantum ordering component such that the dominant simulation overhead results from the non-commutative parts of the Hamiltonian dynamics. Motivated by this decomposition, we achieve an $\approx70\%$ error-reduction using the counting-component for small systems whereas our tensor-network simulations of $n=30$ spin-chain dynamics use coarser statistics tailored to the observable and estimator attaining a negligible bias and a reduction of $\approx 80\%$ leading to $\approx91\%$ and $\approx96\%$ sampling-cost reductions, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces continuous TE-PAI, a bias-free randomized Hamiltonian simulation method that removes Trotter error with finite-depth circuits. It decomposes variance into classical counting and quantum ordering components, enabling variance reduction techniques that achieve ~70-80% error reduction and ~91-96% sampling cost reductions in tensor-network simulations.
AI.motivation: Randomized Hamiltonian simulation methods suffer from a trade-off between systematic bias (e.g., Trotter discretization error) and sampling overhead. The authors aim to apply classical variance-reduction techniques without introducing additional bias, and to understand the sources of variance in randomized product-formula-based estimators.
AI.method: The authors formulate continuous TE-PAI (time-evolution probabilistic angle interpolation), a quasiprobabilistic random-circuit protocol with purely statistical Monte Carlo error. They decompose the variance of randomized product-formula estimators into a classical counting component and a quantum ordering component. Classical variance-reduction techniques are applied to the counting component without changing the mean channel, thus avoiding bias.
AI.result: Continuous TE-PAI removes Trotter discretization error with finite-depth random circuits, avoiding the exponential bond dimension growth seen in deterministic Trotterized tensor-network simulations. Variance decomposition reveals that dominant overhead comes from non-commutative Hamiltonian parts. Experiments show ~70% error reduction for small systems and ~80% error reduction for n=30 spin-chain dynamics, yielding ~91% and ~96% sampling-cost reductions respectively.
AI.conclusion: Classical variance-reduction techniques can be effectively applied to randomized Hamiltonian simulation without introducing additional bias. The variance decomposition provides clear guidance for optimizing sampling overhead, and continuous TE-PAI offers a practical, bias-free alternative to Trotterization in tensor-network simulations.

title: Genuine Global Kochen-Specker Contextuality as Classical Coordination Cost
comment: Comments and suggestions are welcome on alphaXiv
summary: Classical simulations of quantum correlations can fail because no low-communication local hidden-variable model exists, or because no single noncontextual hidden state can explain all compatible measurement contexts. This manuscript studies a third regime: genuine global Kochen-Specker contextuality, where local subsystems are noncontextual and the tested multipartite blocks are generalized-Bell-local, but the whole empirical model admits no global noncontextual hidden-variable explanation. We propose a coordination-cost framework in which communication, memory, and local computation are treated as different ways for a classical simulator to maintain a global classical explanation from locally available information. We introduce coordination bits, global contextual covering numbers, scaling laws for task families, and an abstract lifting theorem showing how classical simulation lower bounds for KS-contextual seed families can be transferred to genuinely global-KS models. As worked examples, we analyze a polarization-path Hardy obstruction and postselected KCBS-type tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a third regime of quantum contextuality—genuine global Kochen-Specker (KS) contextuality—where local subsystems are noncontextual and tested blocks are generalized-Bell-local, yet no global noncontextual hidden-variable model exists. A coordination-cost framework is proposed treating communication, memory, and computation as resources for classical simulation, with concepts including coordination bits, global contextual covering numbers, scaling laws, and a lifting theorem. Examples include a polarization-path Hardy obstruction and postselected KCBS-type tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing work on quantum contextuality focuses on either non-locality (requiring communication) or Kochen-Specker contextuality (requirement of noncontextual hidden variables). This paper identifies a missing regime: genuine global Kochen-Specker contextuality, where local subsystems are individually noncontextual and multipartite blocks are generalized-Bell-local, but the whole empirical model is globally contextual. The goal is to characterize and quantify this phenomenon using classical simulation resources.
AI.method: The authors propose a coordination-cost framework that quantifies classical simulation resources (communication, memory, local computation) needed to reproduce quantum correlations. They introduce: (1) coordination bits—the minimal information exchange required for a classical simulator; (2) global contextual covering numbers—a measure of how many noncontextual fragments are needed; (3) scaling laws for task families; (4) an abstract lifting theorem that transfers lower bounds from KS-contextual seed families to genuinely global-KS models.
AI.result: The paper presents worked examples: a polarization-path Hardy obstruction and postselected KCBS-type tasks, demonstrating that these systems exhibit genuine global KS contextuality despite local noncontextuality and block-wise Bell locality. The coordination-cost framework provides lower bounds on classical simulation resources needed to replicate the observed correlations.
AI.conclusion: Genuine global Kochen-Specker contextuality is a distinct phenomenon from both Bell nonlocality and standard KS contextuality. The coordination-cost framework offers a systematic way to quantify classical simulation overhead, with the lifting theorem enabling transfer of lower bounds across model families. This opens new avenues for understanding quantum-classical separations in terms of coordination resources.

title: Random dimension reduction and learning symmetric properties of quantum states
summary:
We introduce a procedure called random dimension reduction that simultaneously reduces the dimensions of many, potentially distinct quantum states while preserving properties invariant under the tensor power action of an isometry. This provides a black-box method to replace the dimension with the maximum rank in the sample complexity of learning symmetric properties, even those depending on multiple input states. We show that dimension reduction followed by full state tomography yields improved upper bounds for estimating distances, fidelities, and relative entropies between pairs of states. We also give an efficient quantum circuit implementation of the procedure using the Schur transform.
  Expressing the action of our procedure through the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism reveals an intimate connection with the recently introduced random purification channel by Tang, Wright, and Zhandry. This perspective also completes an end-to-end analysis of sample-optimal tomography without requiring a reference to the Schur transform or Schur polynomials. Finally, we prove that there does not exist a random purification channel that simultaneously purifies copies of multiple, potentially different input states. Hence, random dimension reduction is related to, but distinct from, random purification.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a random dimension reduction procedure that reduces dimensions of quantum states while preserving tensor power invariants, enabling improved sample complexity bounds for learning symmetric properties and connecting to (but distinct from) random purification.
AI.motivation: To develop a black-box method that replaces dimension with maximum rank in the sample complexity of learning symmetric properties of quantum states, particularly for tasks involving multiple input states where direct tomography is costly.
AI.method: Introduces random dimension reduction via the Schur transform, which reduces dimensions of multiple quantum states while preserving isometry-invariant properties. The procedure is analyzed through the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism, revealing connections to the random purification channel.
AI.result: Improved upper bounds for estimating distances, fidelities, and relative entropies between pairs of states; an efficient quantum circuit implementation using the Schur transform; a complete end-to-end analysis of sample-optimal tomography without reference to Schur polynomials; and a proof that no random purification channel can simultaneously purify multiple distinct input states.
AI.conclusion: Random dimension reduction is a useful tool for learning symmetric quantum properties with improved sample complexity, and while related to random purification, it is fundamentally distinct in its ability to handle multiple input states.

title: A quantum algorithm for one-shot signatures
summary: We provide a pre-obfuscation circuit-level implementation of an efficient one shot signature scheme, which has known applications to delegated signatures, secured token transfer, and publicly verifiable randomness. The algorithm consists of two stages: a key generation stage where a classical public key/quantum secret key pair is produced, and a signing stage where the quantum secret key is processed with a message string to produce a classical signature. There is no algorithmic error in the construction and the signed message can be efficiently checked by a classical verifier. Our scheme works by preparing a superposition over elements of a random affine coset determined by the output of a puncturable pseudorandom function, together with a circuit that tests coset membership. The logical qubit number scales like $Θ( κ\log(r) + n + l)$ and the gate complexity scales like $Θ(n^3 + nl)$, where $r$ is the public key size, $n+l$ is the signature size, $l$ is the message size, and $κ= Ω(n)$ is the cryptographic security parameter. We provide explicit qubit and gate counts for varying $n$ and identify the circuit components where obfuscation would be required for security against classical and quantum polynomial time attacks.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a pre-obfuscation circuit-level implementation of an efficient one-shot signature scheme, featuring classical public key/quantum secret key generation and classical signature production, with explicit qubit and gate complexity analysis.
AI.motivation: To provide a concrete, error-free circuit implementation of a one-shot signature scheme with applications to delegated signatures, secured token transfer, and publicly verifiable randomness, while analyzing the specific components requiring obfuscation for security.
AI.method: The scheme uses a two-stage algorithm (key generation and signing), preparing a superposition over elements of a random affine coset determined by a puncturable pseudorandom function, combined with a coset membership testing circuit.
AI.result: Logical qubit count scales as Θ(κ log(r) + n + l) and gate complexity as Θ(n³ + nl), with explicit counts provided for varying n. The scheme has no algorithmic error and supports efficient classical verification.
AI.conclusion: The implementation identifies circuit components that require obfuscation to achieve security against classical and quantum polynomial-time attacks, providing a concrete pathway for building one-shot signature schemes.

title: Log-concavity and tunneling: adiabatic quantum optimization for convex functions (with a spike)
summary:
Quantum tunneling is expected to provide a computational speedup in quantum computing, a phenomenon that Adiabatic Quantum Optimization (AQO) aims to leverage. While some academic proofs of concept have been studied, such as the "Hamming weight with a spike" (HWS) problem, the algorithmic gains of this effect remain underexplored. In this work we extend the analysis underlying HWS to more general potentials.
  In the first half of the work, we establish (discrete) log-concavity of the ground state as a key structural property in this context. We devise a framework for establishing log-concavity of the ground state for a large family of discrete, 1-dimensional Schrödinger operators. The family includes convex potentials, but also certain potentials with local minima. In the convex case, this provides a discrete version of a continuous result by Brascamp and Lieb ('76). We demonstrate the utility of our result by establishing new spectral gap bounds, going beyond related results by Jarret and Jordan ('14) for convex potentials.
  In the second half of the work, we use our results on log-concavity to extend the perturbative analysis of HWS by Reichardt ('04) to the larger family of potentials with log-concave ground state. As a concrete instantiation, we use our result to extend the HWS analysis from a linear potential (which is exactly solvable) to a quadratic potential (which is no longer solvable). Our result strongly suggests the broader applicability of tunneling to convex potentials with spikes

AI.tldr: This work extends the analysis of quantum tunneling speedups in Adiabatic Quantum Optimization (AQO) from the "Hamming weight with a spike" (HWS) problem to more general potentials. The authors establish discrete log-concavity of the ground state as a key structural property for a large family of 1D Schrödinger operators, including convex potentials and some with local minima. They prove new spectral gap bounds using this property, and extend the perturbative analysis of HWS to potentials with log-concave ground states, demonstrating tunneling effects in convex potentials with spikes (e.g., quadratic potential).
AI.motivation: Quantum tunneling is expected to provide a computational speedup in adiabatic quantum optimization, but beyond specific proof-of-concept problems like the Hamming weight with a spike (HWS), the algorithmic gains of this effect remain underexplored. This work aims to extend the theoretical understanding to more general potentials.
AI.method: The paper establishes discrete log-concavity of the ground state for a large family of discrete, 1-dimensional Schrödinger operators, including convex potentials and certain potentials with local minima. This provides a discrete analog of a continuous result by Brascamp and Lieb ('76). Using log-concavity, the authors then extend the perturbative analysis of HWS (Reichardt '04) to the larger family of potentials with log-concave ground state, and demonstrate the extension from a linear potential (exactly solvable) to a quadratic potential (no longer solvable).
AI.result: New spectral gap bounds are established, going beyond related results by Jarret and Jordan ('14) for convex potentials. The analysis of tunneling in HWS is extended from linear potentials to quadratic potentials, strongly suggesting the broader applicability of tunneling to convex potentials with spikes.
AI.conclusion: Log-concavity of the ground state is a key structural property enabling the analysis of tunneling speedups in AQO for a broader class of potentials beyond exactly solvable cases. The results strongly suggest that quantum tunneling benefits extend to convex potentials with spikes.

title: Genuine certification of incompatible quantum instruments through sequential communication tasks
summary: Quantum instruments constitute the general description of quantum dynamics, encompassing both quantum measurements and quantum channels as special cases. Consequently, the incompatibility of quantum instruments represents a fundamental manifestation of nonclassicality in quantum theory. Here, we establish the operational significance of this notion by demonstrating communication tasks with classical inputs and outputs that enable the semi-device-independent certification of incompatible quantum instruments. We introduce a class of three-party communication tasks involving a sender, a relayer, and a receiver, and derive the tight upper bound of the figure of merits of these tasks achievable by all compatible instruments implemented by the relayer and this bound coincides with the optimal performance attainable in a classical communication subject to the same dimensional constraints. Violation of this bound certifies the incompatibility of the pair of quantum instruments implemented by the relayer. This identifies certification of incompatible instruments as a manifestation of quantum advantage in communication. This certification protocol is genuine as it is able to certify the incompatibility of a pair of instruments where the measurements and channels induced by the instruments are pairwise compatible and, therefore it does not depend on the incompability of measurements and channels induced by the instruments. Finally, we identify the simplest instances of our communication scenario that enable the certification of incompatible quantum instruments.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a semi-device-independent certification protocol for incompatible quantum instruments using three-party communication tasks, achieving a tight upper bound that coincides with classical limits, thereby identifying instrument incompatibility as a source of quantum advantage in communication.
AI.motivation: To establish the operational significance of quantum instrument incompatibility by demonstrating communication tasks that enable semi-device-independent certification of incompatible quantum instruments.
AI.method: The authors introduce a class of three-party communication tasks (sender, relayer, receiver) and derive tight upper bounds on the figure of merit achievable by all compatible instruments. The bound coincides with optimal classical performance under same dimensional constraints.
AI.result: Violation of this bound certifies the incompatibility of the pair of quantum instruments implemented by the relayer. The certification is genuine—it works even when the induced measurements and channels are pairwise compatible. The simplest instances of the communication scenario enabling certification are identified.
AI.conclusion: Certification of incompatible quantum instruments is a manifestation of quantum advantage in communication, and the proposed protocol does not rely on the incompatibility of the induced measurements or channels alone.

title: Robust Structure Learning of $k$-local Lindbladians
summary: We present an efficient protocol for learning an unknown $k$-local Lindblad generator on $n$ qubits using only product-state preparations, short-time evolution, and single-qubit Pauli measurements, without prior knowledge of the interaction structure. For fixed $k$ and bounded weighted interaction strength, the protocol estimates all Hamiltonian and dissipative Pauli--GKSL coefficients to entrywise accuracy $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-δ$ using $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_k(\varepsilon^{-2}n^{2k}\log(1/δ))$ samples and polylogarithmically many evolution times. A semidefinite projection converts these estimates into a valid $k$-local Lindblad generator with diamond-norm error at most $\varepsilon$ using $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_k(\varepsilon^{-2}n^{4k}\log(1/δ))$ samples and polynomial-time classical postprocessing. If a suitable set of influential coefficients is supplied and satisfies a stable sparsity condition, the dependence on $n$ can improve from polynomial to logarithmic; in particular, exact supports of bounded intersection degree require only $\widetilde{\mathcal O}_k(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/δ))$ samples, with analogous reductions in system-size dependence for sufficiently decaying long-range interactions. We also provide a robust structure-learning procedure, extend the guarantees to model misspecification, and prove complementary sample-complexity lower bounds. To our knowledge, these are the first efficient learning guarantees for general $k$-local dissipative quantum dynamics under such limited experimental control.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an efficient protocol for learning unknown k-local Lindblad generators on n qubits using product-state preparations, short-time evolution, and single-qubit Pauli measurements, achieving sample complexity that scales polynomially with n for general cases and logarithmically under sparsity conditions.
AI.motivation: To develop the first efficient learning guarantees for general k-local dissipative quantum dynamics under limited experimental control (product states, short-time evolution, single-qubit measurements) without prior knowledge of interaction structure.
AI.method: The protocol estimates all Hamiltonian and dissipative Pauli-GKSL coefficients via product-state preparations, short-time evolution, and single-qubit Pauli measurements. It uses a semidefinite projection to convert estimates into a valid k-local Lindblad generator, and includes robust structure-learning and handling of model misspecification.
AI.result: Achieves entrywise accuracy ε with Õ_k(ε^{-2} n^{2k} log(1/δ)) samples and polylogarithmic evolution times. Semidefinite projection yields diamond-norm error at most ε using Õ_k(ε^{-2} n^{4k} log(1/δ)) samples. Under sparsity conditions, sample complexity reduces to Õ_k(ε^{-2} log(n/δ)).
AI.conclusion: These are the first efficient learning guarantees for general k-local dissipative quantum dynamics under such limited experimental control, with complementary sample-complexity lower bounds proving optimality.
